The English version reached readers through a translator who warns of the task's difficulty. Tagore's manner and matter, the translator says, combine in a way no second language easily carries. The effort was ventured anyway, from admiration for the original.

Tagore recalls a sheltered childhood in a great Calcutta house, servants, lessons, and early verses. He writes of his father's travels, his first songs, and the slow birth of a poet. The book is gentle, musical, and self-knowing. It remains the pleasantest door into Tagore's world for English readers.
22226-the-whispering-spheres:
The Whispering Spheres appeared in Comet magazine in July 1941, in that short-lived pulps attempt at wonder. An alien life form advances on Earth in the tale's opening picture, something like an inner eye glowing for a moment. In a factory town the whistle stays silent when it should blow. Three short blasts meant fire; one long blast, a breakdown; five toots, a layoff — but now nothing sounds.

The spheres whisper, and men must learn what the sound means before worse follows. The story works the classic pulp vein of first contact and strange invasion. Comet lasted only five issues, and tales like this one are nearly all that remains of it.
22278-a-master-of-mysteries:
L. T. Meade and Robert Eustace wrote A Master of Mysteries together, joining girls' fiction's queen to a master of scientific crime. Meade opens with a visitor laughing at his friend's special hobby. Yesterday, he admits, it struck him that those strange experiences might help him in a difficulty. The master of mysteries is that friend: a man whose trade is solving what looks supernatural.

Case by case, the tales explain hauntings, curses, and impossible crimes by science and patience. Eustace, a doctor, supplied the technical tricks; Meade supplied the storytelling. Their partnership fed the magazines with a new kind of detective tale. This set is an early, enjoyable sample of the scientific mystery story.
22290-me-and-nobbles:
Amy Le Feuvre wrote 'Me and Nobbles' as a story for children about a small narrator and her dog. The book opens inside a grand, gloomy house. The drawing room is awe-inspiring, its blinds nearly always down, with a musty, unused scent that says its grandeur is not for daily use. The library is gloomier still, with stained glass and dingy books lining the walls.

Through that gloom the child and Nobbles make their own cheerful world. Le Feuvre, whose Teddy's Button sold by the million, wrote faith and feeling in a child's own voice. This slighter tale shows her domestic vein: a dog, a lonely child, and a house learning to be a home.
22315-slain-by-the-doones:
R. D. Blackmore, famed for Lorna Doone, also wrote Slain by the Doones. The tales return to the wild West Country world of the Doone outlaws. One passage recalls a hard fanatic known as the Brewer.

The narrator's father, disgusted with England and banished from her, lost all his property. He took service on the Continent in exile. There he wandered for many years, until the throne was restored. Such backstory gives these short tales their sweep of loss and loyalty. Blackmore mixes family ruin, old violence, and moorland scenery into compact stories for readers who wanted more of the Doones.
22320-oldtown-fireside-stories:
Harriet Beecher Stowe wrote Oldtown Fireside Stories from the tales of old New England. The setting is a hearth, with crickets filling each pause. Aged tellers pass their memories down to the young by firelight.

The stories cover early life, war, and adventure in the forest. They tell of Native captivities and escapes, and of bears and panthers. Rattlesnakes appear, along with witches, wizards, and strange dreams. Appearances and providences round out the stock of tales. Stowe, famous for a very different book, here preserves village storytelling. Readers hear how old communities kept their past alive through winter nights.
22338-the-impossibles:
The Impossibles is a science fiction story preserved from Project Gutenberg. Its hero, Malone, is caught lying curled up and daydreaming. He drifts toward a wonderful dream and hates to interrupt it.

In that dream stands a girl more wonderful than anything he had imagined. She has big blue eyes and long blonde hair. Her figure, Malone thinks, shames the average pin-up girl. Such a start mixes fantasy with a wry, male daydream voice. The title hints that impossible things drive the plot. Readers get a light period tale where longing and the impossible meet, told with a wink.
22357-danger-and-other-stories:
Danger and Other Stories gathers short fiction preserved from Project Gutenberg. Its title story opens with a summons to a royal Presence. Horli has been called in, and the narrator goes with him.

Horli knew the narrator had clear ideas on England's weak points. He also had schemes for taking advantage of those points. Only four men sat at that meeting. They were the King, the Foreign Secretary, Admiral Horli, and the narrator. Such a start promises invasion plans and high stakes. The other stories share the volume's taste for risk. Readers get compact tales built around danger at sea and court.
22475-tortoises:
D. H. Lawrence wrote Tortoises, a small book of poems on the tortoise. Lawrence watched these creatures closely during his years in Italy. The opening poem addresses a baby tortoise in tender terms.

Voiceless little bird, he calls the resting creature fondly. Its head rests half out of its wimple in slow dignity. Alone, with no sense of being alone, it pauses eternally. Hence, he writes, it is six times more solitary. It pitches its little round house through immemorial ages. Such lines turn a small animal into a figure of endurance. Readers get Lawrence's intense, wondering nature poetry at close range.
22519-christmas-every-day-and-other-stor:
Christmas Every Day and Other Stories, dated 1892, opens with a father's tale. A papa rouses himself from his writing with great effort. His little girl wants a story before anything else will do.

Well then, he says, he will tell about a certain girl. She was the little girl who wanted Christmas every day. How would you like that, he asks his daughter slyly. The wish granted becomes the tale's comic and moral engine. Too much of a good thing teaches its own sharp lesson. The other stories share that playful, instructive spirit. William Dean Howells wrote the title tale. It remains a holiday favorite about gifts, greed, and enough.
22522-artists-wives:
Alphonse Daudet wrote Artists' Wives, a set of stories about creative men's marriages. Daudet knew Parisian art and literary life from inside its circles. One husband's outburst shows the book's dramatic, teasing tone.

You dare say that, he cries, and the lamp stays lit! The walls, he marvels, do not fall on your head. For two hours, he protests, she has shown him enviable happiness. It is the very happiness she forbids him to enjoy himself. Such scenes probe what artists demand of their wives. Sacrifice, patience, and rivalry run through these marriages. Daudet treats them with wit and a touch of cruelty. Readers get Paris studio life in sharp little portraits.
22559-the-day-of-the-boomer-dukes:
The Day of the Boomer Dukes is a time-travel story with a bored hero. Its narrator peers back and back through the centuries seeking interest. He finds no time better than his own to live in.

Back he peered as far as the Numbered Years themselves. The twenty-eighth century was boredom unendurable to his searching eye. The twenty-sixth was a morass of dullness without relief. Twenty-fifth and twenty-fourth centuries offered the same tedium everywhere. Wherever he looked, the narrator complains, tedium was the finding. That comic despair drives his hunt through future history for excitement. Frederik Pohl wrote the tale. Readers get future ages reviewed by their toughest critic.
22608-a-book-for-all-readers-an-aid-to-t:
A Book for All Readers is a practical guide to forming, using, and preserving libraries, public and private. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Written when public libraries were spreading across America, it taught new librarians and home collectors how to choose, arrange, and care for books.

The author calms the fear that books multiply beyond all use. Truly important books, the text reflects, form only a small share of the mass; most books repeat what has already been written, many times over. Originality is the rarest of literary qualities. Around that sober thought, the manual builds advice on selection and upkeep. It is a handbook from the heroic age of library building.
22660-king-candaules:
King Candaules is a tale by Théophile Gautier, the French master of lush, pictorial prose, set in the ancient kingdom of Lydia. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Its subject is the old story told by Herodotus: a king so proud of his wife's beauty that he shows her, unseen, to a favored courtier, with ruin to follow.

The sample paints the royal wedding day in Gautier's richest manner. The road for the procession lies strewn with fine yellow sand, while brazen tripods send up smoke of cinnamon and spikenard, the only clouds allowed in the pure azure sky. Such splendor is the trap's bait. Readers who love gorgeous surfaces with a cold fate beneath them will find Gautier in full flower.
22673-plantation-sketches:
Plantation Sketches is a set of reminiscences of the Old South, written as that world faded from living memory. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Its opening sets the tone: as the New South rises with all its changes and improvements, hearts that still cling to the old order look sadly backward.

The Old South, the writer sighs, fades into dimness. Soon it will survive only in the memory of the few who knew it. Sketches of plantation life, its people, and its customs follow from that elegiac start. Such books were written in great numbers after the Civil War, and they must be read with care, since nostalgia softens what slavery made brutal. As a record of how the region chose to remember itself, the volume is revealing.
22682-secret-armies:
Secret Armies is John L. Spivak's exposé of fascist and propaganda networks inside the United States, published on the eve of the Second World War. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Spivak, a muckraking reporter, devoted his pen for years to uncovering evidence of fascist activity in America.

The book's framing credits his reporting with setting off several official investigations into un-American, foreign-run propaganda. Secret Armies is presented as the climax of those exposures. Its pages name agents, front groups, and money trails as Spivak traced them. The book belongs to the alarmed literature of the late 1930s, when Americans first reckoned with organized extremist movements at home. It remains a document of that awakening.
22683-practical-pointers-for-patentees:
Practical Pointers for Patentees is a 1901 guidebook for inventors who hoped to profit from their ideas. The catalog record names no author. America's patent system promised that a good invention could make its maker's fortune. A small industry of guides arose in answer. They explained the path from workshop to patent office to market.

The opening insists there can be no doubt that demand for inventions of merit, ready to sell at a fair profit, is real. Never, the writer claims, was the demand for worthwhile inventions so great as at the present time. Around that promise the book builds cautions and steps: searching prior patents, drafting claims, and avoiding sharp dealers. It is a period handbook from the golden age of the lone inventor.
22782-the-buddha-a-drama-in-five-acts-an:
The Buddha is a drama in five acts and four interludes, telling the life of Siddhartha Gautama in verse for the stage. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Western writers of the era, stirred by translations of Buddhist texts, repeatedly tried the Buddha's story in poetry and drama.

The opening scene is set with a painter's care: a tropical garden in Kapilavastu, mountains behind, and in the distance, the Himalayas lift their snow-capped peaks. A marble bench stands among bushes. Behind it rises the Raja's palace entrance. At the left stands a fortified gate with its guard house. All is built in antique Indian style. From that luxury the prince's great renunciation proceeds. The play offers the Buddha's life as pageant and meditation.
22818-an-alphabet-of-celebrities:
Oliver Herford wrote and pictured An Alphabet of Celebrities, printed in Boston in November 1899. Bertram Grosvenor Goodhue designed the border and initial letters, and E. Bird handled the end papers and cover. The result is a small, handsome gift book built around the alphabet itself.

Letter by letter, famous names of the day get brief, witty treatment in verse and drawing. Herford was known for light satire, and the fun here lies in seeing which celebrity he pairs with each letter and what joke he makes of them. The book doubles as a snapshot of who counted as famous in 1899. Many of its stars have faded, and that fading is half the charm now.
22829-no-animal-food-and-nutrition-and-d:
Meat is the enemy in No Animal Food, a health manual pairing arguments on nutrition and diet with vegetable recipes. Its authorities speak bluntly. One quoted physician warns against cheating. Add butter, cream, cheese, eggs, or lard to vegetables, he says, and the meal stops being vegetarian. It becomes mixed fare, with effects much like meat.

Readers get both doctrine and dinner. The early pages press the case that humans thrive without animal food, drawing on doctors and reform journals. The later pages turn practical, with recipes meant to prove the diet workable at an ordinary table. The book captures the vegetarian movement of its day at full confidence. Modern readers can test its claims, and its menus, for themselves.
22885-hindu-gods-and-heroes:
East meets West by design in Hindu Gods and Heroes, part of a series meant to build goodwill and understanding between the two. The editors state their aim plainly in the front matter. Their small books would serve as ambassadors, following, in their own sphere, the highest example in the land.

Inside, the gods and heroes of India take the stage in retelling and explanation. English readers of the period often knew Hindu religion only through mission reports and rumor. A sympathetic survey, written to be read by general readers, filled a real gap. The volume keeps a respectful, introductory tone throughout. It remains useful as both a primer on its subject and a record of early cross-cultural publishing.
22886-cinderella-in-the-south-twenty-fiv:
A barroom question opens Cinderella in the South, Arthur Shearly Cripps's set of twenty-five South African tales. What's the good of him, the bar-tender asks, of a man who might explain how the Ruins came to be. A man who could explain the great ruins, he reckons, might earn a handsome monthly cheque for the knowledge alone.

Cripps lived in Southern Africa as a missionary priest, and his tales grow from that ground. Settlers, Africans, ruins, and veld talk fill the pages, with the great stone ruins of the region haunting several stories. His sympathy often ran against settler opinion of his day. The tales preserve a voice both inside and uneasy within colonial Africa, which gives them interest beyond their plots.
22891-simple-simon-silhouette-series:
Simple Simon meets the pieman in this little silhouette picture book for children. The hosted text presents the old nursery rhyme in the Silhouette Series format, where black paper-cut style figures act out the verses against the page. Simon's simple questions and the pieman's plain answers carry the whole joke.

Silhouette books were a cheap, cheerful staple of the nursery shelf. Their stark black shapes let even very young readers follow the story in pictures alone. Simon, the famous fool of rhyme, asks to taste the wares first and pay later, which never ends well for him. The charm lies in economy. A few lines, a few shapes, and a rhyme children have repeated for centuries.
22893-pygmalion-s-spectacles:
A philosopher argues about sight itself in Pygmalion's Spectacles. Sensations are mental phenomena, he insists. They exist in our minds. How, then, do we know the objects themselves do not exist only there too? That wall is never truly seen, he tells his listener. What reaches us is a visual sensation, and the mind supplies the rest.

Out of that argument grows one of early science fiction's most retold inventions, spectacles that make imagined scenes feel real. The story, first printed in the 1930s, plays with virtual experience long before the term existed. Its talk stays lively because the stakes stay personal. Readers who enjoy ideas dressed as conversation will find a small classic of the form.
22939-the-gypsies:
Charles G. Leland reports a discovery in The Gypsies, published in 1882. The Romanies of the East, he claims, speak a language much like the Gypsy speech of England, in vocabulary and in the slang of the roads. He learned this, he says, from a Hindu man who had himself been a Gypsy in his native land.

Leland traveled, listened, and wrote down lore, tales, and spells as insiders shared them. His book ranges across countries, always chasing the thread of Romany language and custom. Modern scholars treat parts of it cautiously, since Leland loved a good story. Yet few Victorian writers took Gypsy life so seriously. The book remains a rich, flawed, firsthand record of its subject.
22998-janet-of-the-dunes:

gildas-on-the-ruin-of-britain-giles:
Gildas, a British monk of the sixth century, wrote On the Ruin of Britain as a sermon of blame against his own kings and priests. J. A. Giles translated the Latin for the modern reader. The work is the only connected narrative source for Britain after the Romans left. Everything else for those years is scraps and saints' tales.

Gildas tells of Roman rule, the coming of the Saxons as hired swords, their revolt, and the wars of Ambrosius and the siege of Badon. Then he turns on the five kings of his day and scourges their sins. His Latin is hot, tangled, and full of scripture. Later ages mined him for Arthur's age, though he never names Arthur.
glasses: Henry James's 1896 story about a beautiful woman whose charm depends on no one knowing she is nearly blind. The narrator's fascination and the lady's secret build to a quietly devastating revelation. A small masterpiece about seeing and not seeing.
govdocs-archive_org-PaulFosterCaseGreatS:
Paul Foster Case, an American occultist and founder of the Builders of the Adytum, wrote The Great Seal of the United States. His subject is the history, symbolism, and message of the national emblem. Case read public symbols as carriers of hidden teaching. The Great Seal, with its pyramid and eye, drew him strongly.

He traces the seal's making in the 1780s and reads its parts: the eagle, the shield, the unfinished pyramid, and the Latin mottos Annuit Coeptis and Novus Ordo Seclorum. For Case the seal announces a new age for mankind. The book decodes the nation's emblem for readers of his school, in the archive's collection.
govdocs-archive_org-SpanishUFOFiles_Span:
Spain investigated unidentified flying objects through official channels for decades, and its files on those cases were later released to the public. The Spanish UFO Files gather that material: reports and investigations kept in the government's own records.

The papers cover sightings brought to official attention and the inquiries that followed, recorded in the dry language of state paperwork. Read together, they show how a modern government handled reports it could not easily explain. For UFO researchers, official releases like these matter because they rest on documents rather than retellings, and claims can be checked against the record.
govdocs-archive_org-TheFBIAndCISPES_The_:
In July 1989 the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence issued its report on the FBI's investigation of CISPES, the Committee in Solidarity with the People of El Salvador. The inquiry, from the 101st Congress, reviewed how the Bureau had treated an American group opposed to United States policy in Central America.

The report sets out what the FBI did, on whose authority, and where the committee found fault with the investigation. It became part of the wider record of 1980s fights over domestic surveillance of political groups. Readers get Congress's own oversight findings, drawn from the Bureau's files and testimony.
govdocs-archive_org-Volume3Part2HowHelpC:
Cisco Wheeler, who presented herself as a survivor of Illuminati mind control, wrote Deeper Insights into the Illuminati Formula as a companion to the conspiracy literature around that book. Part 2, How Help Comes About, turns from the alleged system itself to escape from it.

Wheeler writes about how help supposedly reaches people caught in the programming she describes, drawing on her own claimed experience. The volume assumes readers know the earlier Illuminati Formula books and their framework of handlers, alters, and secret networks. It is held as an archive holding, without endorsement, as part of the 1990s mind-control literature.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-BankRobberies_B:
The FBI's King assassination file, MURKIN, generated teletypes long after the shooting, as agents ran down leads to build and close the case. This teletype, dated November 14, 1968, reports a registration-records check at a motel in Indiana, under file 44-38861.

Agents were looking for any record of James Earl Ray or his associates at the motel, and the check found none. Negative results fill much of the MURKIN file, because proving where Ray had not been mattered to a case built on his movements. The single teletype is preserved as issued, one page of the Bureau's legwork.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-BurkeJW_Burke_J:
On June 8, 1977, an angry citizen wrote to J. W. Burke Jr. about the House Select Committee on Assassinations, then in the first year of its reinvestigation of the Kennedy and King murders. The author's name is garbled in the scan, but the temper survived intact.

The letter denounces the committee as dishonest and irresponsible, a charge the HSCA heard from both directions: some thought it a whitewash, others a witch hunt. Citizen mail in the files shows the second investigation never enjoyed the public's full trust. The single letter is preserved as written, heat and all, for researchers of the committee's reception.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-DomesticIntelli:
A news article reports a demand from Maryland Governor Marvin Mandel. Mandel ordered Baltimore Police Commissioner Donald Pomerleau to deliver a full report on his department's secret intelligence and surveillance activities. The governor wanted the covert work of the city police brought into the open.

The demand put a police commissioner under public pressure from his own governor. Domestic intelligence units in American cities operated with little oversight in this period, and Baltimore's was no exception. The article records the moment that secrecy was challenged from the top of state government.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FoxJames_Fox_Ja: A personal letter dated August 6, 1991 was written to a man named David. The writer enclosed a copy of another letter and mentioned Sciambra, a member of Jim Garrison's staff, and the judge in the Shaw case. The author's name cannot be recovered from the text, so the letter survives as an unsigned note among researchers still trading Shaw case material in 1991.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-GochenauerJames: nsia-GochenauerJames Gochenauer James: the made public government document, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, kept as issued. An obscure item, complete, filed. From the archive shelves, for readers of the files and readers.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-JohnsonHaynes_J:
Haynes Johnson reported from New Orleans for the Washington Star in 1967 on two vacant offices on Lafayette Square. One had been used by Cuban exiles. The other was the headquarters of Guy Banister Associates, the detective agency of a former FBI man. Johnson explains their place in the Kennedy assassination story.

An address can carry a case. The square put exile politics and Banister's office within steps of each other, and Oswald's New Orleans summer ran through that ground. Johnson's article walks readers through the geography while the Garrison investigation made it famous.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-KirkwoodJames_K: James Kirkwood's interview with Clay Shaw survives in this file, under the heading 'Surviving.' Shaw was the New Orleans businessman whom District Attorney Jim Garrison put on trial in 1969 over the Kennedy assassination. He was acquitted. Beyond the title and Kirkwood's name, the file gives little detail about when the interview was made or what Shaw said in it.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-LeavelleJames_L: Canada's Maclean's magazine devoted its November 22, 1993 issue to the Kennedy assassination, thirty years after Dallas. The special issue appeared under the line 'JFK — 30 Years Later.' Anniversary issues like this one gathered essays, photographs, and argument about the case for a general audience. The file preserves the issue as a record of how the anniversary was marked in print, though the evidence here does not list its individual articles.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Queries_Queries: A letter filed under the heading 'Queries' concerns geese donated to Peace Corps projects. The project was nicknamed 'Geese for Peace.' The letter discusses the publicity the donations generated. Geese went abroad as breeding stock and as symbols, and the press noticed. The file gives the project, the nickname, and the letter's concern with coverage. It does not name the writer, so the letter stands as one page of that project's correspondence.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Sources_Sources: Days after President Kennedy was shot in November 1963, FBI staff in Dallas faced a legal problem. Their report, filed as DL 89-43 and linked to Anton Pavrlka Jr., records the search for a federal statute that actually covered an assassination. At the time, killing a president was not clearly a federal crime. The report shows investigators working through the law books while the case was already underway.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Turtles_Turtles: nsia-Turtles Turtles: the declassified government document, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, preserved as released. An obscure item, complete, filed. From the archive's collection, for researchers of the files and readers.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Witnesses_Witne: Howard Leslie Brennan was the witness who said he saw a rifleman in the Texas School Book Depository window. A study examines his Warren Commission testimony, given in March 1964. Brennan's account helped the commission place a shooter in that building. Because so much rested on his words, researchers have tested them for decades. The study works through what he said and how well it holds up.
govdocs-archive_org-the-odessa-signal-si: The Odessa Signal SIGMA 6 UMBRA: the declassified government document, subject: government records, a single volume, dated material, filed, an obscure item, complete. From the archive's collection, for researchers of the files and readers, a single volume.
govdocs-archive_org-topdeclassified_Top_:
The CIA wrote the Human Resource Exploitation Training Manual in 1983 to teach its officers the work of interrogation. It covers techniques for questioning prisoners and human sources, set out in the agency's own calm, procedural language.

Once secret, the manual was later declassified and became one of the most notorious training texts of the Cold War. Human rights groups cite it in debates over coercive questioning, because later detention programs echoed its methods and its euphemisms. The library presents the full text as an archive holding. Readers can study exactly what the agency taught its people, rather than rely on summaries or accusations about it.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_chile_CH: CHILE: The Barnes House - the National Security Archive briefing-book page capture. The archivists capture, complete. A single capture. Dated material. From the archive's collection, for researchers of the records, filed. An obscure item and readers.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_colombia:
Colombia set up a Truth Commission to account for decades of armed conflict, alongside a special court and a unit hunting for the disappeared. A Constitutional Court ruling said all three bodies could see every record they needed. This briefing book reports that the promise ran into a wall.

Despite the ruling, Colombia's armed forces kept key files off limits. The blocked records included military intelligence files tied to serious abuses. Those same agencies were linked to illegal paramilitary groups and drug traffickers. The posting shows how access to paper can decide whether a truth process can do its job.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_cyber-va:
How should a military choose targets for cyber operations? Michael Martelle edited this briefing book, number 683, published in September 2019. It presents a freedom of information release on that question.

The released material discusses considerations inside United States military targeting doctrine as applied to cyberspace. Targeting rules decide what may be hit, what must be avoided, and who approves. Seeing those considerations in an official release helps readers understand how cyber attacks are planned as formal military operations, not improvised hacks. Releases of this kind are uncommon, since targeting doctrine is usually kept classified.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_foia-int:
Gina Haspel ran a CIA black site where detainees were tortured, and cables from that program were later declassified. The evidence for this posting centers on the legal cover the program needed. Top CIA lawyer John Rizzo worked the Justice Department for secret opinions approving the proposed methods.

Those opinions were ultimately repudiated by the Justice Department itself, but only years later. That sequence is the core of the record: lawyers blessed harsh methods in secret, the blessing was withdrawn long after the acts, and the cables survived to be read. The posting ties Haspel's name to the paper trail of the program she oversaw.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_iran_Ira: Iran's 1979 Revolution Revisited: Failures (and a Few Successes) - the National Security Archive briefing-book page capture. The archivists capture, complete. A single capture. Dated entry. From the archive shelves, for readers of the records and readers.
great-catherine-whom-glory-still-adores: Bernard Shaw's Great Catherine: the Russian empress. Whom glory still adores. A Shavian historical trifle. Short and witty, shaw's Russian empress, short and witty, a historical trifle, Shaw, Bernard Shaw, Catherine, empress, Russia, trifle, adores.
grim-tales:
E. Nesbit was famed for bright tales for young readers, such as her books of child quests. In 1893 she showed a far more dark face in this set of horror tales. The change shocked some fans who knew just the gay side of her pen.

The best known tale, 'Man-Size in Marble,' turns on two stone knights in a church who may not stay still. Dread in wed life, in homes, and in love runs through the set as its core theme. The set is the dark twin of her famed books for the young.
half-past-seven-stories: Robert Gordon Anderson's Half-Past Seven Stories are bedtime tales for children, told with gentle fancy and warm humor. His story-hour favorites — of toys, animals, and small wonders — delighted young listeners. Parents will find them perfect for reading aloud. A sweet collection for the nursery shelf.
hans-brinker-or-the-silver-skates: Mary Mapes Dodge's beloved 1865 children's novel set in Holland. Poor Hans and Gretel Brinker dream of winning the great ice-skating race, while their family struggles and a famous surgeon holds the key to their father's cure. Full of Dutch canals, windmills, and winter fun, it taught generations of American children to love Holland.
heckewelder-lenape-dialogues:
Words, Phrases, and Short Dialogues in the Lenape tongue appeared in 1819. Heckewelder gathered the material at Moravian stations on the frontier. Missionaries there had to preach and teach in the people's own language.

Word lists give the core terms of daily Lenape life and speech. Useful phrases cover travel, trade, food, and greetings between strangers. Short talks between speakers show the tongue in real use. The slim book was a working tool, not a work of show. Today it keeps early Lenape speech on record for new students of the tongue. Linguists still value its plain, field-gathered forms and phrases.
hell-fer-sartain-and-other-stories: Murfree's Hell-fer-Sartain (1897) tales Appalachian mountain feuds. Dialect rings. The Tower library holds the full text. It sartained hell. Mountains echoed. Feuds burned. Stories rang. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
hieroglyphic-tales: Hieroglyphic Tales, Horace Walpole's fables. The pictured tales. This book preserves that collection. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact.
hinton-scientific-romances-first-series:
Charles Howard Hinton, a British mathematician, issued his Scientific Romances in essays between 1884 and 1886. Hinton coined the word 'tesseract' for a four-dimensional cube. His tales were the first great push to make the fourth dimension known to general readers.

The essays mix story and study: flat worlds, beings who pass through solid walls, and drills for picturing four dimensions. Hinton thought training the mind to see past three dimensions could free it. His work fed later writers of higher-space fiction, and Abbott's Flatland appeared in the same years.
homespun-tales: Kate Douglas Wiggin's Homespun Tales: New England stories. The beloved author's village tales. Sweet and true. A charming collection, wiggin's New England stories, sweet and true, a charming book, Wiggin, New England, tales, village, true.
hospital-sketches: Louisa May Alcott's Hospital Sketches recalls her brave Civil War nursing. The young author tended wounded Union soldiers in crowded Washington hospitals. Warm humor and deep pathos fill these true and lively sketches. A beloved classic of American literature.
hunt-popular-romances-west-england-1865-:
Robert Hunt, a Cornish man of science, made this first set of the folk tales of the west of England in 1865. He heard most of the tales in Cornwall, from miners, fish wives, and old folk. His aim was to save the lore of old Cornwall before it died out.

The set holds the famed tale of the Mermaid of Zennor, who lured a choir man to the sea. Giants, saints, mine sprites, and strange dreams fill the rest of the Cornish store. Hunt's work is the chief book of the folk lore of the Cornish coast.

Robert Hunt brought out the second set of his Cornish folk tales in 1865, in the Hotten print of that year. It stands as mate to the first set of the same year. Hunt spent years in the lanes and ports of Cornwall to gather his store.

More drolls, as Cornish folk name their sly tales, fill this set with fresh lore. Saints, giants, sea tales, and old rites of the Cornish year all find a place here. With the first set, it forms the full record of old Cornwall as its folk told it.
hunting-sketches: Anthony Trollope's stories and essays about fox hunting, the sport he loved. Drawing on his own years in the saddle, he writes of hunts, horses, and country characters with affectionate humor. For Trollope fans it is a delightful sidelight; for others, a vivid picture of Victorian rural England at play.
in-divers-tones: Sir Charles G. D. Roberts — the father of Canadian poetry — gathers lyrics in divers tones, from nature and love to patriotism. His musical verse helped give the young Dominion a literature of its own. A graceful collection from a major and much-loved voice.
in-midsummer-days-and-other-tales: August Strindberg — the great Swedish dramatist — shows his mastery of the short story in this collection. Tales of midsummer light and shadow explore love, nature, and the mysteries of the human heart. Though best known for his fierce plays, Strindberg's stories reveal a tender, observant artist.
in-the-days-when-the-world-was-wide-and-: Lawson's verses sing Australia's bush and wide horizons. Ballads roam. The Tower library holds the full text. It sang the bush. Swags walked. Horizons widened. Ballads rang. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
in-the-heart-of-the-rockies: In the Heart of the Rockies, G, a, henty's western tale, the mountain adventure. This book preserves that novel. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. It awaits future readers. The paper lived through the years and remains here.
indian-fairy-tales: Joseph Jacobs gathers the fairy tales of India — clever jackals, brave princes, and magical transformations — retold with charm. His collection opened the riches of Indian folklore to English children. Stories as bright as jewels. Tigers, princes, and clever maidens dance through these sparkling Eastern stories.
irish-fairy-tales: James Stephens's 1920 Irish Fairy Tales: Finn, the Fianna, and Ireland's wonder. Retold with wit and poetry, they enchant all ages. The great Irish storybook. Finn and the Fianna live again, ireland's wonder tales, Ireland's wonder tales retold.
joan-of-naples-celebrated-crimes:
Joan of Naples is Alexandre Dumas's account of Queen Joan of Naples, covering the years 1343 to 1382. It forms one piece of his Celebrated Crimes set, here in eight chapters. The story opens on the night of January 15, 1343. Bells from three hundred churches wake sleeping Naples to pray for a passing soul.

The dying man is the king, and dread has gripped Castel Nuovo for days. Crown officers meet twice daily, and courtiers leave the royal rooms bowed with grief. Dumas builds the scene like a novel, with a whole city listening in the dark. From this deathbed, the tale moves into Joan's reign of splendor, love, and crime in medieval Naples.
joe-tilden-s-recipes-for-epicures:
Joe Tilden's Recipes for Epicures is a cookbook printed at San Francisco in 1907. Major Joseph Tilden was famed on the Pacific Coast as a Bohemian and a fine cook, an epicurean. After his death, friends hunted for the recipes behind his famous dinners. One close companion, among the few who held them, gave this full set for publication.

The book opens with soups and chowders. Onion soup stews four white onions slowly in butter, then adds stock, milk, and egg yolks beaten with Parmesan. Palestine soup uses Jerusalem artichokes, rubbed through a colander and finished with flour, butter, and milk. The recipes are short, rich, and written for cooks who already know their kitchen.
joe-wilson-and-his-mates:
Joe Wilson and His Mates is a set of stories by Henry Lawson, Australia's bush writer. The sample opens with a glossary of Australian and older terms for far-off readers. It explains words like jackaroo, a newcomer learning station work, and Anniversary Day, now Australia Day. Even slang for pubs, possums, and visiting cards gets a careful note.

That care shows how foreign Lawson's world once seemed to outsiders. His Joe Wilson is a working man of the outback, moving through drought, loneliness, and mateship. Lawson's tales are spare and dry-humored, built on the code of mates helping mates. This glossary stands at the front like a guide, preparing readers for the plain speech of the bush stories.
john-bull-on-the-guadalquivir-from-tales:
John Bull on the Guadalquivir is a story by Anthony Trollope, taken from his Tales from All Countries in the 1864 edition. The narrator is John Pomfret, an Englishman whose family traded with Spain for years. His father's firm had works at Seville, and one partner always lived there. The Daguilars, the firm's Spanish partners, became family to the Pomfrets.

Maria Daguilar visited the Pomfret house at seventeen, and John soon decided to go after her. Their match met no resistance; both families plainly wanted the alliance. Yet John felt something lacking, the flower of romance that a little opposition adds. Maria herself had a quiet decision of character unlike English girls he knew. Trollope turns an Anglo-Spanish marriage into gentle comedy about national habits.
john-ingerfield-and-other-stories:
John Ingerfield, and Other Stories gathers five tales by Jerome K. Jerome. The contents list the title story, The Woman of the Saeter, and Silhouettes. Variety Patter and The Lease of the Cross Keys complete the set. In a note to the gentle reader, Jerome warns that three of the tales are not meant to be amusing.

He tells of a critic who praised one solemn tale as not as funny as his other things. So he asks readers to judge the serious stories by another measure than humor. The title story, a tale of old London, remembers John Ingerfield and Anne, his wife. Jerome, famous for laughter, here shows his grave and tender side on purpose.
joinville-memoirs-st-louis-johnes:
Jean de Joinville, a French knight, finished his Memoirs of Louis IX in 1309, nearly sixty years after the events. Thomas Johnes's English translation is the text here, from Bohn's Chronicles of the Crusades. Joinville sailed with King Louis on the Seventh Crusade and knew him as a friend.

The memoir mixes the king's holy sayings and just deeds with Joinville's own adventures in Egypt: battles on the Nile, captivity after Mansourah, and ransom talks. Louis appears praying, judging under an oak, and washing the feet of the poor. The book is the most intimate life of any medieval king. Its appendix adds knight lists and a Saracen account of the crusade.
jorrocks-jaunts-and-jollities:
Jorrocks' Jaunts and Jollities is Robert Smith Surtees's comic book about a London sportsman. Thirteen chapters follow Mr. Jorrocks through the Surrey hunt, shooting, and the turf at Newmarket. Other jaunts take him to Cheltenham, Margate, Paris, and a ride to Brighton. A dinner party and the day after the feast close the set.

The opening chapter asks what true-bred city sportsman has not put off urgent business for the Surrey foxhounds. Surtees writes as the bard of Eastcheap, cheering the hardy exploits of his fellow Londoners. Jorrocks, a cockney grocer with a passion for sport, became one of English fiction's great comic figures. The book's slang, pace, and hunting lore made it a sporting classic.
karl-ludwig-sand-celebrated-crimes:
Karl-Ludwig Sand is Alexandre Dumas's account of the German student who murdered the writer Kotzebue in 1819. It belongs to Dumas's Celebrated Crimes set, in the 1910 edition. The tale opens on March 22, 1819, about nine in the morning. Sand, twenty-three or twenty-four, pauses on the road between Kaiserthal and Mannheim, within sight of his goal.

Dumas paints him closely: smallpox-marked face, gentle eyes, long black hair over a broad forehead. Sand lifts his cap to feel the fresh air from the Neckar valley. He notes in his little book that he left Wanheim at five that morning. Then, lips moving as if in prayer, he walks on firmly toward Mannheim. Dumas builds dread by calm, step by step.
katherine-s-sheaves:
Katherine's Sheaves is a novel by Mrs. George Sheldon, copyrighted by the author in her later name, Mrs. George Sheldon Downs. She dedicates it to her teacher, F.S.K., placing the book wholly in his keeping. Marginal references to Mary Baker Eddy's Science and Health run through the text. The story is set at Hilton Seminary, and opens in Katherine's room there.

Hilton matters at once: Katherine talks with her roommate, and Dorothy Gordon's strength of character wins early praise. Dr. Phillip Harris Stanley stands central in the cast named by chapter titles. A chapter called Katherine Makes a Demonstration signals the book's Christian Science teaching. Mrs. Seabrook's problem and the Hilton Volunteers carry the later action. Sheldon's novels often mixed romance with moral instruction, and this one teaches openly.
keckley-behind-the-scenes:
Elizabeth Keckley published Behind the Scenes in 1868, with a subtitle that sums her life: thirty years a slave, four years in the White House. Keckley bought her freedom with her needle, then became Mary Todd Lincoln's dressmaker. She was also the First Lady's closest confidante.

She tells of slavery in Virginia and North Carolina, her son's death in Union uniform, and the Lincoln household at war. Lincoln's assassination and his widow's grief fill the closing chapters. The book caused a scandal for its private details. Today it is prized as a rare insider view of the Civil War White House.
king-john-of-jingalo-the-story-of-a-mona:
King John of Jingalo: The Story of a Monarch in Difficulties is Laurence Housman's satirical novel, published by Henry Holt in 1912. Sixteen chapters follow a king whose crown sits uneasily. Early titles include A Domestic Interior, Popular Monarchy, and Church and State. A Royal Commission and a game of heads or tails come next.

Later chapters name a deed without a name, a new bishop, and Maximilian. Housman, known for fairy tales and plays, here mocks modern monarchy gently. His king of the imaginary Jingalo faces parliaments, bishops, and newspapers like any real ruler. The satire stays playful: a fairy-tale kingdom used to tease the politics of Housman's own England.
king-of-the-khyber-rifles:
King of the Khyber Rifles is Talbot Mundy's romance of adventure on India's northwest frontier, in its 1916 Imperial edition. Captain Athelstan King, the hero, serves among the hill tribes of the Khyber country. The sample opens deep in the book, at chapter nine, inside a tunnel action. A verse headpiece tells of Abdul standing guard at a gate.

Rifle-fire sweeps the tunnel's floor on both sides, and terrified men huddle in the dark. A mule breaks loose in panic, and the hillman guide tries to master the scene. Mundy drops the reader into frontier fighting at full speed. His King moves through spies, secret missions, and tribal politics in the passes between India and Afghanistan.
king-solomons-mines:
H. Rider Haggard wrote this adventure tale in a rush of work in 1885, to match a bet on the style of Treasure Island. It was his first big hit, and it made his name at a stroke. Allan Quatermain, a dry and tough hunter, tells the tale in his own voice.

Quatermain leads two English men deep in Africa to find the lost mines of King Solomon. Maps, deserts, a lost tribe, and a vast hoard of gems fill the road there and back. The book made the lost world tale a set form for a hundred years of thrills.
kitty-s-class-day-and-other-stories:
Louisa May Alcott, author of Little Women, wrote the short stories gathered here. The book first appeared as Proverb Stories in 1882. Its eight tales include Aunt Kipp, Psyche's Art, and A Country Christmas.

The title story follows Kitty, who longs to attend a class day with her cousin Jack. She worries most about what she should wear. Other stories cover picket duty, a baron's gloves, and what bells saw and said. Each tale opens under a proverb, giving young readers a lesson inside a lively story. Alcott writes for young people without talking down to them. Work, duty, and kindness recur across the varied settings.
knock-knock-knock-and-other-stories:
Ivan Turgenev's short fiction fills this volume, translated from Russian by Constance Garnett. It gathers five pieces: Knock, Knock, Knock, The Inn, and Lieutenant Yergunov's Story. The Dog and The Watch complete the set.

The title story is framed as a tale told among friends. Its narrator recalls his student days in Petersburg in the 1830s. He stayed with his brother, an officer stationed near Krasnoe Selo. Turgenev builds quiet unease from memory, talk, and small events, which suits readers who like subtle, eerie stories. Garnett's translation keeps Turgenev's calm surface and quiet dread. Small gestures and pauses do much of the work in these tales.
korolenko-birds-of-heaven-and-other-stor:
Exiles, wanderers, and ordinary people enduring great hardship fill Birds of Heaven and Other Stories by Vladimir Korolenko, in English. Korolenko wrote as the humane conscience of Russian literature, and Chekhov counted him a favorite among living writers. Siberian roads and steppe villages supply most of the settings in this selection.

His tales observe convicts, pilgrims, and peasants with moral clarity and steady sympathy. No character is too small for his full attention, a quality readers noticed at once. The title story lifts its eyes from hard lives to the birds passing over them. Together the stories show why contemporaries trusted Korolenko's judgment on Russia itself. His kindness on the page was earned in a life of exile and advocacy.
korolenko-makar-s-dream-and-other-storie:
A Siberian peasant dies drunk before Christmas and argues his case in heaven in Korolenko's famous tale Makar's Dream, which heads this English collection. Makar, a poor dreamer cheated by life and by the local powers, pleads before the Great Toyon with peasant cunning. His scales of sins and good deeds produce the story's famous, tender verdict.

Funny, moving, and profound at once, the tale ranks among the great Russian short stories. Other pieces in the volume carry Korolenko's Siberian exile experience into fiction. He knew the taiga settlements he describes from years of banishment there. The collection makes a perfect doorway into his work. Few writers judge their characters so justly and forgive them so much.
la-constantin-celebrated-crimes:
Alexandre Dumas wrote La Constantin as part of his Celebrated Crimes series. This printing comes from the eight-volume set issued in 1910. The tale is set in the year 1660.

Dumas warns readers not to hunt for its people in real records. Marie Leroux, widow of Jacques Constantin, was no great criminal of history. Her accomplice Claude Perregaud was likewise obscure. Dumas builds nine chapters of drama from their small, dark story, in his lively storyteller's manner. Dumas openly prefers a good story to strict record keeping here. That honesty helps readers enjoy the tale on its own terms.
la-le-gende-des-sie-cles:
Victor Hugo's La Légende des Siècles is a vast French poem cycle. This school and university edition was edited by G. F. Bridge. It appeared in the Oxford Higher Series of French works.

The series aimed at upper forms of public schools and private students. Hugo's poems sweep across the ages of human history. They retell legends, Bible stories, and great events in verse. Even in extracts, the cycle shows Hugo's huge range and his faith in human progress. Bridge's edition suits students who read French with help. Notes and selection make Hugo's vast design easier to approach.
la-mere-bauche-from-tales-of-all-countri:
Anthony Trollope wrote La Mère Bauche for his Tales of All Countries. This text comes from the Chapman and Hall edition of 1864. The story is set near the baths of Vernet, in the Pyrenees.

Trollope notes that few English travelers reach that valley. Tour guides, innkeepers, and horse owners there can bewilder visitors. Against that mountain setting he builds a tale around an innkeeper known as La Mère Bauche. It shows his skill at drawing character in a small foreign place. The inn and its keeper give Trollope a tight stage. Manners, money, and family pride drive the small drama there.
laches:
Plato's dialogue Laches takes courage as its subject. Benjamin Jowett translated this edition. His introduction sets the scene: two older men want the best education for their sons.

Lysimachus and Melesias have watched a man fight in heavy armor. They ask two generals, Nicias and Laches, whether such training helps boys. Socrates joins the talk and presses everyone to define courage itself. The answers shift as the men test each claim. Readers meet Plato's method at its clearest: a common word slowly becomes a hard question. The talk never reaches a final, neat answer. That open ending invites readers to keep testing their own ideas of bravery.
lady-john-russell-a-memoir-with-selectio:
Desmond MacCarthy and Agatha Russell edited this memoir of Lady John Russell. It first appeared in a second edition dated 1910. Ten pictures illustrate it, six of them in color.

Selections from Lady John's diaries and letters fill the book. Early chapters cover her youth, Paris, and her father's posting to Berlin. Lord Minto, her father, served as minister there. The record follows a well-placed family through public life. Readers get both a personal portrait and a window on British politics. Family editors shaped the selection with care and loyalty. Public events appear through the lens of home and kinship.
late-lyrics-and-earlier-with-many-other-:
Thomas Hardy published Late Lyrics and Earlier with Macmillan in 1922. An apology, his word for a preface, explains the mix inside. About half the verses were written quite lately, he says.

The rest are older poems held back from past volumes. Hardy had kept them in manuscript for years. He thought earlier books held enough pages for one reading. Distractions of the time also delayed this issue. The collection lets readers compare Hardy's late voice with work from across his long life. Hardy was in his eighties when this volume appeared. Age, memory, and lost love color many of its verses.
laughing-bill-hyde-and-other-stories:
Rex Beach published Laughing Bill Hyde and Other Stories in 1917. Beach had already won fame with The Spoilers and Heart of the Sunset. The title story opens as Bill Hyde leaves Deer Lodge Penitentiary.

Hyde leaves prison a changed man, as theory says he should. His humor toward the law has turned to lasting hatred. His cheeks are pale, his lungs weak, and he coughs often. Beach sets that bitter freedom against tales of the North. Adventure, rough justice, and second chances run through the collection. Beach knew mining camps and the northern frontier firsthand. That knowledge gives his ex-convict hero a hard, believable world.
lawn-tennis-for-ladies:
Dorothea Lambert Chambers wrote Lawn Tennis for Ladies, first published in 1910. She dedicated it to her father, whose keenness helped her career. Twenty-three illustrations show strokes, dress, and famous players.

Early chapters treat athletics for girls and how to practice. Match and tournament play come next, with practical detail. She also covers rackets, courts, dress, and training. Personal memories and great matches close the book. As a Wimbledon champion, Chambers taught women players from hard-won experience. Her own most memorable matches receive a closing chapter section. Fellow leading players add theirs, widening the book's authority.
legends-and-tales:
Bret Harte gathered his Legends and Tales from California's early days. The Legend of Monte del Diablo opens the collection. Other pieces tell of Padre Vincentio and Devil's Point.

A devil and a broker meet in one comic tale. The Ruins of San Francisco and A Night at Wingdam follow. Harte admits that documentary proof for these tales is thin. He tells them anyway, with a storyteller's wink at cautious readers. His California legends mix Spanish missions, gold country, and tall talk. An ogress of silver land adds a stranger folk note. Harte's ease with legend helped invent the literary West.
letters-of-two-brides:
Honoré de Balzac's Letters of Two Brides tells its story through correspondence. A dedication praises a friendship that survived travel and separation. Balzac says that friendship triumphed over the busy malice of the world.

Two young women, friends from a convent school, write to each other. One chooses love and poverty, the other a rich, prudent match. Their letters compare those paths across many years. Joy, loss, and second thoughts fill the exchange. Balzac builds a whole novel from two voices and their changing hearts. The two friends' choices invert by the story's end. Balzac lets each woman judge her own bargain honestly.
library-of-the-world-s-best-mystery-and-:
Julian Hawthorne edited this 1907 gathering of mystery and detective tales. Its subtitle promises one hundred and one tales by famous authors of East and West. The six-volume set sorts stories by national schools, from American to Oriental. Guy de Maupassant leads the contents with seven tales, including The Horla.

Readers meet Voltaire, Balzac, Pliny the Younger, Alarcón, and many others here. Ghosts, crimes, and strange puzzles fill the pages in turn. Hawthorne's plan shows how wide the mystery field had grown by 1907. The collection suits readers who enjoy sampling many masters in short sittings.
lifted-masks-stories:
Susan Glaspell published these thirteen stories in 1912. She dedicates the volume to her friend Jennie Preston's memory. One of Those Impossible Americans opens the collection. The Plea, Freckles M'Grath, and From A to Z follow.

How the Prince Saw America offers a comic immigrant angle. The Last Sixty Minutes and The Anarchist: His Dog close the list. At Twilight ends the volume on a quieter note. Glaspell's fiction, like her plays, watches ordinary people closely. The Man of Flesh and Blood and Out There vary the moods. His America and The Preposterous Motive close the middle tales.
lincoln-s-yarns-and-stories:
Alexander K. McClure gathered the anecdotes that made Lincoln famous. The John C. Winston Company published the collection, profusely illustrated. Its introduction praises Lincoln as statesman, diplomatist, and judge of men. Lincoln, born in a Kentucky log cabin in 1809, had little schooling.

His Emancipation Proclamation freed more than four million slaves, McClure notes. John Wilkes Booth shot him on April 14, 1865. McClure's preface prizes anyone who makes laughs grow. Lincoln's wholesome fun, he argues, served serious purposes too. Without school education, Lincoln rose by merit and will-power alone. McClure ranks him a thorough judge of men and affairs.
literary-lapses:
Stephen Leacock packs this volume with short comic sketches. My Financial Career leads a long, playful contents list. Lord Oxhead's Secret and Boarding-House Geometry follow. The Awful Fate of Melpomenus Jones promises mock tragedy.

How to Make a Million Dollars spoofs the advice genre. Companion pieces promise long life, doctoring, and avoiding marriage. The Force of Statistics and Men Who Have Shaved Me continue the fun. Leacock's humor stays gentle while everyday absurdities pile up. A lesson in fiction and helping the Armenians vary the sketches. Half-hours with Wordsworth, Tennyson, and Longfellow parody the poets.
literary-love-letters-and-other-stories:
Robert Herrick opens this story collection with literary love-letters. A character called Eastlake renews an episode from his past. Carnations lie beyond his page among confused manuscripts. The flowers recall a house on Grant Street and its mistress.

He takes up their message before they shrivel by tomorrow. She entered the Goodriches' hot room triumphantly that afternoon. Roses drooped in plutocratic profusion around the passive guests. Herrick blends letter, memory, and desire into his modern account. Departed delights grow rosy with deceitful hopes, the letter muses. A woman's heart grows heavy with living, Eastlake writes her.
little-annie-s-ramble-from-twice-told-ta:
Nathaniel Hawthorne tells this short tale from Twice Told Tales. A town crier's bell rings at a distant corner. Little Annie listens from her father's doorsteps below. He announces an elephant, lion, royal tiger, and horned horse.

Annie tires of her wide, pleasant, tree-shaded street. She longs for the mystery of the great world beyond. Hawthorne offers his hand and leads her rambling outward. Her blue silk frock flutters as she bounds across the street. Other strange beasts from foreign countries will receive visitors, he cries. Annie's blue silk frock flutters above her white pantalets.
little-saint-elizabeth-and-other-stories:
Frances Hodgson Burnett published these children's stories in 1888. Little Saint Elizabeth leads the small collection. Reginald B. Birch drew the illustrations for it. Elizabeth had not been brought up in America at all, readers learn.

The Story of Prince Fairyfoot follows her tale. The Proud Little Grain of Wheat offers a fable. Behind the White Brick closes the four-story volume. Aunt Clotilde, found sunk at prayer, opens the illustrations' drama. Eh, eh, the illustrations quote Tootsicums in comic confusion. Fairyfoot kneels in love at first sight in one picture.
little-travels-and-roadside-sketches:
William Makepeace Thackeray, writing as Titmarsh, sketches his travels here. The first piece journeys from Richmond in Surrey to Brussels. Ghent and Bruges, visited in 1840, follow. Waterloo closes the little collection of roadside pieces.

Thackeray quits Richmond's Rose Cottage Hotel with deep regret. He prefers it a thousand times to the Star and Garter. Sneering waiters and ten-shilling claret await the bolder traveler there. An omnibus ride opens his sunny, satirical holiday abroad. Veal cutlets and a dear little bowling-green endeared the inn. Splendor at the Star and Garter knocked visitors down, he jokes.
liza-or-a-nest-of-nobles:
Ivan Turgenev's novel appears here in W. R. S. Ralston's translation. Ralston published it in 1873 in the Leisure Hour Series. He dedicates the translation to Turgenev, his friend. His preface calls Turgenev a writer Russia may proudly claim.

Turgenev seizes character's most fleeting expressions, Ralston writes. A few rapid touches fix appearance and scene vividly. Conscientious workmanship earns him respect beyond mere artistry. Liza gives the heroine's name to the Nest of Nobles story. Fathers and Sons and Smoke headline Turgenev's other translations. Virgin Soil and Annals of a Sportsman complete the series list.
lourdes:
Lourdes is a Catholic account of the famous French shrine by Monsignor Robert Hugh Benson. The book was printed in 1914, with full-page pictures. Benson wrote the pages six years before, after going to Lourdes himself. His preface tells of a famed French scientist who studied the shrine's wonders.

That scientist judged that no known science explains what happens there. Benson describes the pilgrims, the baths, the processions, and the claimed cures. He writes as a believer, but he reports with care and detail. The book asks what faith and fact each say about Lourdes. It stands as a thoughtful English guide to the shrine.
love-and-other-stories:
Love, and Other Stories is the thirteenth volume of Chekhov's tales in English. Constance Garnett translated these stories by Anton Chekhov. The title story opens at three in the morning, with a man too happy to sleep. Around it stand more than twenty short tales of Russian life.

The contents include 'Fat and Thin' and 'The Death of a Government Clerk.' Clerks, singers, soldiers, and country folk pass through these pages. Chekhov can make a tiny scene funny, sad, and true at once. Some tales end with a joke; others end with a sting. Together they show his gift for the brief, perfect story.
love-of-life-and-other-stories: Jack London's collection led by the famous title story: a starving prospector in the Arctic crawls toward survival with a wolf stalking him, in one of the grimmest tales ever written. The other stories roam the Yukon, the sea, and the South Seas, all celebrating endurance against merciless nature. Published in 1907, it shows London's raw power at its peak.
love-stories:
Love Stories gathers short fiction by Mary Roberts Rinehart, printed in 1919. The stories first ran in magazines between 1912 and 1917. Seven tales appear here, opening with one called 'Twenty-Two.' Others include 'Jane,' 'In the Pavilion,' and 'God's Fool.'

Rinehart was famous for mysteries, but these are tales of love and people. Nurses, patients, and young lovers move through several of them. 'The Miracle' and 'The Game' close the book on warm notes. Her touch is light, her people kind, her plots neat. Readers who enjoy gentle magazine fiction of the era will like these stories.
loyalties:
Loyalties is a play by John Galsworthy, in his fifth series of plays. The scene is Meldon Court, Charles Winsor's house near Newmarket. Guests include Lady Adela, General Canynge, and the rich newcomer Ferdinand De Levis. Captain Dancy, a retired officer with a fine war record, is also there.

Money is stolen during the house party, and suspicion falls hard. An inspector comes, lawyers are called, and friends close ranks. Each group in the play protects its own kind first. Race, class, regiment, and club all pull against plain justice. Galsworthy turns a theft into a sharp study of group loyalty. The play asks what honesty costs when loyalty speaks louder.
luther-and-the-reformation-the-life-spri:
Luther and the Reformation calls the Reformer's work the life-springs of our liberties. Joseph A. Seiss, a Philadelphia Lutheran pastor, wrote the book. Its first part grew from his memorial oration in New York. He spoke there on November 10, 1883, Luther's four-hundredth birthday.

The second part came from discourses for Pennsylvania's bicentennial. Seiss traces free government and free conscience back to Wittenberg. He presents Luther as the champion of the open Bible and the free mind. The style is that of a learned pulpit oration. The book shows how strongly America honored Luther in 1883. It joins church history with a plea for liberty.
lydia-of-the-pines:
Lydia of the Pines is a novel by Honoré Willsie, later Honoré Morrow. Frederick Stokes published it, and this text follows the 1917 Burt edition. A color frontispiece by Eric Papse once graced the book. Chapters follow Lydia from a toy balloon to cap and gown.

Readers watch her through cooking class, high school, and a military hop. Politics runs beside her growing up: an election and a Republican candidate. An Indian celebration and an investigation deepen the story's stakes. Love of country sounds in one chapter's Latin title. Lydia grows into the youngest scholar of her college class. The novel mixes a girl's coming of age with public wrongs.
madame-de-mauves:
Madame de Mauves is a tale by Henry James, set near Paris. It opens on the terrace at Saint-Germain-en-Laye in mid-spring. Paris spreads below in dusky vastness, girdled by the silver Seine. A young American sits there, wistful for the great city's life.

He has come to meet the spring, yet his eyes stay on Paris. Soon he meets Madame de Mauves, a young American married to a French baron. Her marriage is cold, and her spirit is quietly starved. The young man must weigh love against honor and pity. James handles the tale with delicate, searching care. It is an early jewel of his art of the novella.
madame-de-treymes:
Madame de Treymes is a short novel by Edith Wharton, set in Paris. John Durham waits in a hotel doorway on the Rue de Rivoli. Across the street the Tuileries gardens shine in spring brightness. Durham is an American who loves Fanny de Malrive, a friend from youth.

Fanny is trapped in a marriage to a French marquis. She seeks a divorce so that she and Durham may marry. Her sister-in-law, Madame de Treymes, holds the family's secrets and power. Wharton shows old French pride meeting American plain dealing. The price of freedom proves higher than either lover guessed. It is a brief, perfect tragedy of manners.
made-over-dishes:
Made-Over Dishes is a cookbook by Mrs. S. T. Rorer, in a revised edition. Rorer also wrote the Philadelphia Cook Book and other kitchen manuals. Her preface calls wise economy the first of domestic duties. Poverty, she insists, need not spoil good cooking.

Chapters work through stock, cooked fish, beef, and mutton. Chicken, game, bread, eggs, and potatoes each get their turn. Sauces, salads, cereals, vegetables, and fruits close the list. Leftover scraps become flavorings instead of garbage. Rorer teaches the housekeeper to waste nothing and serve well. The book is a classic of thrifty American home cooking.
main-street-from-the-snow-image-and-othe:
Main Street is a sketch by Nathaniel Hawthorne, from The Snow Image and Other Twice-Told Tales. A showman steps forward and makes his bow to the public. He walks daily along the main street of his native town. Now he offers its whole history as a moving picture show.

His machine, part panorama and part puppet-show, turns with a crank. Ghosts of forefathers pass in scenes from two centuries. Salem's street fills with processions, fires, and famous days. Hawthorne turns local history into a small theater of time. The piece charms with its mix of fact and fancy. It shows his love for the old town that raised him.
makers-of-madness-a-play-in-one-act-and-: Hermann Hagedorn wrote Makers of Madness, a play in one act and three scenes. The Macmillan Company published it in New York in 1914, as the title page shows. Hagedorn is billed there as the author of Faces in the Dawn. The hosted sample stops after the title and copyright pages, so the play's scenes cannot be described from evidence. This note keeps to the title page.
manners-and-monuments-of-prehistoric-peo:
Manners and Monuments of Prehistoric Peoples surveys the Stone Age world. The Marquis de Nadaillac, a French scholar, wrote the book. Nancy Bell translated it, and Putnam issued it in 1894. One hundred thirteen pictures show tools, dwellings, and the fossil man of Mentone.

Author and translator brought the text up to date together. The translator calls it an epitome of all then known. Chapters treat caves, lake dwellings, weapons, art, and burial customs. Nadaillac wrote for general readers, not only for scholars. His book made deep prehistory vivid to Victorian audiences. It remains a learned classic of early archaeology.
manners-and-social-usages:
Manners and Social Usages is an American etiquette book by Mrs. John Sherwood. The author, Mary Elizabeth Wilson Sherwood, revised this enlarged edition herself. A transcriber dates the first copyright to 1884 and this version to 1887. Her frontispiece shows the modern dinner table in full array.

Chapters guide readers through calls, dinners, dances, and weddings in every season. She explains the German, or cotillon, and contrasts European with American ways. Servants, dress, and the single woman past girlhood all get counsel. Her preface notes how many Americans ask what is proper to do. The book answers with confidence and fine detail. It is a window on Gilded Age social life.
many-cargoes:
Many Cargoes is a book of sea tales by W. W. Jacobs, in a second edition of 1894. Some two dozen stories crowd its contents page. Titles promise a captain's exploit, contraband of war, and a black affair. The skipper of the Osprey and the cook of the Gannet appear.

The night-watchman opens the first yarn, about a 'cute skipper of the barque John Elliott. That skipper, he chuckles, should never have sailed without his mother. Jacobs mixes sailors, smugglers, and elaborate elopements with dry delight. Limehouse Reach and mid-Atlantic anchor his wandering crews. His sea stories made him famous before his shore tales did. They are salt water comedy at its best.
mappo-the-merry-monkey-his-many-adventur:
Mappo, the Merry Monkey tells of a monkey's many adventures, by Richard Barnum. Harriet H. Tooker illustrated the book, issued in 1915. It belongs to the Kneetime Animal Stories for children. The frontispiece shows Mappo hurling a coconut shell at a tiger's head.

Chapters follow Mappo from his jungle home into a net and a box. A ship carries him to a new world of wonders. He meets Tum Tum, the jolly elephant, on the way. The circus claims him at last, and he learns tricks there. Barnum also wrote of Squinty the pig and Slicko the squirrel. His animal tales were bedtime favorites for years.
mark-of-the-beast-other-fantastical-tale:
Mark of the Beast and Other Fantastical Tales gathers Rudyard Kipling's eerie stories. This edition, Fantasy Masterworks volume fifty, carries an introduction by Neil Gaiman. Contents include 'The Phantom Rickshaw' and 'The Strange Ride of Morrowbie Jukes.' 'The City of Dreadful Night' evokes a sleepless, haunted Calcutta.

Most tales rise from Kipling's years in British India. Ghosts ride in rickshaws, and curses work in the house of Suddhoo. 'The Bisara of Pooree' and 'The Sending of Dana Da' mix magic with barrack-room humor. 'My Own True Ghost Story' closes the haunting in lighter vein. The title tale is among the most frightening Kipling ever wrote.
mark-twain-s-speeches:
Mark Twain's Speeches gathers the platform pieces of America's favorite humorist. The contents open with a story of a speech and Plymouth Rock. 'The Horrors of the German Language' appears under its German title. 'The Weather' and 'The Babies' stand among his best-known turns.

He speaks on books, authors, hats, poets, and policemen. A dramatized Pudd'nhead Wilson and the Daly Theatre get their say. Dress reform and copyright draw his comic fire. Twain was the most sought after-dinner speaker of his age. His timing lives even on the printed page. These speeches are funny, wise, and endlessly quotable.
marquise-brinvillier-celebrated-crimes:
The Marquise de Brinvilliers opens Alexandre Dumas's tale from Celebrated Crimes. This set of eight volumes was issued in 1910. The scene is Paris, toward the end of 1665. A crowd gathers on the Pont-Neuf around a closed carriage.

Police force the door while sergeants hold the plunging horses. A young captain leaps down, shutting the door too late. Spectators glimpse a veiled woman cowering at the back. So Dumas stages the arrest that shook old Paris. The marquise had poisoned her father and her brothers for gold. Her beauty and her crimes made her a legend of horror. Dumas paints her in glittering, ghastly hues.
marquise-de-ganges-celebrated-crimes:
The Marquise de Ganges, from Dumas's Celebrated Crimes, is dated 1657. A very plain carriage stops one evening in the rue Hautefeuille. A lady muffled in black satin peers out for a sign. Satisfied, she alights with her companion at the dark house.

The young marquise has come in secret to a fortune-teller. What she hears there shadows all her years to come. Beauty and a great fortune make her a prize for schemers. Her husband's own brothers will murder her for her wealth. Dumas calls her story one of innocence destroyed by greed. Few of his crime tales are so pathetic. The 1910 Celebrated Crimes set keeps it in print.
martin-guerre-celebrated-crimes:
Alexandre Dumas told the tale of Martin Guerre for his Celebrated Crimes set. The text here came out in 1910 in that eight volume series. Dumas starts with a long thought on how alike two strangers can look.

He cites false claims and famed frauds, from Perkin Warbeck to the false Demetrius. Then he turns to the French case that gives the piece its name. A man comes home who may not be the man who left, and doubt spreads fast. The wife, the kin, and the court must weigh face, voice, and memory. Few crime tales turn so fully on the proof of a man's name.
mary-stuart-celebrated-crimes:
Alexandre Dumas told the tale of Mary Stuart for Celebrated Crimes. The set of eight volumes came out in this form in 1910. Ten chapters carry the story, under the date 1587.

Dumas opens with a grim thought on fated royal names. In France, he says, the ill starred name is Henry. In Scotland, it is Stuart, and he lists their ends. Kings of that house die by blade, by burst cannon, and on the field at Flodden. James IV falls at Flodden in that dark royal list. The roll of deaths builds the fate that waits for Mary herself.
masques-phases:
Robert Ross published Masques and Phases in London in 1909. Arthur L. Humphreys of Piccadilly printed the book that December. Ross thanks past editors for the leave to reprint his pieces.

Pieces came from the Cornhill, the Westminster Gazette, and college papers. They include A Case at the Museum and How We Lost the Book of Jasher. His note to Harold Child jokes about fear of editors and their blue pencils. Wit and art talk run through the whole set of essays. The Brand of Isis stands among the reprinted pieces too. Ross writes as a critic at ease in print and in art rooms.
massacres-of-the-south-1551-1815-celebra:
Alexandre Dumas wrote Massacres of the South for Celebrated Crimes. The 1910 text spans the years 1551 to 1815. Nine chapters hold a tale of faith wars in the south of France.

Dumas says the south kept its feud like a book of accounts. One side was writ in Catholic blood, the other in Protestant blood. Nimes stands at the core of the tale, he tells readers. The story leaves that town at times, but it always returns to it. Two and a half centuries fit inside his wide frame. Each new clash, he says, grew from an old wound left unhealed.
matisse-picasso-and-gertrude-stein-with-:
Gertrude Stein's Matisse Picasso and Gertrude Stein holds three prose works. The title piece is also known by the short name G.M.P. Two shorter stories stand with it in the one volume.

A Long Gay Book, from 1909 to 1912, comes first in the list. Many Many Women, from 1910, and G.M.P., from 1911 to 1912, follow. The first pages circle round birth, infancy, and the loss of a first whole feeling. Stein's loops of phrase build sense by echo more than by plot. A note warns that odd spellings stand as found in the source. Readers meet Stein's style with no smoothing of its hard edges.
may-day-and-other-pieces:
Ralph Waldo Emerson's May-Day, and Other Pieces came out in an 1867 Routledge edition. Les Bowler prepared the text used here. May-Day leads, and The Adirondacs comes second in the contents.

A set of stray pieces follows, with Brahma, Nemesis, and Fate. Freedom, the Boston Hymn, and an ode sung at Concord in 1857 stand there. Merlin's Song and a group named Nature and Life close the book. The Romany Girl and a poem named Nature sit in that last part. Love and Thought, Una, and Rubies add softer notes between odes. Emerson moves from public song to close, brief lyrics with ease.
may-day-with-the-muses:
Robert Bloomfield published May Day with the Muses in London in 1822. Bloomfield had won fame with The Farmer's Boy and Rural Tales. His preface makes light of its own need to exist at all.

He jokes of a baronet who took rent in butterflies and grubs. That tale, from the Rambler, frames his own cast of village poets. Few spots, he grants, hold so many poets in one small place. The book stages their May Day contest of song for a kind patron. T. Park's lines on Thanet stand in the preface as praise. Bloomfield frames the contest with humor about his own trade.
melchior-s-dream-and-other-tales:
Juliana Horatia Ewing wrote Melchior's Dream and Other Tales. A church press in London and New York issued the book. Ewing gave it to her four brothers and four sisters.

Melchior's Dream leads the set of eight short tales. The Blackbird's Nest and Friedrich's Ballad come next in the list. A Bit of Green and The Yew-Lane Ghosts add nature and fright. A Bad Habit and A Happy Family close the contents page. The Viscount's friend brings a French air to the set. Ewing's tales mix moral turns with ghost lore and garden scenes.
memories:
