Fannie A. Beers wrote Memories, a record of four years of war. J. B. Lippincott printed it in Philadelphia in 1888. She calls it a record of personal experience and adventure.

She gives the book to the boys who wore the gray. Friends among Confederate soldiers urged her for years to write. Some pieces first ran in the Southern Bivouac magazine. She vows to tell the truth, but not always the whole truth, in its pages. She served the defenders of the Cause with a full heart. Duty to posterity, not mere fame, is her stated spur.
memories-and-anecdotes:
Kate Sanborn wrote Memories and Anecdotes, printed by Putnam's in 1915. Sixteen pictures stand in the book, with her greeting at the front. She had written Adopting an Abandoned Farm and books on wall papers.

She gives the book to all her friends, and to her pupils. Smith College and Packer Institute girls stand in that list. Chapter one recalls her early days and odd village characters. Two story tellers of Hanover and famed Dartmouth guests fill its start. Dartmouth men who liked her father gave her a hand up. Gratitude to teachers and kin fills her long gift list.
memories-of-canada-and-scotland-speeches:
The Marquis of Lorne wrote Memories of Canada and Scotland, in speeches and verses. He later held the title of Duke of Argyll in the record. The book is given to the members of the Royal Society of Canada.

Verses on Canadian subjects lead the contents page. Canada, 1882, and Quebec stand first in that list. A Canadian national hymn and river rhymes on Canada follow. Legends of the St. John River and the Mohawk guide add tales in verse. The Qu'Appelle Valley and the Song of the Six Sisters follow. Prairie roses and Cree fairies show the range of his Canadian verse.
men-s-wives:
William Makepeace Thackeray wrote these comic tales of marriage, first told under the pen name G. Fitz-Boodle. The longest, The Ravenswing, follows Miss Crump, a singer who rises toward fame as Morgiana. Around her circle suitors, managers, and her husband Mr. Walker. Two shorter tales complete the volume.

Mr. and Mrs. Frank Berry turns on a fight and its tangled aftermath. Dennis Haggarty's Wife closes the set with another study of wedded folly. Thackeray mocks vanity and money-hunting on all sides, yet treats his fools kindly. The stories show his satiric voice forming before his great novels.
merton-of-the-movies:
Harry Leon Wilson's comic novel follows a young would-be actor toward Hollywood. Its hero dreams of serious dramatic fame on the screen. Chapter titles promise western stuff, outlaws, and shattered illusions. Wilson dedicates the book to fellow humorist George Ade.

The joke is that the hero succeeds in exactly the wrong way. Studios and audiences take his earnest acting as comedy gold. One chapter even bills his triumph as five reels and five hundred laughs. The novel gently mocks both movie-struck dreamers and the young film industry itself. It remains a warm, funny portrait of silent-era moviemaking.
miscellaneous-pieces:
John Bunyan's shorter religious writings fill this volume, taken from an 1845 Nelson edition of Puritan works. The contents list four pieces only. Two treat doctrine: Of the Trinity and a Christian, and Of the Law and a Christian. The others preserve Bunyan's last sermon and his dying sayings.

The Trinity essay counsels a young or shaken Christian under heavy thoughts about God's nature. Bunyan urges the doubter to keep close to the Word of God. His directions are plain, numbered, and practical. These pieces show the Pilgrim's Progress author as pastor and teacher, not only as allegorist.
miscellanies:
Oscar Wilde's Miscellanies appeared in this 1908 edition, shepherded by his friend Robert Ross. Ross's dedication asks a collector friend to blame the editor, not the printers, for any errors. The volume opens with The Tomb of Keats, first printed in the Irish Monthly in 1877. It begins at the pyramid tomb near Rome's Porta San Paolo.

Wilde describes the gaunt pyramid of Caius Cestius, once mistaken for Remus's sepulchre. Near it lies Keats, the real subject of the young Wilde's pilgrimage. These early and occasional pieces show Wilde before the plays and the downfall. Ross gathered them as part of his long labor to restore Wilde's works.
miss-elliot-s-girls-stories-of-beasts-bi:
Mrs. Mary Spring Corning wrote these nature stories for children, copyrighted in 1886. The title page names her as the author, though the catalog record differs. In the first story, Miss Ruth Elliot asks young Sammy Ray a favor. She wants a large green tobacco worm, brought carefully on its leaf.

Ruth, who leans a crutch against her porch chair, studies the worm with her girls. Sammy warns that it spits tobacco juice and shows its tail horn. Each chapter turns a creature into a lesson: worms, birds, and butterflies alike. The book teaches natural history through story, in the Sunday-school publishing tradition.
miss-mink-s-soldier-and-other-stories:
Alice Hegan Rice published this story collection with the Century Company in 1918. Rice was known for Mrs. Wiggs of the Cabbage Patch and Mr. Opp. The title story, Miss Mink's Soldier, heads a table of five tales. The others are A Darling of Misfortune, Pop, Hoodooed, and A Matter of Friendship.

The dedication recalls happy days spent together east of Suez. Some stories carry earlier copyrights, from 1905 onward, gathered here anew. A soldier in the title story places the collection in the First World War years. Rice writes about humble, warm-hearted people, mixing humor with pathos in her familiar Kentucky manner.
miss-prudence-a-story-of-two-girls-lives:
Jennie M. Drinkwater published this story of two girls' lives in 1883. The title page gives her name, though the catalog record garbles the credit. An epigraph from Epictetus sets the theme: we are not to lead events, but to follow them. Chapters begin after school and introduce Marjorie, asleep and awake.

Other chapters bring an evangelist, a wedding day, and a budget of letters. Characters named Linnet, Jeroma, and John Holmes cross the girls' paths. Maple Street closes the table of contents. Drinkwater writes a Christian coming-of-age tale, in which two girls learn faith and patience through ordinary trials.
mogens-and-other-stories:
Jens Peter Jacobsen's stories appear here in Anna Grabow's 1921 translation from the Danish. Jacobsen lived from 1847 to 1885 and published the collection in 1882. Four pieces make up the volume. The title story, Mogens, stands first, followed by The Plague at Bergamo, There Should Have Been Roses, and Mrs. Fonss.

The introduction places Jacobsen in Denmark's stormy literary decade after 1870. Brandes lectured, Ibsen probed, and Darwinism echoed from England. Jacobsen, the introduction says, stood aside from the fighting, content to be an artist. His sensuous, melancholy tales of love and loss made him Denmark's master of the short story.
moments-of-vision-and-miscellaneous-vers:
Thomas Hardy first published this collection of poems in 1917. The Macmillan edition here was reprinted as late as 1929. The title poem, Moments of Vision, stands first in the contents. Poems follow with titles like The Voice of Things and Why Be At Pains?

Other pieces gather at Mellstock for an afternoon service, and pause at a wicket gate. Heredity, a rival, and a first sight of her show Hardy's lifelong subjects. He was in his late seventies when the book appeared, famous as a novelist turned poet. These late verses are spare, wry, and haunted by memory and chance.
monkey-jack-and-other-stories:
Palmer Cox edited this collection of stories for young children. The title tale is told in verse, with words split into syllables for new readers. A little maid cries because her precious ball is stuck in a tree. Every boy shrinks back afraid, until Monkey Jack comes, nimble and plucky, admired by all.

Jack leaps from bough to bough and catches the ball as the branch gives way. He keeps his prize clasped to his breast through the fall. The poem ends with him in bed, his leg broken, no longer Monkey Jack. His comrades bring books and toys, and little Rosa shyly brings her ball.
mont-saint-michel-and-chartres:
Henry Adams wrote this meditation on medieval faith and architecture, first printing it privately. Editor Ralph Adams Cram's note tells how the guarded volume reached the public. The American Institute of Architects arranged an edition for general sale in 1912. Adams himself thought publication unnecessary, and took no part in it.

Cram calls the book a revelation fusing theology, philosophy, art, and romance. Mont-Saint-Michel stands for the age of faith and force; Chartres, for the Virgin's church. Adams reads Gothic building as the outward form of medieval belief. The result became America's most distinguished study of the medieval mind, written as a uncle's guide for his nieces.
moon-face-and-other-stories:
Jack London gathers eight stories in this collection, named for its opening tale. The contents add The Leopard Man's Story, Local Color, and Amateur Night. The Minions of Midas, The Shadow and the Flash, All Gold Canyon, and Planchette complete the set. Moon-Face itself begins with a confession of irrational hatred.

The narrator hates John Claverhouse, a round-faced, ever-laughing optimist, on sight. He admits Claverhouse never did him any wrong society would recognize. The hatred is deeper and subtler, and it maddens him waking and sleeping. London turns that obsession toward murder, in one of his coldest tales of human nature.
more-english-fairy-tales:
Joseph Jacobs collected and edited this second volume of English fairy tales. John D. Batten illustrated it, and Putnam's published it in New York and London. The front matter plays a game with young readers. They must knock, pull the bell, and find a key marked J. J. before walking in.

Jacobs, editor of the journal Folk-Lore, dedicated the book to his son Sydney, aged thirteen. The contents begin with The Pied Piper of Franchville. Hereafterthis and The Golden Ball follow. Jacobs retold tales from English tradition in plain, lively prose, and his collections helped define the English fairy tale for modern children.
more-fables:
George Ade published this second book of his fables in slang in 1900. Clyde J. Newman illustrated it. The contents promise fables of Uncle Brewster, too shifty for the tempter, and of a grass widow and her mesmeree. An honest money-maker and his partner of joys get their own tale.

Other fables treat a corporation director's mislaid ambition and the night men came to the women's club. A Michigan counterfeit who was neither one thing nor the other closes the sample list. Ade tells each story in the era's slang, then lands a moral. His fables made him America's favorite humorist of the new century's opening years.
more-jataka-tales:
Ellen C. Babbitt retold these Buddhist birth stories for children, with illustrations by Ellsworth Young. She dedicates the book to Rudyard Kipling, in the name of all children who troop to his call. Her foreword says the first Jataka Tales, ten years earlier, drew cries for more. Children, she found, could read the stories to themselves.

The Jataka tales tell of the Buddha's former lives, often as animals. Scholars at Cambridge translated them from the ancient texts for the University Press. Babbitt calls them the oldest collection of folklore extant, treasured since the third century BC. Professor Rhys Davids named them a priceless record of the childhood of our race.
more-seeds-of-knowledge-or-another-peep-:
Julia Corner wrote this instructive book for children as a sequel to her Seeds of Useful Knowledge. Charles is now a year older and wiser. He can write well, read long words without spelling them, and work his multiplication sums. Seven elegant coloured engravings embellish the London volume.

New lessons concern Black slaves, a conversation on history, and missionaries. One engraving shows an Inca's surprise at seeing a watch. Corner's method is the family conversation: papa and mamma teach, and Charles asks questions. Such books carried Victorian children through geography, history, and morals at home, in the improving manner of their day.
morning-bells-or-waking-thoughts-for-lit:
Frances Ridley Havergal wrote this devotional book of waking thoughts for little ones. She dedicates it to twin brothers, Willie and Ethelbert, with Aunt Fanny's love. Each numbered reading opens with a short Bible verse. The first is Thy Holy Child Jesus; the second, Even Christ pleased not Himself.

Thirty readings give a month of mornings. Verses promise that the Lord will fight for you, and that He careth for you. Others urge children to bear one another's burdens and be faithful over a few things. Havergal, a hymn writer, shaped each day's thought as a small bell calling children to prayer and kindness.
mother-west-wind-where-stories:
Thornton W. Burgess wrote these animal tales for his Bedtime Story-Books, copyrighted in 1918. Harrison Cady illustrated them. Grosset and Dunlap published the volume by arrangement with Little, Brown. Each chapter answers a where question about a creature of the Green Meadows.

Where did Grandfather Frog get his big mouth? Where did Miser the Trade Rat first set up shop? Other chapters explain Yap-Yap the Prairie Dog's wits and Yellow-Wing's liking for the ground. Little Chief learns to make hay, and Glutton the Wolverine earns his name. Burgess teaches natural history through storytelling, as Mother West Wind carries the tales.
mother-west-wind-why-stories:
Thornton W. Burgess published these why stories with Little, Brown in Boston in 1920. Harrison Cady supplied illustrations in color. The volume belongs to Burgess's Bedtime Story-Books, listed at length in the front matter. That list runs from The Adventures of Reddy Fox through dozens of animal heroes.

Why stories explain how animals got their markings, habits, and homes. Mother West Wind tells them to the creatures of the Green Forest and Green Meadows. Burgess, a conservationist, slipped real nature knowledge into each fable. Generations of children met Peter Cottontail, Jimmy Skunk, and Grandfather Frog through these bedtime chapters.
mr-achilles:
Jennette Lee published this novel in 1912, dedicating it to Gerald Stanley Lee. Its hero is Achilles Alexandrakis, a Greek fruit seller in Chicago. Chapter one finds him arranging oranges into a yellow pyramid on Clark Street. Figs, dates, melons, and grapes take their places under his deft fingers. His helpers' pushcarts have already rolled north and south.

A sigh escapes him as he surveys the sooty street. For a moment he had almost fancied himself back in Athens. Lee contrasts Chicago's grime and meagre sky with the glorious curve over the Parthenon. Her immigrant hero carries Greece in his heart through an American working day.
mr-hawkins-humorous-adventures:
Edgar Franklin's comic novel from 1904 follows a narrator named Griggs and his neighbor Hawkins. Hawkins is rich, kind, and full of wild inventions. Griggs builds a quiet summer home in the Berkshires. He then learns that Hawkins owns the villa next door.

Each chapter puts Hawkins and his latest scheme in Griggs's path. Steam cars, trials, and bright ideas go wrong in funny ways. Griggs tells the tales in a dry, amused voice. He is always pulled in just as trouble starts. The book is light period humor about invention, money, and a neighbor no one can escape.
mr-justice-raffles:
E. W. Hornung published this Raffles novel in 1909, told by Bunny Manders. Raffles is a famed cricketer and a secret burglar. He steals fine jewels from rich hosts who trust him. Bunny, younger and more ideal, aids him and tells the tale.

The book opens after Raffles has vanished from London. He cables Bunny to meet a train from Carlsbad. Raffles steps off thin, ill, and hungry for British beef. From there the pair face debt, blackmail, and the law. Hornung turns the detective pattern around, so readers root for the thief.
mrs-caudle-s-curtain-lectures:
Douglas Jerrold created Mrs. Caudle as a comic wife who lectures her husband in bed. In his preface Jerrold tells how ladies asked what made him invent her. He says the idea fell on him like rain, with no plan at all. He then recalls a bleak schoolyard scene that fed the fancy.

A curtain lecture was the talk a wife gave after lights out. Mrs. Caudle scolds, pleads, and reasons while Mr. Caudle longs for sleep. Jerrold turns small home grievances into long, funny speeches. The sketches were a hit in Punch. They still show Victorian home life through one wife's tireless voice.
mrs-korner-sins-her-mercies:
Jerome K. Jerome wrote this comic sketch about Mrs. Korner of Acacia Villa. The sample opens at breakfast, with eggs, a teapot, and a grumbling servant. Mrs. Korner declares she likes a man to be a man. Her friend doubts she would like it in her own husband.

Talk turns to Mr. Korner hunting a lost collar stud. Mrs. Korner fears he may be swearing to himself. Jerome draws the house in a few quick, kind strokes. V1 summed up her good deeds that end in mishaps. The piece laughs at kind hearts whose help goes wrong, with warmth on every page.
mrs-overtheway-s-remembrances:
Juliana Horatia Ewing wrote these tales for young readers, issued by a Christian press. The contents list Ida, Mrs. Moss, and The Snoring Ghost. Rek a Dom and Kerguelen's Land close the set. Ewing dedicated the book to her husband, recalling 1866 and 1867.

Ida opens with a small old lady who lives over the way. She passes a green gate each day at eight for Morning Prayer. The church bell chimes as she climbs three white steps. Ewing tells of neighbors seen through a child's eyes. The tales mix faith, play, and gentle wonder in a clear, kind style.
mrs-skagg-s-husbands-and-other-stories:
Bret Harte fills this book with California tales, led by the Mrs. Skaggs story. The contents add Santa Claus at Simpson's Bar and The Iliad of Sandy Bar. The Poet of Sierra Flat and Rupert's Christmas gift follow. Harte sets his stage in the Sierra foothills near Angel's.

Dawn comes to the mining town with coaches and crowded barrooms. A faded lamp and a worn reveler open the title tale. Harte mixes miners, wives, and drifters in short plots. Humor and pathos share each story, as in his best work. The set is classic mining-camp fiction from the Gold Rush's long shadow.
mudfog-and-other-sketches:
Charles Dickens wrote these early sketches as Boz, here in a 1903 edition. The lead piece tells the public life of Mr. Tulrumble of Mudfog. Full reports of the Mudfog Association fill much of the book. Its sections mock zoology, medicine, statistics, and machines.

Mudfog sits in a hollow by a river that smells of tar. Dickens jokes about its drunks, barges, and damp charms. A fake section on Umbugology gives the game away. He is parodying proud learned societies and town boosters. V1 called it fun young work, with the master of comic character already clear in every sketch.
murad-the-unlucky-and-other-tales:
Maria Edgeworth's tales appear here in the 1891 Cassell edition. The contents list Murad the Unlucky, The Limerick Gloves, and Madame de Fleury. A long introduction tells Edgeworth's own life first. She was born on January 1, 1767, near Maidenhead.

Her father raised his first son by Rousseau's bold plan in Emile. The family moved to Ireland, to estates at Edgeworthstown. Maria was schooled at Derby and then in London. That keen, teaching home shaped her tales for the young. Murad, an Eastern tale of luck and character, leads a set that taught generations of children.
murat-celebrated-crimes:
Alexandre Dumas tells the fall of Murat in this tale from Celebrated Crimes. The set of eight volumes came out in this form in 1910. Three chapters trace Toulon, Corsica, and Pizzo in 1815. The tale opens on the day of Waterloo, June 18, 1815.

A man dressed as a beggar walks the road to Marseilles. He stops above the Gorge of Ollioulles to view the sea. A war brig races for Italian seas below him. Dumas builds doom from that lone, ragged figure. Murat had been Napoleon's bold marshal and king of Naples, and his last ride ends in glory and ruin.
musical-memories:
Camille Saint-Saens looks back on a long life in music in this memoir. Edwin Gile Rich translated it into English. Small, Maynard of Boston issued it in 1919. The first chapter recalls the composer's own childhood.

Later chapters treat the old Conservatoire, Victor Hugo, and a comic opera's fate. Saint-Saens writes on the organ, on Haydn, and on art for art's sake. He scolds anarchy in music and praises craft. His voice is dry, proud, and full of sharp tales. Few composers left so clear a record of the Paris music world they helped to shape.
my-book-of-favourite-fairy-tales:
Captain Edric Vredenburg edited this book of favorite fairy tales for children. Jennie Harbour painted its many pictures. Raphael Tuck and Sons issued it in London and Paris. One plate shows the Goose Girl in full color.

Tales here are retold by the editor and others. Such gift books gathered the best-loved stories in one rich volume. Kings, geese, and lost children fill its pages. The art leads, with bright plates made to charm young eyes. It is a fine sample of the lush story books British children got at Christmas in the age of color printing.
my-book-of-indoor-games:
Clarence Squareman wrote this handbook of indoor games, issued in 1916. Photographs came from the Chicago Park Commission. Its index runs from Acting Proverbs to card games and charades. Blind Man's Buff, Bingo, and Buzz all appear.

Dozens of games fill the list, for parlor, hall, and classroom. Some need boards or blackboards, and some need nothing at all. Squareman gives rules plain enough for leaders to use at once. The book served parties, schools, and park programs. It shows how Americans amused themselves indoors before radio, with games of wit, luck, and quick hands for all ages.
my-man-jeeves:
P. G. Wodehouse gathers eight Jeeves tales in this 1919 book. Bertie Wooster tells them in his own loose, cheerful voice. Jeeves, his man, knows all and fixes all. Leave It to Jeeves opens the set.

Bertie swears he could not manage without Jeeves at all. He compares him to an inquiry clerk who is never wrong. A check suit like Monty Byng's starts one fine clash. Jeeves calls the suit unwise, and Bertie calls it rot. Other tales aid Freddie, George, and Clarence. Wodehouse's perfect comic pair begins here, master foolish and servant wise.
myth-and-romance-being-a-book-of-verses:
Madison Julius Cawein published this book of verses with Putnam's in 1899. He dedicated it to his friend William Warwick. The first part is called Visions and Voices. Poems named Myth and Romance and Genius Loci lead it.

The Rain-Crow, the Harvest Moon, and an Old Water-Mill follow. An Anthem of Dawn and a Hymn to Desire raise the key. Jotunheim, the giants' home of Norse myth, closes the sample list. Cawein was known as a Kentucky nature poet. His verses blend woods, weather, and old romance in rich, musical lines for quiet reading.
nancy-macintyre-a-tale-of-the-prairies:
Lester Shepard Parker wrote this prairie tale in verse and prose, dated 1910. He inscribed it with love to his wee daughter Rachel. The contents run from Billy's Revery through a quarrel and a search. Nancy's own story closes the short book.

Pictures show a parting in the night outside Nancy's dug-out. One grim plate drags a man through a cactus bed. A prairie schooner loads up for the trail in another. Parker mixes poem, tale, and frontier hardship in one slim volume. It is a fond, rough sketch of prairie love and loss for young readers.
nasa-tm-19640009344-nasa-program-plannin:
NASA's Office of Space Sciences prepared this planning document in September 1963. Discipline subcommittees of the Space Sciences Steering Committee wrote it. It holds the approved NASA program in space sciences at that date. The document replaced an edition from December of the prior year.

Its stated uses are budget work and future program planning. Funds for data study flow to experimenters once their craft flies well. That rule is spelled out in the introduction. Catalog notes list the fields covered, from astronomy to biosciences. Solar physics, planetary air, particles and fields, and radio physics all appear. The plan shows how NASA sorted its science bets at the Apollo era's start.
nasa-tm-19650012058-bibliography-of-part:
W N Hess, G D Mead, and M P Nakada of the Theoretical Division at Goddard compiled this bibliography of particles and fields research. It gathers published work on the solar wind and radiation belts. Aurora, solar energetic particles, and galactic cosmic rays are also covered. Geomagnetism and neutrons round out the list.

A bibliography was a working tool before online search existed. It told a new researcher what had already been done and where to find it. In a field growing as fast as space physics, that map mattered. This one preserves the shape of the field as Goddard staff saw it.
nasa-tm-19650012604-micrometeorites:
Tiny dust grains that strike Earth, called micrometeorites, are the subject of this survey. Satellites and rockets had added much new information about them, the author notes. Larger interplanetary material was already known from meteors seen by eye and by radio. Meteorites themselves were thought to come mainly from the breakup of comets.

The survey follows how dust is spread and removed in space. Light pressure, the solar wind, and collisions all play a part. Near Earth, the grains move at roughly forty kilometers per second. Their paths, makeup, and numbers matter for spacecraft, which these grains can damage over time.
nasa-tm-19660005487-radial-density-and-t:
Roman Krawec at Lewis Research Center set out how density and temperature vary across a plasma near a special resonance point. The paper was offered for a plasma meeting in California in March 1966. At the ion cyclotron resonance point, ions absorb wave energy strongly. The catalog note links the theory to an electrostatic probe, called a Langmuir probe, in a plasma held by magnetic fields.

Profiles across the plasma show where it is dense and where it is hot. A probe reading means little without such a profile behind it. Krawec gives the theory that connects the two. Plasma devices for research and propulsion both depend on that link.
nasa-tm-19660022059-program-for-calculat:
Thor T Semler at Lewis Research Center described a computer program that finds neutron ages from laboratory activation data. Neutron age is a measure used in reactor theory. It states how far a neutron wanders while slowing down from birth to heat speeds. Activation data come from foils or samples made radioactive by the neutrons themselves. The program turns those readings into the age value.

Semler details the numerical schemes and the error analysis behind them. Curve fitting methods are also covered, with a best fit drawn from statistical decision theory. Reactor designers need the age for the basic equation of a working core. A documented program let any laboratory repeat the computation the same tested way.
nasa-tm-19660027755-shadow-shield-experi:
R. H. Knoll, E. R. Bartoo, and R. J. Boyle, of NASA's Lewis Research Center in Cleveland, prepared this paper for a 1966 conference in Huntsville, Alabama. The conference dealt with storing cryogenic propellants in space for long periods. Their part of that problem is shielding cold fuel from heat.

The paper reports experiments on shadow shields, including flat plate shields against thermal radiation. A shadow shield blocks heat the way a parasol blocks sunlight. Keeping radiant heat off stored propellant slows boil-off during long missions. The authors present their experimental studies so designers could judge how well such shields work.
nasa-tm-19670019470-oscillator-strengths:
Sidney O. Kastner, of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, wrote this paper in April 1967. It gives oscillator strengths for resonance lines of some silicon and sulfur ions. Oscillator strength measures how strongly an ion absorbs or emits light at a given wavelength.

Kastner opens by noting where these lines appear. Resonance lines of silicon and sulfur ions show up in the far ultraviolet spectrum of the solar corona. That is the Sun's hot outer atmosphere, seen during eclipses and by instruments. Knowing the strengths lets astronomers turn line brightness into physical information about the corona.
nasa-tm-19670030323-acoustic-linear-stud:
Bert Phillips, of NASA's Lewis Research Center in Cleveland, presented this paper at a combustion conference in Menlo Park, California, in October 1967. Despite the catalog title's wording, the work concerns acoustic liners, panels of small resonators that soak up sound inside rocket engines. Violent combustion noise can shake an engine apart, so understanding liner behavior mattered.

Earlier work had exposed poor understanding of how mean flow and high sound wave amplitudes change liner behavior. Lewis attacked the problem two ways. Arrays of isolated Helmholtz resonators were tested inside a hydrogen-oxygen rocket engine firing at twenty thousand pounds of thrust. Stability was rated by cooling the incoming hydrogen until oscillations broke out. Separately, a single resonator went through cold flow testing. The hot tests asked whether flow effects belong in the resonant frequency calculation, and where along the chamber a liner works best.
nasa-tm-19680002399-sensitivity-of-quart:
Lloyd W. Canfil and William C. Nieberding, at the Lewis Research Center in Cleveland, calibrated pressure sensors across an extreme temperature span. The sensors are quartz, piezoelectric transducers, which turn pressure into electric charge. Their sensitivity was checked from near absolute zero up to several hundred degrees.

Slow, steady calibrations showed the sensitivity barely moved. At the cold end it differed from the room value by only a few percent, and somewhat more at the hot end. Repeated temperature trips left the room value essentially unchanged. This kind of transducer, they conclude, suits dynamic pressure measurement at cryogenic temperatures especially well.
nasa-tm-19680009667-solar-spin-down-and-:
Dilhan Ezer, of Middle East Technical University in Ankara, and A. G. W. Cameron, of Yeshiva University and the Goddard Institute for Space Studies, puzzle over missing solar neutrinos. Davis had failed to detect the expected boron neutrino flux from the Sun. Either the Sun models were wrong, or the experiment was.

The authors suggest the failure may reflect the Sun's inner state. A high central hydrogen abundance could be maintained inside the Sun. Circulation currents tied to the Sun's spin-down might keep fresh hydrogen mixed inward. That would lower the neutrino output to match the null result. The paper ties solar rotation to the neutrino problem.
nasa-tm-19680014432-a-review-of-transpor:
Bruce G. Powers of NASA's Flight Research Center at Edwards reviewed transport handling qualities rules in this 1968 memorandum. He judged the rules against early flight experience with the XB-70, a large supersonic aircraft. The question was whether standards written for transports still fit such a machine.

Powers draws on preliminary XB-70 flights, including work with the unaugmented aircraft. He compares how the aircraft behaved with what the criteria predicted. Cases where the rules matched flight results sit beside cases where they did not. The review gives designers a flight-based check on handling standards before those standards guide new transport designs.
nasa-tm-19680018431-damping-of-thermoela:
William Mitchell Gillis, of the Aero-Astrodynamics Laboratory at Marshall Space Flight Center, wrote this April 1968 memorandum, TM X-53722. His subject is damping in thermoelastic structures, where heat flow and elastic motion affect each other. He studies lengthwise waves moving through a solid cylindrical rod, a simple shape that reveals the basic physics.

Gillis first reviews classic results for waves in elastic solids and cylinders. He then shows that heat changes wave speed only slightly, yet heat conduction steadily drains energy from the wave. That damping grows large for very high frequency waves in thin bars. He sums the effect up in a new measure, the thermoelastic bar number.
nasa-tm-19690031850-thermal-anomalies-an:
Thermal Anomalies and Geologic Features of the Mono Lake Area, California, as Revealed by Infrared Imagery is NASA Technical Letter NASA-82, dated September 1968. The author's name does not appear in the hosted sample. Aircraft infrared imagery reads ground heat patterns invisible to ordinary cameras. Around volcanic Mono Lake, warm ground can betray hidden geologic activity.

Early chapters review previous investigations, state objectives, and describe procedures. The geology of the Mono Lake and Mono Craters area is then laid out, with lunar analogues for comparison. Long sections weigh which geologic factors shape image tone, radiative transfer first, then convective transfer. Other anomalies, many plates of imagery, and a summary complete the letter.
nasa-tm-19700025218-an-investigation-of-:
Apollo titanium pressure vessel welds are the subject of this Houston working paper, number 1333, dated January 1968. The welds were made with a filler wire of commercially pure titanium. The question mattered because a suspect vessel of this kind sat at the center of a booster explosion the year before.

The S-IVB stage carried nine spherical helium vessels around its thrust cone, working at very high pressure. Three recovered vessels had split at the girth weld in a brittle way after the March 1967 explosion. Checking showed they had been welded with pure titanium wire instead of the specified alloy wire. An eddy current screening then found five more such vessels that had not failed.
nasa-tm-19700026407-study-of-lem-abort-t:
Abort transfer paths for the lunar landing module are worked out in this Houston study, dated May 31, 1965. The module was then called the LEM. If a landing had to be called off, the module needed a sound path back to the command ship.

The study takes up aborts at three points in the flight. They are the coasting descent, the powered descent, and a stay on the surface. For each case it gives the transfer paths and compares their ranges, flight times, and thrust needs. A closing section states the conclusions for planners.
nasa-tm-19710018632-design-of-sert-2-spa:
Lewis Research Center engineers described the SERT 2 spacecraft structures in this technical memorandum. SERT 2 tested electric thrusters in Earth orbit. Its frame had to be simple, rugged, and cheap. The team also wanted a frame that could change easily when parts were swapped. Weight was not a tight limit on this mission, which freed the design.

Both structures used riveted aluminum and magnesium sheet. They took a drum like half shell form called semimonocoque. Design, building, and vibration testing all finished in a very short time. Stress analysis stayed minimal by choice. The report argues such simple structures may see wider use. Cheaper launch vehicles would make that trade more common.
nasa-tm-19720018180-short-arc-optical-su:
Short Arc Optical Survey Techniques is a NASA report on fixing ground station positions from brief satellite passes. Surveyors watched the GEOS 1 satellite through optical instruments at thirteen stations. From such short arcs of observation, they computed where each station sits, a foundation for satellite geodesy.

The report lays out the optical tracking network and its data reduction, then tests three choices that shape the results. Those choices are the gravity value used, the accuracy of the fixed origin station's own survey, and the starting reference frame, or initial datum. Result sections examine errors in each choice separately. Tables preserve the starting surveys used, drawn from North American, Smithsonian, and Mercury program sources, alongside the computed solutions.
never-again-a-protest-and-a-warning-addr: Never Again! A Protest and a Warning Addressed to the Peoples of Europe is a work by Edward Carpenter. The hosted sample holds only a Project Gutenberg header, so it preserves no readable content from the work itself. The full title alone states its stance: a protest, and a warning, spoken to the peoples of Europe. No year for the work is given in the sample or the record. Readers should treat this note as a title level guide only.
new-collected-rhymes:
Andrew Lang published New Collected Rhymes with Longmans, Green in London in 1905. His preface calls the book a poor little flutter of rhymes. He says a friend urged him so warmly that he let the verses go rather than drop the plan.

Lang warns that his loyal lyrics on Charles, James, and the White Rose sing symbols, not revolt. They stand, he says, for dear things that live on in loyal memory. Of the ballads, The Young Ruthven and The Queen of Spain were written to vie with street singers of an older age. The Queen of Spain retells the tale of the ship Florencia.
new-comedies:
Lady Gregory wrote the five short plays in New Comedies, copyrighted in 1913 and tied to the Abbey Theatre. Their titles are The Bogie Men, The Full Moon, Coats, Damer's Gold, and McDonough's Wife. Notes follow the plays at the back of the book.

The Bogie Men opens in a shed near a coach stop. Darby Melody, a chimney sweep, hides a showy suit when he hears a step. Taig O'Harragha, a fellow sweep, enters with a greeting. Each man doubts the other at once. Gregory builds her comedy from Irish speech, small trades, and quick suspicion between neighbours.
new-faces:
Myra Kelly published New Faces in New York in 1910, with pictures by Charles F. Neagle. Kelly had earlier written Little Citizens and Little Aliens. A verse by Andrew Lang opens the book, begging for new faces after a fortnight of the same ones. Boredom with known faces sets the theme.

Eight stories follow, starting with The Play's the Thing and There's Danger in Numbers. Misery Loves Company and The Christmas Guest come next, then Who Is Sylvia? The Spirit of Cecelia Anne and Theodora, Gift of God close the set, with Great Oaks from Little Acorns. The titles promise school, home, and city tales told with a light hand.
nick-baba-s-last-drink-and-other-sketche:
George P. Goff published Nick Baba's Last Drink and Other Sketches at Lancaster, Pennsylvania, in 1879. The Inquirer Printing and Publishing Company printed the book, with pictures. Goff entered it for copyright that same year. He inscribed the volume to the Raymond Hall Shooting Club.

A Latin tag on the title page warns that books meet their fate by the reader's grasp. The title piece gives Nick Baba a last drink as its hook. The rest are sketches, short prose pieces of the kind local papers loved. Goff wrote for readers who knew his ground and its people. The club dedication hints at sport and camp life among his themes.
nisida-celebrated-crimes:
Alexandre Dumas wrote Nisida as part of his Celebrated Crimes set, shown here from the eight volume edition of 1910. The tale is dated 1825 in its heading. It opens not with a crime, but with Naples on a feast day.

Dumas cites the proverb about seeing Naples and then dying. Land at Mergellina, he advises, on a fine summer day, as a solemn procession leaves the cathedral. The town decks herself like a bride, in silk hangings and flower festoons. Rich and poor alike dress with pride. Bells, bands, and sherbet sellers fill the air. Against that bright scene, the crime of Nisida will stand out.
no-and-yes:
Mary Baker Eddy, author of Science and Health, wrote No and Yes as a short statement of her teaching. Trustees under her will published it in Boston in 1919. The book counts as authorized literature of the First Church of Christ, Scientist, in Boston. Its contents are framed as questions and answers.

Heads include Disease Unreal and Science of Mind-Healing. Eddy asks if Christian Science shares lineage with spiritualism or theosophy. She asks if it comes from beneath or from above, and if it is pantheistic or blasphemous. Personal deity, personal devil, soul, and sin each get a head. The book defends her system in brief, direct replies.
norse-tales-and-sketches:
Alexander L. Kielland's Norse Tales and Sketches came out in London in 1896, translated by R. L. Cassie. The contents list A Siesta, A Monkey, and A Tale of the Sea. A Dinner, Trofast, and Karen follow. Letters from Master-Pilot Seehus and Old Dances sit near the end, with Autumn last.

A Siesta opens far from Norway, at dessert in the Rue Castiglione in Paris. Senhor José Francisco de Silvis hosts a merry party there. He is a short, dark Portuguese who came from Brazil with incredible wealth. His guests scarcely know each other, or him. Kielland's sketches move between home waters and foreign drawing rooms.
not-pretty-but-precious-and-other-short-:
Not Pretty, but Precious, and Other Short Stories appeared in 1872, with several hands at work. John Hay, Clara F. Guernsey, Margaret Hosmer, and Harriet Prescott Spofford are named on the title page. Lucy Hamilton Hooper and others join them. The book is illustrated, as the title page notes.

Contents assign each tale to its maker: the title story to Margret Field, The Cold Hand to Guernsey. Hay wrote The Blood Seedling, and De Forrest The Hungry Heart. Spofford wrote Louie, and Hooper Under False Colors. The title tale opens as a letter to Mr Norval, four weeks after his accident. A doctor has cleared him, broken bones aside, for hard news.
notes-to-shakespeare-volume-01-comedies:
Samuel Johnson's Notes to Shakespeare appear here in volume one, on the comedies, in an Augustan Reprint Society edition. Arthur Sherbo edited the volume and wrote its introduction. A general introduction recalls that Johnson's Preface to Shakespeare is a famous critical essay of the eighteenth century. Too many students, it says, forget what that preface was.

The Preface stood before plays edited by Johnson himself, the introduction argues. The edition has been obscured by the fame of its own front essay. These notes give Johnson's comments play by play on the comedies. Readers can watch the great critic judge scenes, words, and characters in short, sharp remarks. Sherbo's frame helps place each note.
notes-to-shakespeare-volume-iii-the-trag:
Volume three of Samuel Johnson's Notes to Shakespeare covers the tragedies. The Augustan Reprint Society issued this copy at Los Angeles in 1958. It came from the William Andrews Clark Memorial Library of the University of California. Arthur Sherbo edited the volume, with an introduction of his own.

Johnson made his name as a critic with his edition of Shakespeare and its famous preface. The notes in such volumes follow the plays scene by scene. They gloss hard words, weigh readings, and judge characters in plain prose. Only front matter is sampled in this copy, so the note treats the book's frame. Students of Johnson still read these volumes beside the plays.
noughts-and-crosses-stories-studies-and-:
Arthur Thomas Quiller-Couch, signing Q, gathered Noughts and Crosses as stories, studies, and sketches. Two tales first ran in Longman's Magazine, he notes, and the rest came from the Speaker. He thanks both editors for leave to reprint. The book is dedicated to his wife.

The Omnibus and Fortunio open the contents, then the Outlandish Ladies. A statement by Gabriel Foot, highwayman, gives a rogue his say. The Return of Joanna, Psyche, and the Countess of Bellarmine follow. A Cottage in Troy runs as four linked pieces. Old Aeson and the affair of Bleakirk-on-Sands close the sampled list. Q mixes Cornish life with fancy.
novel-notes:
Jerome K. Jerome published Novel Notes in 1893, in the Leadenhall Press edition sampled here. He dedicates it to a big hearted, big souled, big bodied friend, Conan Doyle. A prologue reaches back to his small childhood. The family lived in a great house on a long, straight, brown street in London's east end.

By day that street was noisy and crowded, Jerome recalls. By night it fell silent and lonesome, with gas lights few and far between. A policeman's tramp on his long beat drew near and faded. The back windows faced an ancient, much peopled churchyard. The child author peered at grey tombstones, fearing ghosts among them.
nsa-manhattan-project-director-files:
In 2024 the National Security Archive published this Nuclear Vault briefing book from the files of General Leslie Groves, director of the Manhattan Project. The declassified documents open a window on the atomic bomb's early history. Groves ran the project from 1942 with near-total power and a passion for secrecy.

The papers cover the project's organization, its vast sites and security web, and the choices that led to the Trinity test of July 1945. Letters and memos show Groves settling fights over science, labor, and spies. The briefing shows how one office steered the largest secret enterprise of the war. The documents are United States government records.
old-english-libraries:
Ernest Albert Savage wrote this history of English libraries. Methuen first published it in London in 1911. The full title stresses the Middle Ages. Savage studies how books were made, kept, and used. Fifty-two pictures show old libraries and their keepers.

The preface says the book is a popular, discursive treatment. It covers monastic collections and the libraries of Oxford. Savage worked with James Hutt on the Oxford chapter. Book lovers learn how chained books reached readers. Savage writes for general readers, not only for trained scholars of books. Clark's Care of Books covers gear and rooms, Savage notes. His own aim is books in the life of that age.
old-fashioned-fairy-tales:
Juliana Horatia Ewing wrote these new fairy tales for children. The preface stresses that the tales are not old ones retold. They first appeared in Aunt Judy's Magazine for young people. Ewing used only shared fairy props and ideas. She kept close to tradition in color and detail.

Ewing names themes found in myths of all countries. The weak outwit the strong in her plots. Wishes often lead choosers into trouble. Sprites long for a human soul and its hopes. The tales teach gently through wonder and humor. They suit families who like moral fairy stories.
old-fires-and-profitable-ghosts-a-book-o:
Arthur Quiller-Couch gathered fifteen stories in this book. The contents mix sea tales, ghosts, and Cornish scenes. Titles include The Seventh Man and Frozen Margit. Other stories treat mirrors, prisoners of war, and a lugger. The first story, Oceanus, opens as a letter.

The letter writer tells Violet that grief has changed him. His friend Harry has died, and laughter feels lost. Yet cheer returns in a calmer, steadier form. Such loss and haunting run through the collection. Quiller-Couch writes with grace, pathos, and quiet mystery. Several tales first draw readers in with an ordinary, calm opening scene.
old-greek-stories:
James Baldwin retold Greek myths for children in simple language. The American Book Company published the book in New York. Baldwin tells tales of Jupiter and his mighty company. He also tells tales of old Greek heroes. Each story stands alone, yet the set feels complete.

Baldwin refuses to explain the myths as science lessons. He says such analysis kills a child's delight. He keeps the supernatural element in the background. He never calls Jupiter and his company gods. The preface argues that pleasure alone justifies early reading. Teachers and families used the book for generations.
old-news-from-the-snow-image-and-other-t:
Nathaniel Hawthorne wrote this reflective sketch called Old News. It comes from The Snow-Image and Other Twice-Told Tales. Hawthorne studies a bound volume of old colonial newspapers. The small half sheets are yellow, stained, and coarsely printed. He marvels that such frail pages outlived their whole town.

Hawthorne pictures a colonial reader before his fire. The major reads the king's speech with grave reverence. Ship news and trade notices draw his sharper eye. Hawthorne smiles at hopes that time proved false. The sketch turns old papers into a mirror of vanished life. It rewards readers who love quiet, thoughtful prose.
old-peter-s-russian-tales:
Arthur Ransome collected these Russian fairy tales for English children. Dmitri Mitrokhin drew the pictures and cover design. Frederick Stokes published the book in New York. Ransome wrote it while living beside the Volkhov River. Old Peter tells the tales to his grandchildren at night.

Ransome says Russian peasants tell such tales to all ages. Even soldiers told them on the road to war. He retells his favorites freely, mostly from memory. Versions appear in chapbooks and in Afanasiev's great collection. Wise princesses, forests, and wonders fill the stories. The book is meant for children, not for scholars.
on-land-and-sea-at-the-dardanelles:
Thomas Charles Bridges wrote this war adventure for young readers. Indian troops at Alexandria open the picture captions. The contents follow a ship called Cardigan Castle. Chapters treat a landing, a ruse of war, and promotion. Guns, sweepers, and prisoners drive the action forward.

A hero named Ken meets an old friend late on. Battles by rocks and above the Narrows fill scenes. The Dardanelles campaign joins land and sea fighting. Bridges writes fast, patriotic adventure in a boy's-book style. The tale honors courage under fire in wartime. It reflects British views of the Great War campaign.
on-picket-duty-and-other-tales:
Louisa May Alcott published these tales in Boston in 1864. The title tale opens on a Civil War picket post. Four guards rest beneath a scarred, moss-draped tree. Camp fires twinkle behind them on a distant plain. A river and a Southern swamp frame the scene.

Two friends, Phil and Dick, think of their wives. Quiet hours turn soldiers toward home and honesty, Alcott suggests. Thorn, a grim Massachusetts volunteer, hides a warmer nature. The men differ in schooling, character, and tastes. Shared danger binds them in strong fellowship. Alcott writes war from the heart, not just battle.
on-the-economy-of-machinery-and-manufact: Charles Babbage wrote this study of machinery and manufacturing. The hosted sample preserves only the Project Gutenberg header. That header gives the title and Babbage as author. It gives no readable text of the book itself. Readers cannot judge its arguments from this sample alone. Babbage is known for his work on calculating machines and factory methods.
on-the-reception-of-the-origin-of-specie:
Thomas Henry Huxley wrote this account of Darwin's reception. Francis Darwin included it in his father's Life and Letters. Younger readers now rank Darwin with Newton, Huxley says. They honor his genius, industry, and strict honesty. Popular prejudice once raged against him, Huxley recalls.

Struggle for existence has become a household phrase now. Natural selection shapes all teaching of biology today. Darwin's book lights the path of every investigator, he writes. Evolution, long bound by theology, gained new life from Darwin. It captures the triumph of Darwin's theory in science.
one-of-life-s-slaves:
Jonas Lie wrote this Norwegian novel of working life. Jessie Muir translated it into English prose. Hodder Brothers published it in London in 1895. Chapter one is called Neglected Responsibilities, chapter two A Strict Disciplinarian. A fight and its consequences follow in chapter three.

Later chapters move among the unemployed and factory girls. A wedding is postponed again as hardship grows. A fair and a convict close the contents list. Lie was a leading Norwegian novelist of his time. He writes with sympathy for the poor and struggling. The tale shows how small failures can bind a life.
only-an-irish-boy-or-andy-burke-s-fortun:
Horatio Alger Jr. wrote this rags-to-respect tale for boys. Andy Burke is a poor Irish boy in the story. Chapter one introduces Andy, chapter three his mother. Mrs. Preston and Colonel Preston shape his fortunes. Andy obtains a place and makes his school debut.

Andy rides with a highwayman and baffles a robber. A midnight alarm and a Christmas present add excitement. Colonel Preston's will drives the closing chapters hard. Mrs. Preston plots revenge but meets a surprise ending. The final chapter promises that all ends well. Alger rewards honesty, pluck, and steady hard work.
original-letters-and-biographic-epitomes:
J. Atwood Slater was a London art prizeman and a certificated Slade student. He also won a silver medal from the Royal Academy of Arts. His Original Letters and Biographic Epitomes gathers his correspondence and short lives. The sample opens with a letter printed in the Western Daily Press in February 1901. Its subject is Munkacsy's famous painting Ecce Homo.

Slater judges the celebrated picture with a cold eye. He calls it laborious and of average ability. Its lighting is too yellow, he says, where light should lead the beholder to the theme. That theme is Christ as the light of the world. The combative, technical tone sets the volume's flavor. An ambitious Victorian artist-critic argues his case in public, letter by letter.
orpheus-in-mayfair-and-other-stories-and:
Maurice Baring collected the stories and sketches of Orpheus in Mayfair from the pages of the Morning Post and the Westminster Gazette, and dedicated the book to the composer Ethel Smyth. Its two dozen pieces move between London society, music, travel, and fable: a cricket match, a luncheon party, a Chinaman on Oxford, Dr. Faust's last day, and the title tale among them.

Orpheus in Mayfair itself introduces Heraclius Themistocles Margaritis, a professional musician. He sings, composes songs, and writes poetry in Romaic Greek. But none of that, the narrator warns, is how he earns his daily bread. Baring's light, ironic touch treats modern Mayfair as a place where ancient myth can walk in wearing evening dress.
out-of-the-ashes:
Ethel Watts Mumford's novel Out of the Ashes, published in 1913, opens in a Fifth Avenue library of green Genoese velvet and Donatello bronzes. Marcus Gard, the Great Man, sits contemplating a pair of sixteenth-century bronze inkwells. His thoughts, though, are on vast schemes of destruction and reconstruction. The room is sealed and steel-cased. The city's roar never reaches it.

His secretary announces Mrs. Martin Marteen, very anxious to see him about the Heim Vandyke, and Gard, still handsome under silver hair, rises to receive her. Mumford sets her stage among collectors, masterpieces, and money, where art objects carry the plot's weight — a society mystery built in the treasure rooms of the rich.
outdoor-sports-and-games: Claude H. Miller's Outdoor Sports and Games is a handbook for boys on the whole outdoor life. It appeared in 1911 in the Library of Work and Play. The hosted sample shows the title page and contents only. The contents promise the Boy Scouts and how to form a patrol. Camps, camp cooking, and woodcraft follow. The use of firearms closes the plan. No instructional text appears in the sample.
outwitting-our-nerves: Josephine A. Jackson, a physician, and Helen M. Salisbury wrote Outwitting Our Nerves. It is a primer of psychotherapy, published in 1921. The hosted sample shows the title page and a contents list's start only. Part One is The Strange Ways of Nerves. Its first chapter has most of us plead guilty to nerves. Part Two is called How the Wheels Go Round. No chapter text appears.
owindia-a-true-tale-of-the-mackenzie-riv:
Charlotte Selina Bompas, wife of the first Anglican bishop of the Mackenzie River country, wrote Owindia as a true tale of the Mackenzie River Indians of North-West America. It opens on a pretty open spot on the bank of the great river, where Michel the Hunter has pitched his lodge among other camps drawn by the abundant fish.

Bompas paints the seasonal round in affectionate detail. Children snare rabbits. Beaver furs buy tea, tobacco, blankets, and ammunition from the Hudson's Bay Company. Women make birch syrup in spring and dress moose skins. Canoes are readied for the breaking of eight months of ice. Michel, whose swift tread and steady aim no moose escapes, heads the family whose story the tale follows. It is missionary literature, written to bring the North home to church readers.
parmenides:
Plato's Parmenides, given here in Benjamin Jowett's English translation, is often called his hardest dialogue. A young Socrates meets the aged philosopher Parmenides and his follower Zeno. Socrates puts forward his theory of Forms, and Parmenides takes the theory apart with a series of pointed objections.

Jowett's long introduction explains why scholars have argued over the dialogue for centuries. The second half works through what follows if things are one, and what follows if they are many. Readers come to it for the sharpest ancient testing of Plato's own ideas, stated by Plato himself.
pascal-s-pense-es: What is hosted here shows only the front matter of Pascal's Pensées, the contents pages and an editor's note, with none of the fragments themselves. It records a Dutton paperback edition of 1958, with an introduction by T. S. Eliot. The contents divide Blaise Pascal's thoughts into sections on mind and style, the misery of man without God, and the wager. The rest treat the philosophers, morality and doctrine, the prophecies, proofs of Jesus Christ, and the miracles.
peace-manoeuvres:
Richard Harding Davis opens "Peace Manoeuvres" with a scout standing where three roads meet in pine woods. The scout is Private Lathrop of the Bicycle Squad of the Boston Corps of Cadets, out on army manoeuvres. His duty is to wait and watch for the enemy forces from New York, New Jersey, and Connecticut.

His heart pulls another way, since down one road stands the summer home of Beatrice Farrar, who has rejected him. Davis spins the story from that tug between love and duty. He lets a punctured bicycle wheel, spun like a roulette, decide which road the scout will take.
peacock-pie-a-book-of-rhymes: The sample provided here shows only the front matter of Peacock Pie, the title page and contents, with no poems visible. The title page names Walter de la Mare as the author and calls the book a book of rhymes. The contents are divided into sections such as "Up and Down" and "Boys and Girls," and list poems including "The Horseman," "Tired Tim," "The Dunce," "Hide and Seek," and "The Cupboard.
penelope-s-irish-experiences: What is hosted here shows only the front matter of Penelope's Irish Experiences, the title page, dedication, and contents, with no narrative text visible. The title page names Kate Douglas Wiggin, dates publication to 1901, and dedicates the book to her first Irish friend, Jane Barlow. The contents tour all four provinces, Leinster, Munster, Ulster, and Connaught, with chapters on Dublin, the belles of Shandon, the glens of Antrim, and the wee folk.
phantastes:
George MacDonald, a Scots priest and poet, wrote this first of his great tales in 1858. He was then a young man, and the book broke new ground at a stroke. It tells of Anodos, a youth of one and twenty years, on the day he comes of age.

Anodos finds a gate in his room to Fairy Land and walks its woods and streams. Maids of ash and alder, a knight, and a dark shade mark his road of growth and loss. The book is the first great fantasy of the Victorian age, and it shaped C. S. Lewis.
philippine-folk-tales:
Philippine Folk-Tales, as gathered here, reprints four articles from the Journal of American Folk-Lore. Clara Kern Bayliss contributes the title piece, with tales like The Monkey and the Turtle. Berton L. Maxfield and W. H. Millington supply Visayan tales, Fletcher Gardner Tagalog tales, a Filipino version of Aladdin, and games of Filipino children, and Laura Watson Benedict adds Bagobo myths.

The contents promise Juan Pusong the trickster, enchanted rings and shells, and stories explaining why dogs wag their tails. Assembled in the early American period, the collection preserves island storytelling in the words of its first scholarly collectors.
philippine-folklore-stories:
John Maurice Miller's Philippine Folklore Stories, dated Boston 1904, opens with The Tobacco of Harisaboqued, a legend of the volcano Canlaon on Negros. Long before the Spaniards came, an old man with great power over the earth lived on the mountain. Tapping the ground three times summoned dwarfs who obeyed his every wish, and under their nightly care the tobacco fields climbed almost to the crater.

The contents add fourteen more tales: How the World Was Made, Catalina of Dumaguete, The Anting-Anting of Manuelito, and others. Miller collected the stories as folklore, noting where each was told, for American readers new to the islands.
pickle-the-spy-or-the-incognito-of-princ:
Andrew Lang's Pickle the Spy, published by Longmans in 1897, began in his study of the Pelham Papers in the British Museum. Among them were the letters of Pickle, the spy who betrayed the Jacobites, and of James Mohr Macgregor. Lang sent transcripts to Robert Louis Stevenson for a novel Stevenson did not live to finish.

Resisting the temptation of fiction, Lang tells the story with fidelity instead. The letters, with Prince Charles's own correspondence in the Stuart papers at Windsor, reveal the secret of the prince's incognito. It is historical detective work: naming the traitor inside Bonnie Prince Charlie's hidden court.
platform-monologues:
T. G. Tucker, professor of classical philology at the University of Melbourne, published Platform Monologues in Melbourne in 1914. Despite the title, the contents are public lectures on literature. Each one is a platform performance on a large question about reading and writing.

Six lectures make up the book. They are The Supreme Literary Gift, Hebraism and Hellenism, and The Principles of Criticism applied to two successors of Tennyson. Then come The Making of a Shakespeare, Literature and Life, and The Future of Poetry. The first lecture opens with Longinus and the test of true sublimity. A great passage, he says, leaves the mind in proud elation, as if it had itself begotten the thing read. Tucker builds his criticism on that feeling of elevation.
plays-by-august-strindberg-second-series:
August Strindberg's plays appear here in a second series, in English versions by Edwin Björkman, who also wrote an introduction to each play. The volume holds five works: There Are Crimes and Crimes, Miss Julia, The Stronger, Creditors, and Pariah.

The book opens with There Are Crimes and Crimes, a comedy dated 1899. Its cast centers on Maurice, a playwright, and Jeanne, his partner, with their young daughter Marion. Around them stand a painter, a workman, a priest, and a watchman, in a story set in Paris. Miss Julia is printed with the author's own preface.
plays-fifth-series:
John Galsworthy's Plays: Fifth Series holds three plays: A Family Man, Loyalties, and Windows. Galsworthy was an English novelist and playwright whose stage works often test family honor and public respect.

A Family Man, the first play in the book, is set in the town of Breconridge, in the Midlands. Its cast centers on John Builder, a partner in a building firm, and his wife Julia and their two daughters. Around them stand a mayor, a police sergeant, a journalist, and the figure of a poacher. The scenes shift between the Builder study, a studio, and the mayor's office.
plays-first-series:
John Galsworthy's Plays: First Series holds three plays: The Silver Box, Joy, and Strife. The volume opens the set of Galsworthy stage works gathered by series. Each play turns on clashes of class, money, and duty in English life.

The Silver Box, a comedy in three acts, comes first. It centers on John Barthwick, a rich Liberal member of Parliament, and his son Jack. Against them stand a charwoman, Mrs. Jones, and her husband, a stranger in the house. The action runs from Easter Tuesday into the next week. A detective and a police magistrate appear among the cast.
plays-fourth-series:
John Galsworthy's Plays: Fourth Series holds three plays: A Bit O' Love, The Foundations, and The Skin Game. The volume is the fourth in the gathered series of his stage works. Galsworthy often set his plays among the rich and the poor of the same English world.

A Bit O' Love opens the book, set in a village of the West on Ascension Day. Its cast centers on Michael Strangway and his wife Beatrice, among farming families with names such as Burlacombe and Trustaford. Scenes move from a cottage room to the village inn and the church door.
plays-second-series:
John Galsworthy's Plays: Second Series holds three plays: The Eldest Son, The Little Dream, and Justice. It is the second gathered volume of his stage works. The plays share his steady focus on family duty, class, and the law.

The Eldest Son opens the volume, set at the Cheshires' country house on December 7 and 8. Sir William Cheshire, a baronet, heads a large family with three sons and three daughters. The cast also names a head-keeper, his daughter the lady's-maid, an under-keeper, and a village girl, Rose Taylor. A night passes between the first and second acts.
plays-third-series:
John Galsworthy's Plays: Third Series holds three plays: The Fugitive, The Pigeon, and The Mob. It is the third gathered volume of his stage works. The plays turn on marriage, flight, and public pressure in English life of his day.

The Fugitive, a play in four acts, opens the volume. George Dedmond and his wife Clare stand at its center, with his father, a general, and her brother around them. Scenes move from a flat to a writer's rooms and a supper room at a restaurant called The Gascony. Three nights pass between the first and second acts.
podcast-dannyjones-XDDgL0WvtEs:
A car collector tells Danny Jones about chasing a Lamborghini Veneno. The Veneno ranks among the priciest production cars ever sold. The buyer recalls a price above four million dollars.

He says he began calling the moment a related model appeared. He took the steps needed just to be considered for a car. The talk covers waiting lists, status, and desire at the top of the market. Heavy metal plays while the exhaust roars, his favorite music. The episode is a rich man's hunt, told step by step. Desire, not need, drives every step he took.
podcast-joerogan-5QQun2pDQEs:
Writer Michael Pollan joins the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 2467. Pollan is known for books on food, farming, and the mind, and his work on psychedelics helped bring the subject to a broad readership. Rogan has hosted him before and treats him as a trusted guide.

The talk moves between psychedelic research and the food system, two fields Pollan links through nature and care. He discusses what plant medicines may teach about the mind, and how we eat shapes the land. Pollan's calm, reported style gives the episode a steady pace, even when the subjects turn strange.
podcast-joerogan-RB-O0V9djEs:
Has Google created sentient AI? Rogan takes up that startling question in a segment of the Joe Rogan Experience. The debate flared when an engineer claimed a company chatbot had become a person. Rogan treats the claim the way his show treats most: out loud, from every side.

The talk asks what sentience would even look like in software, and how anyone could test it. Rogan weighs the engineer's belief against the firm's denial and the nature of chatbots that mimic feeling. The segment is a snapshot of the first public panic over machine minds, recorded while the story was fresh.
podcast-tuckercarlson-nLCOfT6UXEs:
Pastor Andrew Isker joins Tucker Carlson to talk about the Book of Revelation and states that push Christians out. The title promises the truth about Revelation. Isker reads prophecy as a call to build, not to flee.

Isker lays out his postmillennial read, in which the church wins ground over time. He argues blue states drive out faith by law, tax, and school rules. Carlson asks what Christian families should do in reply. Listeners get a pastor's plan for hard times, tied to a bold read of the last book. The library keeps the talk as a record of his views.
podcast-tuckercarlson-opf790y07Es:
Ukraine's treatment of its churches is the subject of this Tucker Carlson episode. Carlson argues that Ukraine's secret police and its government have moved against the Ukrainian Orthodox Church during the war with Russia. He presents that campaign as an attack on Christianity itself.

The episode lays out raids, arrests, and laws aimed at clergy said to have Russian ties. Carlson questions why Western leaders who praise Ukraine stay silent about it. He frames religious freedom as a test the West is failing. Viewers hear a sharp charge, built on the host's reading of events in wartime Ukraine.
poems-by-emily-dickinson-third-series:
Emily Dickinson's third series of Poems was edited by Mabel Loomis Todd and published at Amherst in October 1896, ten years after the poet's death. Todd's preface explains that Dickinson's output was so large and characteristic that a rich third selection remained possible even after two volumes and the published letters. Verses sent to friends in letters were mostly left out, with a few strong exceptions kept in.

Todd notes that many poems read as spontaneous flashes of insight, unrelated to any outward event. While others grow from clear personal occasions, such as a playful reminder to a friend traveling in Europe who owed her a letter. The volume opens with a small offering poem about bringing her heart and the fields. For readers of the first two series, this book proved the supply of major Dickinson poems was nowhere near exhausted.
present-at-a-hanging-and-other-ghost-sto:
Ambrose Bierce's ghost stories appear in this selection from the 1918 Boni and Liveright edition of Can Such Things Be, under the title Present at a Hanging and Other Ghost Stories. The contents arrange Bierce's supernatural work in three companies. The Ways of Ghosts opens with the title story, about a traveler who finds a hanged man and something worse. Soldier-Folk gathers tales where the Civil War dead refuse their graves. Some Haunted Houses gives a run of his most anthologized horrors.

The frame pretends the tales are a dead man's notes, transcribed by an editor who cannot vouch for them and finds the style too baldly simple for mere literary intention. Inside, Bierce's method never varies and never fails: flat reporting, exact detail, and one impossible fact admitted without comment, tale after tale. No American has written colder ghost stories.
president-wilson-s-addresses:
George McLean Harper of Princeton edited this school edition of President Wilson's addresses for the series English Readings for Schools. Under the general editorship of Yale's Wilbur Lucius Cross, published by Henry Holt in 1918 while Wilson was still in office and the nation at war. The series motto, from Richard de Bury, states the educational creed: the virtue of books is the perfecting of reason, which is indeed the happiness of man.

Contents choose the addresses as literature as much as statecraft: the First Inaugural Address, the first address to Congress. The address on the banking system, and the Gettysburg address, where Wilson stood in Lincoln's shadow and knew it. Harper, a Wordsworth scholar, presents a professor-president whose sentences were already being taught as models of English prose. The volume captures a moment when the president was also, by common consent, its finest living speechwriter.
prime-ministers-and-some-others-a-book-o:
George W. E. Russell published his book of reminiscences in July 1918. Inscribing it to the Earl Curzon of Kedleston with a formula that explains the author: not sharing his opinions but prizing his friendship. Russell, a Liberal MP and man of letters who had served in Gladstone's world, drew the papers from magazines including the Cornhill and the Spectator. The first part walks the century's premierships as personal portraits: Palmerston, Lord Russell, Lord Derby, Disraeli, Gladstone, Salisbury, Balfour, and Campbell-Bannerman.

The second part, In Honour of Friendship, turns from power to affection: Gladstone after twenty years, Henry Scott Holland, Lord Halifax, the Ripons, and college friends remembered for themselves. Russell knew everyone and liked most of them, a glory in a memoirist. His book preserves the talk and temper of the Victorian political class as remembered from inside, by one of its kindest members.
primitive-love-and-love-stories:
Henry T. Finck published Primitive Love and Love-Stories in 1899, dedicating it to one who taught the author that conjugal affection is not inferior to romantic love. His contents outline a provocation in three movements: a history of the idea, with chapters on Burton, Hegel, Shelley, and Herbert Spencer's analysis of love. A survey of how sentiments change and grow, covering honorable polygamy, curiosities of modesty, and indifference to chastity; and a direct answer to the question, what is romantic love.

Finck's thesis runs against the romantics: romantic love is not eternal or universal but the last. Not the first, product of civilization, absent where women are property and present only where they are persons. He calls sensuality the antipode of love and animals higher than savages. The book is a Victorian evolutionist's tour of the world's courtships, still quoted wherever the history of love is argued.
prince-eugene-and-his-times:
L. Mühlbach, the pen name of the German novelist Clara Mundt, wrote Prince Eugene and His Times as one of her vast historical romances. Englished for the wide market that devoured her Frederick the Great and Joseph II cycles. Her subject is Prince Eugene of Savoy, the small, ugly, French-born general who became Austria's greatest soldier. Defeated the Turks at Zenta and Belgrade, and fought beside Marlborough at Blenheim, Malplaquet, and Oudenarde.

Mühlbach builds the era around him in her usual manner: courts, camps, mistresses, and ministers, with documents melted into dialogue and the hero's private feelings supplied by the novelist's license. Her books taught nineteenth-century readers their history and Eugene, the cosmopolitan soldier-statesman who also built the Belvedere and collected books like a scholar, fits her method perfectly. The romance preserves a hero Europe once ranked with Alexander.
princess-polly-s-playmates:
Amy Brooks continued her tales of Polly with a children's story set around Sherwood Hall, which one dreamy girl in the opening chapter wishes could be an enchanted castle. Polly visits Rose, spends time at the shore and in a studio, and shares the days with Gwen and Gyp.

The chapter list runs from a scene in the garden and a little hero to a village nuisance, a small green door, and Gyp running away. Each short episode turns on friendship, small dangers, and making things right. It suits young readers who like mild adventure close to home.
principles-of-home-decoration-with-pract:
Candace Wheeler, a leading figure in American design, published her guide to decorating the home with Doubleday, Page and Company of New York in 1903. She treats decoration as an art and asks how a house gains character rather than mere fashion.

Chapters cover colour as both science and influence, the law of fitness, builders' houses, kitchens and their walls, and the care of walls, ceilings, and floors. A frontispiece shows a dining room in a cottage at Onteora. Homeowners get plain rules, named examples, and a stress on health, light, and harmony.
prose-fancies:
Richard Le Gallienne gathered short prose pieces in a London book of 1894, printed with a portrait of the author and a tender dedication to his late wife. The pieces are brief, bright essays and sketches rather than formal studies.

Titles include A Spring Morning, A Conspiracy of Silence, Life in Inverted Commas, Poets and Publishers, Apollo's Market, Anarchy in a Library, and a plea for the old playgoer. Le Gallienne writes on books, love, fame, and the trade of writing with a light, musical touch. Readers get a sample of 1890s literary charm at its most polished.
prose-fancies-second-series:
Richard Le Gallienne followed his first set of prose sketches with a second series printed at London and Chicago in 1896, dedicated to Maggie Le Gallienne. A poem at the front calls the poet's gifts nothing but words, forty thousand of them, offered with love.

Named pieces include A Seventh-Story Heaven, Spring by Parcel Post, The Great Merry-Go-Round, The Burial of Romeo and Juliet, Variations upon Whitebait, and The Answer of the Rose. The manner stays light and fanciful, turning small scenes into short meditations. Readers get more of Le Gallienne's graceful 1890s essay style.
questionable-amusements-and-worthy-subst:
Questionable Amusements and Worthy Substitutes, by the Reverend J. M. Judy, was issued at Chicago by the Western Methodist Book Concern in 1904, printed for a friend of the author rather than sent to a publisher. George H. Trever's introduction, dated at Whitewater, Wisconsin, on March 2, 1904, commends the papers to young people of the Epworth Leagues.

Trever argues that the church has said "Don't" quite enough without offering something better in place of the amusements it bans. Judy, a Northwestern and Garrett trained preacher who had served on the frontier and among foreign-born people, writes to fill the emptied house with pure occupants before worse spirits rush in.
questionable-shapes:
Questionable Shapes, by W. D. Howells, published in May 1903, gathers three tales of the supernatural: His Apparition, The Angel of the Lord, and Though One Rose from the Dead. Howells treats ghostly visits with a calm, probing realism rather than stage fright.

The first tale opens on Hewson, who has been confronted with an apparition and finds himself oddly unafraid. His hair did not rise, and his trouble comes later, when sense and reason fight over whether the thing happened at all. He notes the details with care, in a central calm amid whirling feelings, and the tale turns on that conflict.
quotes-and-images-from-celebrated-crimes:
Quotes and Images from Celebrated Crimes selects from Alexandre Dumas's Celebrated Crimes, a set of true-crime histories that, the opening note argues, put most romantic novels in the shade. Dumas, it says, was a novelist who knew his history and researched his early works with care, and these histories range over many centuries and many lands.

The contents name the cases. The Borgias and the Cenci head the list. The Massacres of the South and Mary Stuart follow. Karl Ludwig Sand and Urbain Grandier appear. So do Nisida, Derues, and Joan of Naples. The Man in the Iron Mask is treated in an essay, not the novel. Martin Guerre, Ali Pacha, and Murat come next. The Marquise de Brinvilliers closes the list.
raffles: Raffles, by E. W. Hornung, is shown here in the Dover edition of 2018, described on its copyright page as an unabridged republication of The Amateur Cracksman, published by Charles Scribner's Sons in 1909. The catalogue data class the book with jewel thieves and criminals in England. The contents begin with The Ides of March, A Costume Piece, Gentlemen and Players, Le Premier Pas, Wilful Murder, and Nine Points of the Law.
raggedy-andy-stories:
Raggedy Andy Stories, written and illustrated by Johnny Gruelle and published by Little Simon, introduces the little rag brother of Raggedy Ann. The book opens with a letter dated at Gainesville, Florida, on January 8, 1919, addressed to Gruelle at the P. F. Volland Company in Chicago.
