The writer tells how she bought a Raggedy Ann book and doll, read the introduction, and then climbed to her attic for an old trunk. The doll she sends Gruelle had been her mother's. It was treasured and kept, then given to her. The two of them, she writes, often went out under the arbor. They had their little cry together there. They went when the world seemed blue.
raggedy-ann-stories:
Raggedy Ann Stories, written and illustrated by Johnny Gruelle and published by Little Simon, opens with a preface and dedication addressed to the doll herself. Gruelle keeps the old rag doll propped against the telephone on his desk, the same Raggedy Ann his mother played with as a child.

She is a trifle loppy and loose-jointed. She has shoe-button eyes. Her face is smeared with chocolate from a tea party. Her smile is painted on, so that it never fades. Mice have nibbled her and nested in her cotton stuffing. Yet she smiles as broadly as ever. Gruelle credits her with fifty-nine years of wisdom on kindness and patience.
ralph-granger-s-fortunes: Ralph Granger's Fortunes, by William Perry Brown, illustrated by W. H. Fry, was published by the Saalfield Publishing Company in 1902. Only the title page and contents are shown. The chapters carry Ralph far from home. They start with Ending the Feud and his grandfather's house. Moonshiners and his first railroad ride follow. He reaches Columbia and Savannah. Then he goes aboard the Curlew to sea. A brush in the wilderness comes nearing the Gold Coast. The story goes up a river. At last he is left behind.
rataplan-a-rogue-elephant-and-other-stor:
Rataplan, A Rogue Elephant and Other Stories, by Ellen Velvin, F.Z.S., author of Tales Told at the Zoo, with illustrations by Gustave Verbeek, is a book of animal stories for young people. Velvin dedicates it to Grace Gallatin Thompson Seton, whose help and loyal friendship met her as a stranger in a new country.

Her preface argues that young people have always loved animal tales, and that such stories teach humane feeling. There are heroes and tyrants among animals as among men, she writes, and their lives are pastorals or tragedies. She consulted the best authorities, she says, and hopes also to cure the grave blunders children make in caring for their pets.
readings-in-the-history-of-education-med:
Arthur O. Norton, an assistant professor at Harvard, gathered source readings on the rise of universities in the Middle Ages. Harvard University published the book at Cambridge in 1909. His contents open with an introduction and a chapter on the revival of learning in the twelfth century.

Readings then follow teachers and students of that age, with Abelard and John of Salisbury as named examples. Later parts take up the new method of study and the new fields: Aristotle, Roman law, canon law, theology, and medicine. A closing section explains university privileges, from royal protection and tax relief to the right to suspend lectures and to teach anywhere.
records-of-journeys-to-venice-and-the-lo: A publisher's header is all that opens this record, and it presents the work as memoirs of journeys to Venice by Albrecht Durer. The header calls the item the first in a series by that artist. No title page follows it in these pages, and no page of the journeys themselves is shown. A reader can take from it only the artist's name and the kind of work promised. No scene or date from Durer's travels is shown.
reginald-in-russia-and-other-sketches:
Saki followed his first Reginald book with this set of sketches, first published by Methuen of London in 1910. The title piece sends Reginald to Russia; other sketches stand beside it, though their names fall beyond the pages shown. Praise for the earlier book fills the front matter, quoted from the Morning Post, the Athenaeum, and other papers.

The Morning Post finds reason in Reginald's playful paradoxes, while warning that no rich old uncle should take him as a model of conduct. The Athenaeum likens the book, for its steady brilliance, to a Brock's Benefit fireworks show at the Crystal Palace. The Queen calls Saki one of the lightest humorists of the day.
report-of-commemorative-services-with-th:
The Diocese of Connecticut published this report of the services marking the Seabury centenary, covering the years 1883 to 1885. The services marked the centenaries of Bishop Seabury's election and of his consecration. Sermons and addresses from the services fill the book, with an appendix.

Contents list a service of thanksgiving at Woodbury on March 27, 1883, with full addresses by Bishop Williams and Dr. Beardsley. The consecration centenary brought a diocesan convention in 1884 and a service at Hartford on November 14 that year. Dr. Tatlock's address, the bishop's reply, and further sermons follow in the list.
reprinted-pieces:
Short prose pieces are reprinted here from a 1905 Chapman and Hall edition, opening with The Long Voyage. In it the narrator loves, when wind and sleet drive against dark windows, to sit by the fire with books of voyage and travel. Such books, he says, have drawn his mind since his earliest childhood. No author's name is printed on the opening pages.

The contents range widely: The Begging-letter Writer, A Child's Dream of a Star, and pieces on English and French watering-places. The Detective Police and three detective anecdotes follow, with On Duty with Inspector Field. A Walk in a Workhouse, a fairy tale called Prince Bull, and sketches named Our School, Our Vestry, and Our Bore fill out the set.
rewards-and-fairies:
Rudyard Kipling mixes tales and songs in this book, opening with A Charm that begins, Take of English earth as much as either hand may rightly clutch. An introduction follows, then a tale called Cold Iron. Stories and poems alternate through the contents, as in his earlier books of the same kind.

Gloriana, The Wrong Thing, and Marklake Witches stand among the tales, with King Henry VII and the Shipwrights for period color. The Way through the Woods, Brookland Road, and The Knife and the Naked Chalk carry the English countryside through the set. The poem If— stands in the list, beside Brother Square-Toes, Simple Simon, and The Thousandth Man.
riders-of-the-silences:
Max Brand published this western novel in 1919, opening with a prologue on legend in the Great West before the century's turn. Fabled gunmen, tireless stallions, and glorious women fill those tales, Brand writes. The greatest legend of all tells of Red Pierre and the phantom gunfighter McGurk, two men alike in one trait: each was unbeatable.

Fate brings them clashing together, thunder to thunder, on a trail from the northern wastes of Canada to the mountains of the Far West. Chapter one turns to Father Anthony, an inspector of Jesuit houses across Canada. His kindliness beams like a fire men warm their hands at, though his eyes miss nothing.
rienzi-the-last-of-the-roman-tribunes:
Sir Edward Bulwer Lytton built this historical novel on Cola di Rienzi, the last of the Roman tribunes. A stanza from Byron's Childe Harold heads the book, calling Rienzi the friend of Petrarch and the hope of Italy. A passage from Gibbon follows, on the revolution that astonished Europe.

Lytton dedicated the fruits, gathered on the soil of Italian fiction, to Alessandro Manzoni, as to the genius of the place. The dedication is dated at London on December 1, 1835. A second dedication, to his mother, was prefixed to the first collected edition of his works in 1840, thanking her for the pains she spent on his education.
right-ho-jeeves:
P. G. Wodehouse's comic novel is dedicated to Raymond Needham, K.C., with affection and admiration, and is told by Bertie in his own voice. He opens by asking Jeeves if he may speak frankly, then stops himself: he has gone off the rails. His problem, he explains, is always where to begin a story.

The case he reports involves Gussie Fink-Nottle, Madeline Bassett, his cousin Angela, Aunt Dahlia, Uncle Thomas, young Tuppy Glossop, and the cook Anatole. It began, he thinks, with his visit to Cannes. There he met the Bassetts and bought a white mess jacket, and Angela met someone who set the whole tangle moving.
riley-child-rhymes:
James Whitcomb Riley wrote these rhymes for children, with Hoosier pictures by Will Vawter, under copyrights running from 1890 to 1905. He inscribes rhymes and pictures alike to the children everywhere, with hale affection and abiding faith. A frontispiece shows children listening to the witch-tales that Annie tells.

A verse at the front gives the child his wealth: the bird-songs of the hills and the laughter of April rills. Morning's dew and the rainbow's gold are his as well. The contents run in alphabetical order, opening with At Aunty's House, The Bear Story, The Boy Lives on Our Farm, The Boys' Candidate, and The Bumblebee.
riley-farm-rhymes:
James Whitcomb Riley inscribed these farm rhymes, with all grateful esteem, to the good old-fashioned people. A long June poem stands before the contents, thick with the sounds of the country. The thicket boils with June, from the cricket's rattle to the yellowhammer's tune, and the catbird and chipmunk add their music.

The contents gather The Brook Song, A Canary at the Farm, and The Clover. A Country Pathway, Griggsby's Station, and How John Quit the Farm give the set its stories. June and Knee-Deep in June are both listed, beside Old-Fashioned Roses, Old October, and Old Winters on the Farm. No year is printed on the opening pages.
rio-grande-s-last-race-and-other-verses:
A. B. Paterson gathered these Australian verses in the original Sydney edition of 1902, as its title page notes. A signed note says the pieces had appeared in papers around the world. Rio Grande ran in London, most of the war verses in Bloemfontein, and others in Sydney, in Paterson's own account.

The contents print each poem's first line beside its title. Rio Grande's Last Race opens from what Macpherson told, and With the Cattle begins with drought on field and flock. Mulga Bill's Bicycle starts from the cycling craze at Eaglehawk. The Pearl Diver, Saltbush Bill's Gamecock, Hay and Hell and Booligal, and Father Riley's Horse fill out a bush and war set.
rockefeller-reminiscences:
John Rockefeller published his Random Reminiscences of Men and Events in 1909. The founder of Standard Oil was then the first billionaire in American history. Critics expected a defense; instead he offered calm reflections on business and giving.

Rockefeller tells of his start as a bookkeeper, his early oil ventures, and the building of a vast company. He shares his rules: keep accounts, respect partners, and give while you live. Friends, rivals, and church life appear between the business chapters. The book is short and guarded, yet it remains the richest American of his age speaking in his own words.
rolling-stones:
O. Henry's stories are gathered in this book of 1919, fronted by his last photograph, taken by W. M. Vanderwayde of New York in 1909. A sonnet in dialect, written by James Whitcomb Riley in the character of Sherrard Plummer, praises O. Henry as chief of all delight. An introduction follows it in the contents.

The stories named include The Dream, A Ruler of Men, and The Atavism of John Tom Little Bear. Helping the Other Fellow, The Marionettes, and The Marquis and Miss Sally come next. A Fog in Santone, Sound and Fury, Tictocq, and Tracked to Doom keep the set's pace. An Unfinished Christmas Story and The Unprofitable Servant close the list shown.
romance-two-lectures:
Sir Walter Raleigh, professor of English literature at Oxford, lectured on romance at Princeton on May 4 and 6, 1915, under the Louis Clark Vanuxem Foundation. Princeton University Press published the two lectures in October 1916. The first, The Origin of Romance, opens on the fifty years from 1783 to 1832.

Between Pitt's taking office and the passing of the Reform Bill, Raleigh notes, English letters crowded with life. Blake's Poetical Sketches and Crabbe's Village opened the period, and Scott's death closed it. One strain in that plenty gave the age its name, the Romantic Revival. The name itself, he argues, holds a theory of art.
rosa-mundi-and-other-stories:
Ethel M. Dell, author of The Way of an Eagle and The Knave of Diamonds, gathers four tales in this book, opening with the title story, Rosa Mundi. A Debt of Honour follows it in sixteen chapters, from Hope and the Magician to The Coming of Hope. A magician thus stands at that tale's opening and its close.

Its middle chapters name a visitor, a friend in need, her natural protector, and her enemy, then a race and its penalty. The Deliverer, in twelve chapters, moves from a promise of marriage and a grievous wound to Afterwards — Love. The Prey of the Dragon and The Secret Service Man close the set of romances.
russian-rambles:
Isabel F. Hapgood, author of The Epic Songs of Russia, wrote Russian Rambles, issued at Boston and New York in 1895. She gives the notes of her stay to Russia and her Russian friends. She notes that many of her most cherished moments are not recorded in the pages. They stay deeply printed on her heart. In the preface she says the countless questions put to her since her return to America showed her a gap. For all that has been written about Russia, she argues, the common incidents of everyday life are not known. Where known, they are known so poorly that any account of them is a travesty, a false copy.

As proof she takes apart a praised American book of the past two years. Its hero skates to church, gazes down a long aisle, climbs to an organ gallery, and sings a solo with trills.
sacred-and-profane-love-a-novel-in-three:
Arnold Bennett published Sacred and Profane Love in 1905, shaping the story as a novel told in three episodes. He dedicated the book to his friend Eden Phillpotts, praising the dignity of his aims as a novelist. A line from Guy de Maupassant about the kiss, passed down through the ages, stands at the front.

The three parts carry the titles In the Night, Three Human Hearts, and The Victory. Part one opens with the narrator confessing that love has filled his thoughts for years. By love he means a strong, bodily passion that takes over the soul and gives life its purpose. Everything before such a passion, he suggests, shrinks beside it.
sagittulae-random-verses:
E. W. Bowling, rector of Houghton Conquest and late fellow of St. John's College, Cambridge, wrote Sagittulae, Random Verses, issued in London and Cambridge in 1885. A Latin motto asks the kind reader to forgive the jest if it is sweet to play the fool in season. In his preface Bowling says a very few of the pieces appeared in Punch. The rest were written over the past twenty-five years under the signature Arculus, for The Eagle, the magazine of St. John's College. He hopes old college friends will welcome their return.

Bowling expects the general reader to think some apology is due for verses of so crude and trivial a character. The smallest of bows, he answers, should sometimes be unstrung. If his little arrows are flimsy and light, he trusts they will wound no one. The title itself plays on that image of small arrows.
saxe-holm-s-stories-first-series:
Helen Hunt Jackson published Saxe Holm's Stories, first series, in 1873, gathering six tales in one volume. The set opens with Draxy Miller's Dowry and also holds The Elder's Wife, Whose Wife Was She?, and Esther Wynn's Love-Letters. Two more pieces, The One-Legged Dancers and How One Woman Kept Her Husband, complete the list.

The first tale starts with a christening gone wrong. Reuben Miller, a bookish and lonely villager, names his baby girl Darachsa after a Polish heroine from a novel he loved as a boy. The doctor scoffs at the strange name, the nurse predicts bad luck, and the whole village talks. Jackson then sketches the Millers' shrinking fortunes and a wife too gentle to steady her husband.
scattergood-baines:
Clarence Budington Kelland wrote Scattergood Baines. Kelland had earlier written The High Flyers and Sudden Jim. Fourteen chapters follow one man through a small valley town, and most chapter heads begin with what Scattergood does next. He meddles in matchmaking in one tale, borrows a grandmother in another, and puts money into salvation in a third.

The first chapter treats his arrival in Coldriver Valley as local legend, retold at the post office and the grocery. Story says the very fat newcomer walked twenty-four miles from the railroad, sank onto the porch at Locker's grocery near sundown, and pulled off his shoes. There he sat, in no hurry to greet the watching men, content to rest his bare feet.
school-church-and-home-games: George O. Draper, secretary for health and recreation in the county work department of the International Committee of Young Men's Christian Associations, compiled School, Church, and Home Games. The rural edition, headed Community Recreation, was issued in New York in 1923 by Association Press. Draper gives the book to his father, Herbert Edward Draper, whose happy contact with country folks through county duties won their esteem.
scientific-essays-and-lectures:
Scientific Lectures and Essays, as the heading in the pages shown here orders the title, lists six pieces. They are On Bio-Geology, The Study of Natural History, and Superstition Science. They also include Thoughts in a Gravel-Pit, How to Study Natural History, and The Natural Theology of the Future. No author is named in the portion shown here. The first address, On Bio-Geology, opens with doubt. The speaker is not sure the subject of the address is rightly chosen. The speaker is not sure, either, that a question of mere natural history should not have been postponed.

In place of natural history, the speaker longed to address scientific men on questions of life and death forced upon them by the awful warning of an illustrious personage's illness.
scottish-sketches:
Amelia E. Barr gathered these Scottish tales in a volume issued in New York by Dodd, Mead and Company in 1898. The stories first carry an 1883 copyright from the American Tract Society. Each tale turns on faith, money, pride, or family duty in Scottish homes.

Contents list six pieces, among them Crawford's Sair Strait, James Blackie's Revenge, and Andrew Cargill's Confession. The opening tale watches Alexander Crawford pore over his locked ledger book, proud of the thousands of pounds it records. Plain moral conflict drives the plots, and Barr writes for readers who liked earnest fiction with a clear lesson.
sea-power-and-other-studies:
Admiral Sir Cyprian Bridge collected twelve essays on naval war and naval history under this title. Bridge had placed ten of the pieces before in journals and reference works, among them the Encyclopaedia Britannica, the Times, and the Cornhill Magazine. Two key essays came by leave of the Britannica's owners.

Topics run from command of the sea and the press gang to planned invasions of the British Isles. Bridge also writes on Queen Elizabeth's seamen, Nelson at Trafalgar, and how a fleet stays fed and linked at sea. Senior officers and keen lay readers alike get a clear view of British sea strength.
selected-english-letters-xv-xix-centurie:
M. Duckitt and H. Wragg arranged this gathering of English letters from the fifteenth through the nineteenth centuries, issued in 1913. Writers range from Sir Thomas More and Francis Bacon to John Milton and Dorothy Osborne. Each entry in the contents pairs a writer with the person addressed and a hint of the matter.

More writes to his daughter Margaret Roper from prison, and she writes back. Roger Ascham writes to Lady Jane Grey, while John Evelyn writes to Samuel Pepys in old age. Private voices across four hundred years show how English men and women handled love, duty, faith, and daily life.
selected-polish-tales:
Else C. M. Benecke and Marie Busch translated this set of Polish tales, first issued in the World's Classics in 1921. Busch's preface tells how Benecke left rough drafts of Polish stories at her death. Busch then edited the drafts and saw them into print, as her friend had wished.

Stories include The Outpost by Boleslaw Prus and tales by Adam Szymanski, Stefan Zeromski, and Wladyslaw St. Reymont. Village life, soldiers, and plain folk under hard rule fill the pages. English readers gained a path into Polish fiction through two women who had already brought two tale volumes to Oxford readers.
selections-from-erasmus-principally-from:
P. S. Allen chose these passages from Erasmus, drawn mostly from his letters, for readers starting Latin. Allen's preface praises the ease and direct force of Erasmus's Latin, a living tongue for its writer. Allen adjusts some spelling and grammar toward classical norms for learners.

Allen chose passages that light up English life in a rich age, through the eyes of a keen guest. Kings and wars matter less here than what great and small men did and thought in private. Students read real letters on daily events and grave themes, and they meet the age from inside its own correspondence.
sermons-for-the-times:
Twenty-one sermons fill this volume, opening with Fathers and Children and ranging across Salvation, Justification by Faith, Providence, and The True Gentleman. No preacher is named on the pages at hand. The first sermon takes its text from the close of Malachi, the last words of the Old Testament.

The preacher stresses the weight of that placement: no prophet would rise among the Jews for four hundred years after Malachi, until John the Baptist came. Hearts of fathers and children turning to each other form the theme. Later sermons treat public spirit, shame, forgiveness, and England's strength in the same direct pulpit voice.
sermons-on-the-card-and-other-discourses:
Hugh Latimer preached these discourses, issued by Cassell in 1883 with an opening life of the preacher. Latimer, a farmer's son born about 1491 at Thurcaston in Leicestershire, went to Clare College, Cambridge, at fourteen. He first argued for the Pope's power against the new teaching.

Thomas Bilney visited Latimer's rooms and won him to the reformers' faith, a debt Latimer never forgot. With homely force Latimer then preached his new convictions to court and country. The famed card sermon stands among these pieces, where plain speech and sharp wit press hearers toward honest, godly living.
sermons-preached-at-brighton-third-serie:
Frederick W. Robertson, late minister of Trinity Chapel in Brighton, preached these sermons between 1847 and 1853. Kegan Paul issued this third series in a new edition in London in 1884. The book is dedicated to the congregation that heard the sermons across those six years.

The first sermon was preached on April 28, 1850. Robertson's preaching drew crowds for its fresh thought, warm feeling, and bold handling of doubt and duty. These printed recollections of spoken sermons let later readers hear a voice that had moved Brighton deeply before its early silencing by death, and they still repay close reading today.
sesame-and-lilies: John Ruskin's famous 1865 lectures: "Of Kings' Treasuries" on the value of books and reading, and "Of Queens' Gardens" on women's education and influence. Eloquent, earnest, and very Victorian, they shaped how generations thought about literature and womanhood. Ruskin's moral passion burns on every page.
seven-english-cities: W. D. Howells wrote this illustrated travel book on seven English cities. The pages at hand show the title page plus a priced list of Howells's other travel and comment books, among them Roman Holidays, London Films, and Certain Delightful English Towns. No contents list, city names, or chapter text appears in these opening pages. Which seven cities Howells visits, and what he finds in each, cannot be stated fairly from the front pages alone.
seven-icelandic-short-stories:
The Ministry of Education at Reykjavik issued these seven Icelandic tales in English, with an opening essay by Steingrimur J. Porsteinsson. The first tale, The Story of Audun and the Bear, comes from an unknown writer of the thirteenth century, in English by G. Turville-Peire. Six modern tales follow.

Writers include Einar H. Kvaran, Gunnar Gunnarsson, and Halldor Kiljan Laxness, with tales dated from 1905 to 1927. Named translators carried each piece into English. Farm life, the sea, and emigration to a new Iceland fill the pages, giving foreign readers a compact taste of Iceland's fiction old and new.
seven-o-clock-stories:
Robert Gordon Anderson wrote these bedtime tales for children, first told to Jean and Malcolm, to whom the book is given. Stories are grouped by nights, from a first night with three happy children onward. Toymen, willow whistles, and scarecrows fill the early evenings.

Later nights bring fairy tales billed as true, a mother hen against a robber hawk, and the happy close of an oriole's tale. Each short piece fits a single sitting at a child's bedside. Anderson writes in a warm, plain voice, with farm and garden life close at hand and a gentle moral tucked inside the fun.
shakespeare-study-programs-the-comedies:
Charlotte Porter and Helen A. Clarke built these study programs on Shakespeare's comedies, issued in Boston by Richard G. Badger. The programs first ran in the journal Poet Lore and sold out their back numbers. Fresh programs join revised old ones in this book form, by steady demand.

Contents run from The Comedy of Errors and The Two Gentlemen of Verona through The Taming of the Shrew, Love's Labour's Lost, and Much Ado About Nothing. References point to Porter's First Folio edition. Clubs and classes get a guided path play by play, shaped by two editors deep in Shakespeare publishing.
shanty-the-blacksmith-a-tale-of-other-ti:
Mrs. Sherwood published this tale of other times in 1852. The tale opens in the last century, before revolt changed the manners of English forefathers. On the wild border ground between England and Scotland stands an old castle, shrunken to one tower and a few rooms within high walls.

Its moat has dried, though a small stream still threads the hollow below. The house, called Dymock's Tower for its one barrier and its family name, once sheltered freebooters who plundered Scotland. Sherwood sets a blacksmith's tale amid that stern past, where faith and duty test plain folk.
shearing-in-the-riverina-new-south-wales:
Rolf Boldrewood wrote this account of sheep shearing on Anabanco station in the Riverina district of New South Wales. Manager Hugh Gordon speaks the opening words: shearing starts tomorrow. That plain news stirs a large cast awaiting what Boldrewood calls an industrial drama.

Pages recall when a low sand hill looked over grey plains with a few pine huts and a cattle yard. Two or three thousand cattle then grazed the run, moving to mountain pasture when swamps dried. Sheep and shearing changed that spare world. Readers get a close, felt picture of station work in early Australian pastoral life.
short-cruises:
W. W. Jacobs gathered twelve tales in this set, with drawings by Will Owen. Titles include The Changeling, Alf's Dream, The Test, and A Love-Knot. Picture captions promise swapped babies, sharp wives, and lodgers defended against all comers in Jacobs's dockside world.

Sailors, mates, cooks, and cunning landsmen scheme and blunder through the tales. A gold watch lends a man false substance in one caption; in another, a trunk's corner cracks a gesturing head. Jacobs packs each short cruise with a neat turn, told in plain speech that hides fine craft.
short-stories-for-english-courses:
Rosa M. R. Mikels, a teacher at Shortridge High School in Indianapolis, edited this set of tales for English classes, with an opening essay and notes. A preface asks why children's reading must stay bound to old classics. Teachers, Mikels reports, increasingly seek fresh tales with real craft.

Contents join Henry van Dyke and Joel Chandler Harris with Poe's Gold Bug, O. Henry's Ransom of Red Chief, and Stevenson's Markheim. Kipling, Twain, Stockton, Galsworthy, and Wharton all appear. Study helps frame each tale: what a short story must do, and how a class may use the book to learn it.
shorter-prose-pieces:
Oscar Wilde's shorter prose fills this volume, transcribed from a 1920 Methuen printing. Contents lead with a set of phrases and philosophies for the young, dated December 1894. Paradox rules there: duty, art, and wickedness all get turned on their heads in single bright lines.

Later pieces treat Mrs. Langtry on stage, slaves of fashion, and women's dress, with sharper essays on dress reform and costume. An American invasion piece and sermons in stones at Bloomsbury follow. Readers meet Wilde the journalist and wit, arguing that style outranks sincerity in small things and charm can carry a serious point.
sights-from-a-steeple-from-twice-told-ta:
Nathaniel Hawthorne wrote this sketch for his Twice-Told Tales, viewing a town from a church steeple's height. The watcher sighs that he has climbed high for small reward, with earth far below and heaven still far beyond. Clouds in the golden west gather like black air ships freighted with storm.

Thunder rolls from that sky fleet while nearer vapor offers rest to tired pilgrims of the air. Fair spirits might sport among those clouds, the watcher dreams. Hawthorne turns a steeple perch into a meditation on distance, longing, and the small dramas of a town seen from above.
sketches-and-studies:
Nathaniel Hawthorne gathered four pieces in this set, led by his campaign life of Franklin Pierce. A preface owns that Hawthorne, no politician, would not by choice have taken up a party biography. His edge lay elsewhere: he had known Pierce early, when character could be read with clear accuracy.

Chiefly About War Matters, Alice Doane's Appeal, and The Ancestral Footstep complete the set. The Pierce life served a presidential canvass, work far from Hawthorne's tastes, he grants. Readers meet the romancer as biographer of his college friend, judging later acts by the young man he once knew well.
sketches-and-studies-in-italy-and-greece:
John Addington Symonds wrote these travel essays, reissued by John Murray in London in 1914 as the first series of a rearranged set. Horatio F. Brown's note, written at Venice in June 1898, explains the plan: three older travel books were merged, with essays reordered by place for travelers' ease.

Nothing else changed, Brown states, and the joint title departs least from Symonds's own phrasing. Contents open with love of the Alps, winter nights at Davos, and Bacchus in Graubunden. Provence towns, the Cornice, Ajaccio, and Lombard vignettes follow in this opening series.

John Addington Symonds wrote these travel essays, issued by John Murray in London in 1914 as the second series of his Italy and Greece set. A first edition from Smith, Elder in October 1898 had gone through many reprintings by 1914. Ravenna opens the volume, with Rimini and May in Umbria close behind.

The palace of Urbino, Vittoria Accoramboni, Parma, Canossa, and Fornovo follow. Florence and the Medici anchor the later pages. Essays on Tuscan songs, Renaissance verse, Poliziano's Orfeo, and eight sonnets of Petrarch close the set. Place and poem share Symonds's rich attention throughout.
sketches-of-young-couples:
Sketches of Young Couples, drawn from the 1903 Chapman and Hall edition of Sketches by Boz, sorts wedded pairs into comic types. The contents name the Young Couple, the Formal Couple, the Loving Couple, and the pair who dote on their children. Later sketches cover the Cool Couple, the Plausible Couple, and the Old Couple, then a short close.

The book opens with a mock plea to the bachelors and widowers of England. It jokes that Queen Victoria has told her council she will wed Prince Albert of Saxe Coburg and Gotha. Since the year is a leap year, the plea warns, any lady may propose, and a man who says no owes her a fine silk or satin dress.
smith-and-the-pharaohs-and-other-tales:
H. Rider Haggard groups six tales in Smith and the Pharaohs and Other Tales. The contents name Magepa the Buck, The Blue Curtains, Little Flower, Only a Dream, and Barbara Who Came Back. Barbara's tale runs through heads on a rectory blind, a New Year feast, an Aunt Maria, a wedding, a parting, a sin, and an act that makes amends.

The title tale opens with a jab at men of science who claim to know all worth knowing about man. Such men, the narrator says, trace man's bones and shape from a far past and treat his hopes of a next life as fear of death. Man, in their account, is an animal ruled by his setting, like cattle that take the red hue of Devon soil.
snow-flakes-from-twice-told-tales:
Nathaniel Hawthorne watches a storm begin in Snow-Flakes, a sketch from Twice Told Tales. A few light flakes hang in the cold gray air of morning, now near the ground, now whirled aloft. These are not the big, wet flakes that melt at a touch and warn of rain. A true winter storm, he judges, is on its way.

The two or three folk on the walks wear a blue-nosed look of endurance. By night, Hawthorne expects, the street and the small garden will lie heaped with drifts. The soil has been frozen for weeks and can bear the load. All the snow yet fallen, heaped up, would scarce match a grave's small hill, yet great changes come by just such soft and stealthy steps.
snubby-nose-and-tippy-toes: Laura Rountree Smith wrote Snubby Nose and Tippy Toes, dated 1917 and 1922. The contents list ten chapters under the title head, then a run of chapters under More Cotton Tail Stories, with no heads to show their matter. The list of pictures quotes cries for camphor and smelling salts, a Grandpa Grumbles who had not seen Dr. Cottontail for two hundred years, Tippy Toes at the dishes, and a sweep with a long, fine tail.
sologub-the-old-house-and-other-tales:
Fyodor Sologub wrote short tales of fear, decay, and strange beauty, and English readers meet them here in translation. He was a leading Russian Symbolist, a writer drawn to dark and uncanny moods. Schoolrooms, homes, and quiet streets become uneasy places in his hands.

Horror in these stories rarely comes from monsters or gore. It grows out of cruel adults, trapped children, and minds that twist small harms into grand terrors. Sologub mixes pity with dread and finds a cold beauty in rot and failure. Readers who want Symbolist fiction at its darkest will find his voice sharp, elegant, and hard to forget.
some-christmas-stories:
Charles Dickens fills Some Short Christmas Stories with pieces first printed across the season years. The contents name A Christmas Tree, What Christmas Is as We Grow Older, and tales told by a poor relation, a child, and a schoolboy. Nobody's Story closes the list. The set is drawn from the 1911 Chapman and Hall Christmas Stories, Volume 1.

A Christmas Tree, dated 1850, watches glad children round a German tree set on a great round table. Small tapers light dolls hid in the green, real watches on twigs, and tin tables, chairs, beds, and clocks made at Wolverhampton. Broad-faced little men lift off their heads to show sugar-plums inside. Fiddles, drums, tambourines, boxes of all kinds, and bright trinkets for the elder girls crowd the boughs.
some-reminiscences:
Joseph Conrad calls Some Reminisces a little book born of a friend's hint, and of a bit of friendly pressure. In a familiar preface, he says men need small urging to talk of themselves, yet he fought the plan with spirit. The friend's voice held firm: you know, you really must. It was no argument, Conrad grants, but he gave in at once, for the force of a word is a real thing.

That force is his theme. He who would persuade should trust, not the right argument, but the right word, for sound has always had more power than sense. Words such as Glory and Pity, he says, shouted with heat and faith, have set whole nations moving by their sound alone. Give him the right word and the right accent, he writes, and he will move the world, as a writer dreams of doing.
some-short-stories-by-henry-james:
Henry James gathers five tales in Some Short Stories: Brooksmith, The Real Thing, The Story of It, Flickerbridge, and Mrs. Medwin. Brooksmith opens among the scattered friends of the late Mr. Oliver Offord. When they meet by chance, the narrator says, they share a hid sense of respect. To pass the house in Mansfield Street is to recall that Arcadia was there, and that Brooksmith once opened its door.

Offord was a retired envoy who lived on his pension and a bit of his own. Kept by ill health near his fireside, he loved to be found there from five each day by guests Brooksmith let up. Brooksmith, his butler, was also his closest friend, and stood to guests as a prime minister stands to a king's subjects. Offord had been, in far lands, the most winning Englishman any one had known, and guests who came once came again.
song-and-legend-from-the-middle-ages: Only the front matter of this file is present here. Its Project Gutenberg header names Song and Legend from the Middle Ages, by William D. McClintock and Porter Lander McClintock, as etext number 1893, issued in September 1999. No page of the collection itself follows in this record, so its chosen songs and tales cannot be listed or described from what is shown.
songs-of-travel-and-other-verses:
Robert Louis Stevenson wrote the verses in Songs of Travel and Other Verses. He wrote them at many times and places. Most came after his last parting from England in 1887. A note signed S. C. tells their fate. He sent the set home for printing months before his death. He had tried the poems in several orders. He had tried several names for them as well.

Songs and Notes of Travel was one such name. Posthumous Poems was an other. In the end he left naming and order to his editor. The plan is to add the set as Book III. Later issues of Underwoods will hold it so. For now the poems come out apart. Folk who hold Underwoods in its first form gain them here. The Vagabond leads the contents. Its first line gives the tone: give to me the life I love.
south-african-memories-social-warlike-sp: Lady Sarah Wilson wrote South African Memories, social, warlike, and sporting, from diaries written at the time. Edward Arnold printed the London book in 1909. Wilson gives it to the memory of her sister Georgiana, Countess Howe, whose work for the yeomanry hospitals in the South African war broke her health and led to her death. The contents open with a first voyage to South Africa and Cape Town, then Kimberley and the Jameson Raid and its fall-out.
south-sea-tales: Jack London's stories of the South Pacific: pearl divers, beachcombers, and traders living hard under the tropical sun. Drawn from his own sailing voyages, they mix adventure with a clear-eyed view of colonial exploitation. Vivid, salty, and unsentimental, they are among his finest short fiction.
southern-horrors-lynch-law-in-all-its-ph:
Ida B. Wells-Barnett wrote Southern Horrors: Lynch Law in All Its Phases, dated 1892, 1893, and 1894. Wells gives the pamphlet to the Afro-American women of New York and Brooklyn. Their race love, zeal, and free-handed work at Lyric Hall on October 5, 1892, she says, made its printing possible. A letter from Frederick Douglass stands at the front, dated from New York City, October 26, 1892.

Douglass thanks Wells for her faithful paper on the lynch wrong now dealt out to colored people in the South. No word, he writes, has matched it in power to convince, and his own word is feeble beside it. She gives what she knows from first-hand fact, with cool, pains-taking truth, and lets the bare facts speak. He calls her a brave woman who has done her people and his a service that can be neither weighed nor measured.
specimens-of-greek-tragedy-aeschylus-and:
Goldwin Smith turned Greek plays into English in Specimens of Greek Tragedy, dated 1893, taking his texts from Aeschylus and Sophocles. His preface traces Greek drama to the feast of Dionysus, god of wine, kept with dance, song, and spoken lines. The spoken part, done in character, grew into drama, and custom names Thespis as the chief author of that step. Dance and song stayed on as the Chorus.

Smith leans on Thirlwall, whom he calls still the soundest judge among Greek historians. Thirlwall traced the germ to great choral works that joined music and action to high verse in the Dorian cities. From that germ, by adding a player who took a part and shifted his mask, Thespis and those after him unfolded Attic tragedy. In the age of Pericles, Smith adds, drama became the branch of letters that marked the time.
squinty-the-comical-pig-his-many-adventu: Richard Barnum wrote Squinty, the Comical Pig: His Many Adventures, with pictures by Harriet H. Tooker, in the Kneetime Animal Stories. Barnum's other books in the set name Slicko the Jumping Squirrel, Mappo the Merry Monkey, Tum Tum the Jolly Elephant, and Don, a Runaway Dog, each at forty cents in 1915. The contents send Squinty to meet a dog, run away, get lost, get home, meet a boy, and go on a journey to learn a trick.
state-of-the-union-addresses:
John Adams gives four yearly addresses in one set, dated November 22, 1797, December 8, 1798, December 3, 1799, and November 11, 1800. Three stars part each address from the next. The first opens with a worry now past: Adams had feared that the catching sickness in Philadelphia would force Congress to meet at some other place.

To move would have cost much public trouble and coin, and added to the woes of a city whose suffering stirred all hearts. Adams put off his choice while tests were made of the sickness and its fall, and his hopes were met: Congress could sit at Philadelphia without risk to life or health. He still asks whether the law of 1794 should grant a power to put off a meeting in such a case.
stella-fregelius-a-tale-of-three-destini:
H. Rider Haggard wrote Stella Fregelius: A Tale of Three Destinies, first published in 1904, under a Latin motto on the glad man who has learned the causes of things. The contents open with Morris, Mary, and the Aerophone, then the colonel and some musings. Poor Porson, Mary preaching while the colonel holds his ground, and a proposal and a promise follow in the early heads.

Beaulieu, the sunk rocks and the singer, and Miss Fregelius herself carry the tale forward. A morning service, Mr. Layard's wooing, two questions and the answer, and the return of the colonel lead to a marriage and its wake. Stella's diary fills two chapters near the end, and heads named The Evil Gate, Stella Comes, and Dreams and the Sleep close the list. A dedication to John Berwick stands at the front.
stephen-archer-and-other-tales:
George MacDonald leads a set of tales with Stephen Archer. The Gifts of the Child Christ joins it in the contents. The History of Photogen and Nycteris stands there as well. The Butcher's Bills, Poet in a Storm, and If I Had a Father close the list. Stephen Archer keeps a shop in a London suburb. He sells stationery, books, and news there. Newspapers hang in a rack at his door.

The teller came once to test the shop's stock. He wanted many copies of one Shakespeare play at a penny each. Archer shook his head at the ask. He could not in conscience push such sales. That stand pleased the teller at once. Principle should rank above pence in such a man. His stock was all small religious books in gay bindings. A year later, the teller went in again. He scarce knew the man he found there.
stories-from-thucydides:
H. L. Havell retold Stories from Thucydides, opening with a line from Shakespeare's Henry IV about a kingdom sick with civil blows. The prologue recalls how Greece threw back Xerxes, then turns to the war between Athens and her rivals.

Havell calls that war cruel and wasting: it lasted twenty-seven years and broke up the Athenian empire, rising from envy of Athens's power. His contents pick the great episodes. They give the plague at Athens and the siege of Plataea. They give the capture of a hundred and twenty Spartans at Sphacteria. They close with Brasidas in Thrace and the Athenian venture in Sicily. The retelling makes a hard history readable.
stories-of-the-border-marches:
John Lang and Jean Lang wrote Stories of the Border Marches, printed at London in 1916. The book gathers tales and legends from the old border country between England and Scotland, a land of castles, raids, and ghosts.

The contents move from The White Lady of Blenkinsopp and the reiver Kinmont Willie to Grisell Home, a seventeenth-century heroine, and the days of the fifteen rising. Sunken treasure at Sewingshields Castle, the kidnapping of Lord Durie, the Laidley Worm of Spindleston Heugh, and the murder of Colonel Stewart of Hartrigge follow. Snowstorms, wraiths, and packmen round out a store of border lore told for younger readers.
stories-to-tell-children-fifty-four-stor:
Sara Cone Bryant's Stories to Tell Children, in the London printing by George G. Harrap and Company dated 1918, promises fifty-four stories with some suggestions for telling. Bryant also wrote How to Tell Stories to Children, and method matters as much as the tales here.

The opening parts advise the story-teller on method, offer two valuable types of story, and give a graded list of tales to act out and retell. A further piece argues for story-telling in the teaching of English, stressing oral work in the primary grades. Only then do the stories begin, opening with Two Little Riddles in Rhyme and The Little Yellow Tulip.
strawberry-acres:
Grace S. Richmond's Strawberry Acres, dated 1911, is a novel in two parts, Five Miles Out and The Lanes and the Acres. A dedication greets the owner of Grasslands, and the chapter heads trace a group leaving a cramped city apartment for a country place.

Part I moves from arrival and exploring through arguments and answers, telephones and tents, and days in the pine grove, until everybody is satisfied. Part II slows into the old garden, afternoon tea, and evenings in August, with chapters on problems and hearts and on Max compromising. The book is a cheerful country-house story about young people making a home and sorting out love.
struwwelpeter-merry-stories-and-funny-pi:
Heinrich Hoffman's Struwwelpeter first came out in German in 1844. An English version followed in 1848. The undated edition at hand was printed at New York by Frederick Warne and Company. It has color pictures on every page. It is a picture book of cautionary verses for children.

An opening poem promises good children pretty Christmas things and warns that naughty, romping girls and boys who tear their clothes will never see the book. Then come the cases: Shock-headed Peter, whose nails are never cut and whose hair is never combed, and Cruel Frederick, first of several children whose bad habits end badly and absurdly.
studies-of-trees:
J. J. Levison, a lecturer on ornamental and shade trees at the Yale University Forest School and forester to Brooklyn's park department, wrote Studies of Trees, first edition, first thousand, dated 1914. A Wordsworth motto on the frontispiece bids the reader come forth and let nature be the teacher.

The early chapters teach how to identify trees. First come the pines, spruce, and hemlock. Red cedar and arbor-vitae follow. Then come larch and cypress, and horsechestnut, ash, and maple. Later chapters tell trees by their form. Others tell them by bark or trunk. The oaks and chestnut close the set. Hickories, walnut, tulip tree, and many more follow. The book is a field guide built on close looking rather than book terms.
suburban-sketches:
William Dean Howells gathered Suburban Sketches from his early magazine work, drawing on the Boston suburbs he knew as a young editor. The contents list Mrs. Johnson, Doorstep Acquaintance, A Pedestrian Tour, By Horse-Car to Boston, A Day's Pleasure, A Romance of Real Life, Scene, Jubilee Days, Some Lessons from the School of Morals, and Flitting.

The picture captions hint at the humor: a woman lighting a potent pipe, a sweet young blonde arriving by most trains, children stalking ahead with shawls dragging. Howells watches neighbors, servants, and newcomers with a kind, exact eye, finding small dramas in doorsteps and horse-cars. The sketches mark his turn toward the realism he later made famous.
sunday-at-home-from-twice-told-tales:
Sunday at Home, a sketch from Nathaniel Hawthorne's Twice-Told Tales, watches a Sabbath morning from a chamber window facing a church steeple. Every summer Sunday the narrator thrusts back the curtain to see the sunrise steal down the spire opposite.

First the weathercock flashes, then light creeps over tower and dial until the steeple stands glowing while twilight still hides in the nooks of the buildings nearby. Hawthorne muses that living near a church breeds attachment to it, and that men personify its dim, calm spirit. The steeple seems a giant who cares for the great and small concerns of the whole town, and its hourly voice speaks a moral to the quiet street.
sunny-boy-and-his-playmates:
Ramy Allison White wrote Sunny Boy and His Playmates, copyrighted in 1922 by Barse and Company of New York and Newark, with illustrations by Howard L. Hastings. White had already written Sunny Boy in the Country, Sunny Boy at the Seashore, and Sunny Boy in School and Out.

The chapters follow a small boy through a year of play: learning to skate, finding Grandpa Horton, building a snow man on Court Hill, and meeting the Parkney family. Toys go to school, a blizzard catches the children out, and one chapter asks where the horse lived. The frontispiece shows a child carried ashore in someone's arms, promising the gentle rescues and small excitements of the series.
sunny-slopes:
Ethel Hueston wrote Sunny Slopes, a novel of a young minister's wife. The Bobbs-Merrill Company copyrighted it in 1917. Grosset and Dunlap reprinted it at New York. Arthur William Brown drew the illustrations. Hueston wrote it in memory of her husband and dedicated it to the St. Louis Presbytery.

The frontispiece caption catches the tone: a minister's wife, someone exclaims, who looks more like a little girl's baby doll. The chapters move through Mansers and a baby in business. They move through a woman in the church and a minister's son. They reach the heavy yoke. All along they follow a parsonage household. It faces parish duties, money troubles, and small triumphs. Hueston had already written Prudence of the Parsonage in the same warm vein.
superstition-in-all-ages:
Superstition in All Ages is the last will and testament of Jean Meslier. Meslier was a Roman Catholic priest. He served thirty years at Etrepigny in Champagne, France. He wholly gave up the dogmas he had preached. The work, dated 1732, was left to his parishioners and the world, to be published after his death under the title Common Sense.

Anna Knoop made the English version in 1878, and a life of Meslier by Voltaire stands at the front. Voltaire tells how Meslier rose through study to the priesthood. Meslier was born in 1678 at Mazerny. He was the son of a serge weaver. He lived with great austerity. He gave what was left of his salary each year to the poor. The testament argues his secret unbelief at full length.
symphonies-and-their-meaning-third-serie:
Philip H. Goepp's Symphonies and Their Meaning, Third Series: Modern Symphonies, dated 1913, guides concert listeners through the orchestral music of the nineteenth century and after. Goepp wrote the series to give hearers a story and a shape to hold onto while the music played.

The contents open with the symphony during the nineteenth century, then take up Berlioz and Liszt together. Berlioz's Romeo and Juliet dramatic symphony and the symphony on Dante's Divine Comedy get chapters of their own, followed by Liszt's symphonic poems: Les Preludes, Tasso, Mazeppa, and Battle of the Huns. Saint-Saens's Danse Macabre and other tone poems come next, and Cesar Franck's Symphony in D minor closes the list at hand.
tales-and-novels-volume-01-moral-tales:
Volume I of Maria Edgeworth's Tales and Novels, in ten volumes, holds her Moral Tales. Her preface quotes a remark of Johnson's. Merely to invent a story, he said, is no small effort. Edgeworth asks how much harder the work becomes for youth. Such stories must fit the early years of life.

Such fictions must show examples of virtue. They must not initiate the young reader into the ways of vice. They must speak in a style level to his capacity. Tedious detail and vulgar idiom are both barred. Aware of the difficulties, she solicits indulgence for errors that escaped her vigilance. The tales that follow were among the most trusted books of moral schooling in their day, teaching industry, honesty, and kindness through small domestic plots.
tales-and-novels-volume-02-popular-tales:
Volume II of Maria Edgeworth's Tales and Novels, printed in 1857, holds her Popular Tales, written for readers of the middle ranks rather than the nursery. Its long preface, in the voice of her father's household, makes a jesting defense of prefaces themselves.

Some author says a good book needs no apology, the preface begins, yet readers who are epicures rather than gluttons in literature like to see the bill of fare before they dine. Critics, too, are served by a plain statement of the writer's pretensions. The French call the art reading with the thumb; the English call it hunting a book. The tales themselves show tradesmen, servants, and strivers caught in schemes of sudden wealth, and teach prudence by letting folly run its course.
tales-from-two-hemispheres:
Hjalmar Hjorth Boyesen's Tales from Two Hemispheres is dated 1877. It collects six stories. The Man Who Lost His Name leads. The Story of an Outcast and A Good-for-Nothing follow. A Scientific Vagabond, Truls the Nameless, and Asathor's Vengeance complete the set. Boyesen, a Norwegian who made his life in America, draws on both his countries.

The first tale lands a young Norseman, Halfdan Bjerk, on the pier at Castle Garden on the second day of June in the eighteen-sixties. At the gate he is asked his name, birthplace, and how much money he has, and grows very frightened; asked his destination, he answers America, to the official's roar. The immigrant's first hour, timid smile and trembling hand, opens a book about names lost and remade between two worlds.
tales-of-troy-ulysses-the-sacker-of-citi:
Andrew Lang retold the Troy story for young readers in Tales of Troy: Ulysses the Sacker of Cities, printed by Longmans, Green, and Co. in 1912. Fourteen parts run from the boyhood of Ulysses through the theft of Helen to the fall of Troy and her rescue.

Lang begins on Ithaca, a small, rough isle west of Greece ruled by King Laertes, father of Ulysses. He notes its twin peaks, its herds, and why its men fought on foot with no chariots. Readers get the war's great turns in plain, brisk prose, with the horse trick, the death of Achilles, and the sack of the city held to the end.
tales-of-two-countries:
Alexander Kielland, a Norwegian writer, is the author of Tales of Two Countries, rendered from the Norwegian by William Archer with an opening essay by H. H. Boyesen. Ten tales are listed, among them Pharaoh, The Parsonage, The Peat Moor, Two Friends, and The Battle of Waterloo.

Boyesen recalls Kielland as a star pupil at the University of Norway in 1867, whose speech struck all who heard him. Ten years of law, trade, and town life in Stavanger then passed before his fame spread. Readers meet a sharp, poised voice, shaped by coast town life, in tales that move between Norway and the wider world.
tanakh-jps-1917-ecclesiastes:
Ecclesiastes is a wisdom book of the Hebrew Bible, presented in the Masoretic-based English of the Jewish Publication Society from 1917. Its speaker is Koheleth, named as son of David and king in Jerusalem, who weighs all work done under the sun.

Koheleth opens by calling all things vanity, a breath that soon is gone. Sun, wind, and rivers run their rounds and come back, yet no gain lasts and nothing is truly new. He tells how he sought truth by wisdom as king. Readers meet a grave, plain voice that tests wealth, toil, and joy, and finds life short and hard to grasp.
tanakh-jps-1917-i-chronicles:
First Chronicles is a history book of the Hebrew Bible, here in the Jewish Publication Society's 1917 English rendering. Rather than opening with a tale, it begins with long lists of names that trace lines of descent from Adam onward.

Adam, Seth, and Enosh lead to Noah and his sons Shem, Ham, and Japheth, whose lines spread across lands and peoples. Nimrod is marked as the first mighty one on earth, and Eber's sons mark a split of the earth. Readers who want the Bible's own map of kinship get it here, as tribe, king, and temple lines are set in order before the tales of David's reign unfold.
tanakh-jps-1917-ii-chronicles:
Second Chronicles is a history book of the Hebrew Bible, here in the Masoretic-based English issued by the Jewish Publication Society in 1917. It opens with Solomon, son of David, firm on his throne and raised high by God's favor.

Solomon leads all Israel to the high place at Gibeon, where the tent of meeting made in Moses' time still stands. There he offers a thousand burnt gifts on the bronze altar in one day. That night God tells him to ask for what he wants, and Solomon asks for wisdom to rule a vast people. Readers get the royal tale told with the temple at its heart, stressing worship, prayer, and each king's faith.
tanakh-jps-1917-judges:
Judges is a narrative book of the Hebrew Bible, presented in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society English Bible. It opens after the death of Joshua, when Israel asks who should first go up to fight the Canaanites.

Judah is named to lead and takes Simeon along, and the two tribes win a fight at Bezek. Their foe Adoni-bezek flees but is caught, and his thumbs and great toes are cut off. He admits the act mirrors his own past cruelty to seventy kings. Readers then enter a rough age of raids and rescues, where tribes rise and fall and heroes such as Deborah, Gideon, and Samson hold the stage in turn.
taras-bulba-and-other-tales:
Nikolai Vasilievich Gogol's Taras Bulba and Other Tales gathers his long Cossack tale with five shorter pieces, in a volume opened by John Cournos. Alongside Taras Bulba stand St. John's Eve, The Cloak, How the Two Ivans Quarrelled, The Mysterious Portrait, and The Calash.

Cournos calls Gogol, who lived from 1809 to 1852, the great enigma of Russian prose, a peer to Pushkin in verse. He credits Gogol's Cossack blood and Ukrainian myth with giving Russian fiction its path. Readers get wild steppe warfare in Taras Bulba, then tales that swing from folk horror to keen, sad fun at petty clerks and pride.
tarzan-of-the-apes:
Edgar Rice Burroughs launched his most famed hero in Tarzan of the Apes, a novel in twenty-eight chapters. A frame tale opens it: the narrator says he had the story from a man who had no right to tell it.

Wine loosened that man's tongue, and doubt then drove him to show written proof of the strange tale. What follows tracks a castaway child raised by apes, from his savage home and first light of learning to kingship among the apes. Later parts bring his own kind, lost treasure, and the edge of the wider world. Readers get the source novel for a century of Tarzan tales, told at a brisk clip.
tea-leaves: Tea Leaves is credited in its opening line to Francis Leggett and Co. No page of the book itself is present here. The full Project Gutenberg wrapper stands in its place. It gives notes on rights, reuse, and gifts to the Gutenberg fund. It also lists the states where gifts were then sought. No title page appears. No contents or text of the tea book appears.
the-30-000-bequest-and-other-stories: Mark Twain wrote The $30,000 Bequest and Other Stories. His real name was Samuel L. Clemens. The title tale heads the book in eight chapters. A Dog's Tale follows in three chapters. Was It Heaven? Or Hell? comes next in five chapters. More tales follow those three. The contents list gives chapter numbers only. It gives no hint of plot for any tale.
the-adventures-of-ann-stories-of-colonia:
Mary E. Wilkins wrote The Adventures of Ann, stories of colonial times drawn from old records and family lore, printed at Boston by D. Lothrop and Company with rights held in 1886. Four tales are listed: The Bound Girl, Deacon Thomas Wales' Will, The Adopted Daughter, and The Horse-House Deed.

The Bound Girl opens with a real indenture, kept in its old spelling and form. Margaret Burjust of Boston binds out her only daughter, Ann Ginnins, as an apprentice to Samuel Wales, a blacksmith of Braintree, and his wife. The term runs sixteen years, three months, and twenty-three days. Readers get colonial New England life rebuilt from paper trails, with bound service, wills, and deeds made into warm tales.
the-adventures-of-prince-lazybones-and-o: Mrs. W. J. Hays, author of Princess Idleways, wrote The Adventures of Prince Lazybones and Other Stories, printed by Harper and Brothers of New York and London in 1884 with pictures. The contents join the title tale to Phil's Fairies, Florio and Florella: A Christmas Fairy Tale, and Boreas Bluster's Christmas Present.
the-adventures-of-sherlock-holmes:
Arthur Conan Doyle wrote The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, the first set of Holmes short tales, with twelve cases listed in its contents. The set opens with A Scandal in Bohemia and runs through The Red-Headed League, The Five Orange Pips, The Speckled Band, and The Copper Beeches.

A Scandal in Bohemia starts with Watson's famed line that to Holmes she is always the woman, meaning Irene Adler. Watson grants Holmes felt no love for her, since such feelings jarred his cold, exact mind. He calls Holmes the most perfect reasoning machine the world has seen. Readers get the tales that fixed Holmes and Watson in print, from a blackmail case for a king to a snake in a country house.
the-adventures-of-sir-launcelot-greaves: Tobias Smollett wrote The Adventures of Sir Launcelot Greaves. The author's preface stands at the front. An opening essay by G. H. Maynadier stands with it. Maynadier taught English at Harvard University. Chapter heads promise the hero's first entrance. One chapter the reader may wish were the last. The knight proves hard to wake when set on sleep. A late head shows that madness can be catching.
the-arabian-art-of-taming-and-training-w:
T. Gilbert's guide to taming wild and vicious horses was printed at Cincinnati, Ohio, in 1856 by Henry Watkins of West Fifth Street. Its opening calls the horse's first taming one of man's greatest feats in the animal kingdom. That feat, Gilbert says, came not in a day but by slow trials and finds.

Man first subdued the meeker beasts, easy to catch and tame, and for years made do with the ox, the ass, and the camel as drudges. The fleet and fine horse came last under his hand. Gilbert blames man's thin knowledge of the horse's nature for that delay, and takes the delay itself as proof of the animal's high rank.
the-armourer-s-prentices:
Charlotte M. Yonge's tale of Tudor London, printed by Macmillan in London and New York in 1889 with pictures by W. J. Hennessy, opens its pages here deep in the book, near a chapter called Old Haunts. The scene stands in the New Forest, at the home of the Birkenholt family.

Forest officers, Yonge writes, have held some of southern England's pleasantest dwellings since the Conqueror's days. The Birkenholt house sits below a grove of great beeches, their silver trunks rising like columns into a vault of branches. Sunlight gilds a twig here and there, but the floor below stays russet with fallen leaves. A motto from As You Like It, about a poor allotment left by a father's will, heads the scene.
the-awakening-and-selected-short-stories:
Kate Chopin is named on the title page for a volume joining her novel in thirty-nine numbered chapters with a group of shorter tales. Headings after the novel include Beyond the Bayou. No date or publisher is printed in the opening pages shown here.

Readers who open the volume get the long work first, in a steady run of short chapters, and then separate stories. The pairing lets them compare Chopin's novel-length writing with her brief fiction in one place. Because the front pages give no plot or setting, the safest guide is the form itself: one major novel, followed by selected short pieces by the same hand.
the-battle-of-the-books-and-other-short-:
Jonathan Swift's short pieces were issued by Cassell in London, Paris, New York, and Melbourne in 1886. A long introduction gives his life, starting with his birth on November 30, 1667. His father, an attorney in Dublin, died before he was born.

Swift was raised in the household of his uncle Godwin, sent to Kilkenny School, and entered at Trinity College, Dublin. The introduction notes a date misprint in its own text for that entry. When troubles closed the university in 1689, Swift went to Leicester to plan his future with his mother. Links to Sir William Temple at Moor Park then open the next stage of his career.
the-bee-man-of-orn-and-other-fanciful-ta: Frank R. Stockton's writings are listed in a uniform edition at the front, naming The Bee-Man of Orn and Other Fanciful Tales as one of five volumes priced at $1.25 each. Other sets listed include The Lady or the Tiger, The Christmas Wreck, The Late Mrs Null, and Rudder Grange. Prices and formats are given for illustrated and paper editions of several Stockton books. No tale text itself appears in these opening pages, which are publisher's advertisements.
the-bell-in-the-fog-and-other-stories:
Gertrude Atherton published a story collection with Harper and Brothers in New York and London in 1905. She dedicated the book to Henry James, called simply the Master. Atherton is also named for Rulers of Kings and The Conqueror.

Ten pieces are listed, starting with the title story. Others include The Striding Place, The Dead and the Countess, and The Greatest Good of the Greatest Number. A Monarch of a Small Survey, The Tragedy of a Snob, and Crowned with One Crest follow. Death and the Woman, a prologue to an unwritten play, and Talbot of Ursula close the contents.
the-bell-ringer-of-angel-s-and-other-sto:
Bret Harte gathered tales of the American West under a title story set on the North Fork of the Stanislaus River. That tale opens where the river loses its youthful speed and broadens into a plain, forming a calm promontory at high water. Mosses and alders trail in its slow current.

Harte traces the spot from a Digger chief's camp to a pioneer and then a quartz prospector, each taken by violence or flood. Other stories listed include Johnnyboy, Young Robin Gray, The Sheriff of Siskiyou, and A Rose of Glenbogie. A mystery of a hacienda and a piece called My First Book complete the list.
the-best-american-humorous-short-stories:
Alexander Jessup edited a collection of American humorous tales and prefaced it with a survey of recent short fiction. He names O. Henry and Jack London as apostles of the burly and vigorous, and sets Henry James and Edith Wharton in finer fields. George Randolph Chester and Irvin Cobb are grouped nearby.

Jessup also notes Sarah Orne Jewett, Mary E. Wilkins Freeman, George Washington Cable, and Kate Chopin as belonging largely to an earlier period. O. Henry, pen name of William Sydney Porter, began, he says, with a Christmas stocking story in McClure's in 1899. The survey frames the comic tales that follow.
the-best-ghost-stories:
A Modern Library volume copyrighted in 1919 by Boni and Liveright gathers ghost tales with an introduction by Arthur B. Reeve on the fascination of the ghost story. Daniel Defoe's apparition of Mrs Veal opens the contents at page three. Montague Rhodes James follows with Canon Alberic's scrap-book.

Edward Bulwer-Lytton contributes The Haunted and the Haunters, and Leopold Kompert a silent woman. Later pieces include Banshees, E. F. Benson's man who went too far, and Algernon Blackwood's woman's ghost story. Rudyard Kipling's phantom rickshaw, Brander Matthews's rival ghosts, and Ambrose Bierce's damned thing close the list.
the-bible-king-james-version-book-13-1-c:
First Chronicles in the King James rendering, begins with name after name. Early verses list Kenan, Mahalaleel, and Jered, then Henoch, Methuselah, and Lamech. Noah and his sons Shem, Ham, and Japheth follow.

Sons of Japheth include Gomer, Magog, Madai, Javan, Tubal, Meshech, and Tiras. Sons of Ham include Cush, Mizraim, Put, and Canaan, and Cush is said to have begotten Nimrod, who began to be mighty on earth. Genealogy is the book's first labour: lines of descent link the earliest figures to the peoples and kings who follow in later chapters of the history.
the-bible-king-james-version-book-14-2-c:
Second Chronicles , given here in King James English, opens with Solomon strengthened in his kingdom, with God magnifying him greatly. Solomon speaks to all Israel, to captains, judges, governors, and chief fathers.

King and congregation go to the high place at Gibeon, where the tabernacle made by Moses stood. The ark, by contrast, had been brought by David from Kirjathjearim to a tent at Jerusalem. A brass altar made by Bezaleel stands before the tabernacle, and Solomon goes up to it. Worship at an ancient shrine begins a history centred on temple and kings.
the-bible-king-james-version-book-21-ecc:
Ecclesiastes in the King James rendering, begins with the Preacher, son of David, king in Jerusalem, crying that all is vanity. What profit, he asks, has a man from all his labour under the sun?

One generation passes and another comes, while the earth abides forever. The sun rises, goes down, and hastens back; wind turns in circuits; rivers run into a sea that is never full. All things are full of labour, the eye is not satisfied with seeing, and the ear is not filled with hearing. Cycles, not progress, shape the Preacher's first meditation.
the-bible-king-james-version-book-59-jam:
James in King James wording, begins with James calling himself a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ. He greets the twelve tribes scattered abroad.

Count it all joy, he tells his brethren, when you fall into various trials, knowing that testing of faith works patience. Let patience have its perfect work, so you may be perfect and entire, wanting nothing. Anyone lacking wisdom should ask God, who gives liberally and does not upbraid, but must ask in faith without wavering. A wavering man is like a sea wave, driven and tossed, and a double-minded man is unstable.
the-bible-king-james-version-book-7-judg:
Judges , given here in King James English, opens after Joshua's death, when Israel asks the Lord who shall go up first against the Canaanites. The Lord says Judah shall go up, for the land is delivered into his hand.

Judah asks Simeon his brother to come into his lot to fight, promising to go likewise into Simeon's lot. Together they defeat the Canaanites and Perizzites at Bezek, slaying ten thousand men. Adonibezek flees, is pursued, and is caught. Tribal war in parts, rather than one national campaign, characterises the book from its first chapter onward.
the-bicyclers-and-three-other-farces:
Four farces are gathered in one volume, starting with a bicycle play. Other pieces are called A Dramatic Evening, The Fatal Message, and A Proposal Under Difficulties. In the first, Thaddeus Perkins, a beginner, awaits his first lesson in his Gramercy Square drawing room in late October.

Robert Yardsley and Jack Barlow, both experts, are coming at half past eight to teach him. His wife Bess welcomes the plan, saying he needs rest from work. Perkins doubts that learning to ride is restful, citing a friend who dented floors with his head. Bess counters that the same friend dented floors with other people's heads.
the-black-arrow-a-tale-of-the-two-roses:
Robert Louis Stevenson signed a prefatory letter at Saranac Lake on April 8, 1888, to a critic friend who could never read this tale. He says the book was written years earlier for a particular audience, in rivalry with Alfred R. Phillips, and was judged an advance on Treasure Island by story-paper readers.

A prologue called John Amend-All opens in late spring at Tunstall Moat House in the reign of Henry VI. A bell rings at an odd hour, and workers leave forest and fields along the river. Tunstall hamlet, with oak-framed houses, a church among yews, and a road to Holywood Abbey, is described in detail.
the-black-creek-stopping-house-and-other:
Nellie L. McClung copyrighted her story collection in 1912 and dedicated it to the pioneer women of the West. Those women, she writes, fed the hungry, nursed the sick, cheered the dying, and kept the conscience of the neighbourhood alive. Many were old before their time from hard work and privation.

The title story's chapters follow an old trail to a house of bread and a sailors' rest. Farm pupils, a prairie club-house, and ladies' day at the stopping-house follow. Shadows of night, an evil genius, a father's turn, and a blizzard lead to a chapter called When the Day Broke, grounding western tales in women's labour.
the-black-prophet-a-tale-of-irish-famine:
William Carleton set a tale of Irish famine at Glendhu, the Black Glen, in a chapter on domestic affection. Twenty-odd years before, a small cabin stood at the foot of a round hill commanding a fine prospect. A rapid torrent ran through the glen pass beside it.

On a wet autumn afternoon a young woman of about twenty-one leaves the cabin again and again. She climbs a small knob, looks eagerly in every direction for someone expected, and returns disappointed each time. Anger mixes with hope in her watch. The cabin's site is called desolate and linked with wild, supernatural terrors, setting famine hardship inside a gloomy landscape.
the-book-of-missionary-heroes: Basil Mathews wrote The Book of Missionary Heroes, put out in New York by the George H. Doran Company with rights dated 1922. A first part called The Relay Race opens the book. Book I, The Pioneers, tells of St. Paul on the long trail, Wilfrid of Sussex, Raymond Lull, and St. Francis of Assisi. Book II, The Island Adventurers, starts with the ship Duff and beacon fires. It goes on to John Williams, Kapiolani of Hawaii, and Elikana in a canoe. Only the list of parts is shown.
the-borgias-celebrated-crimes:
Alexandre Dumas, père, wrote The Borgias as one part of his eight-book set Celebrated Crimes, in a form dated 1910. The book is built as a prologue, sixteen chapters, and an epilogue. No chapter heads are given beyond their numbers, so the shape is all the list shows.

The prologue opens on April 8, 1492, in a room of the Carneggi Palace, some three miles from Florence. Three men stand grouped round a bed where a fourth man lies dying. The first, at the foot of the bed, half hides his tears in the gold-worked drapes. He is Ermolao Barbaro, who wrote a tract On Celibacy and studies on Pliny. The year before, the tale notes, he had been at Rome on state work. Sorrow, rank, and old learning set the tone at once.
the-boy-allies-under-the-sea-or-the-vani:
Ensign Robert L. Drake wrote The Boy Allies Under the Sea, or The Vanishing Submarines, put out in New York by the A. L. Burt Company in 1916. The first chapter is called A Mystery. Frank Chadwick opens it with a sharp question for Jack Templeton. He wants to know how long England will put up with German submarines in the seas round the British Isles.

Jack says a strong drive on them is under way, but Frank is dry. A big liner, he notes, was sunk off the Irish coast the day before. Then Jack shares news Frank has not heard. In the last thirty days, close to a hundred German boats have vanished, sunk or taken, no one knows which. Word through state channels says many have failed to come back to base, and Berlin is much stirred. Jack heard Lord Hastings talk of it with Mr. Churchill.
the-boy-knight-a-tale-of-the-crusades: The Boy Knight: A Tale of the Crusades, by G. A. Henty, opens with a list of chapters and no tale page. The first heads are The Outlaws, A Rescue, and The Capture of Wortham Hold. The Crusades, making ready, and The Lists come next. Revenge and The Attack lead east: The Princess Berengaria, Pirates, and In the Holy Land. The Accolade, the rite that makes a knight, is the last head shown.
the-brick-moon-and-other-stories:
Edward Everett Hale opens The Brick Moon and Other Stories with a preface on tales written thirty and more years back. The title tale, he says, was begun in his dear brother Nathan's work room at Union College, Schenectady, in 1870. It retells the old chat, dreams, plans, and jokes of their college days, before Nathan left Cambridge in 1838. Hale learned most of what he knows, he says, through his brother's care and love.

The tale ran in the Atlantic Monthly in 1870 and 1871, Hale's last tale for that sheet before he took charge of Old and New. High praise came from Asaph Hall of the National Observatory, the man who found the two moons of Mars. Hall sent Hale their tables with a note: the smaller of those moons is the veritable Brick Moon.
the-brownies-and-other-tales: Juliana Horatia Ewing wrote The Brownies and Other Tales, put out in London by the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge, and in New York by E. and J. B. Young and Company. The book is dated 1871, and Ewing gave it to her very dear and honoured mother. The tales are The Brownies, The Land of Lost Toys, and Three Christmas Trees. An Idyll of the Wood, Christmas Crackers, and Amelia and the Dwarfs complete the set of six. Only the front pages and this list are shown.
the-burglar-s-fate-and-the-detectives:
Allan Pinkerton wrote The Burglar's Fate and the Detectives, put out in New York by G. W. Carleton and Company, and in London by S. Low, Son and Company, in 1884. Pinkerton had a shelf of like books, among them Expressman and Detective and Mollie Maguires and Detectives. His preface is blunt: the tale that follows is a story of actual occurrence.

No touch of fiction, he says, dims the truthful telling. The crime was really committed, in the way and in the setting he relates. Four young men did the deed, and today they are inmates of a prison. Their real names are cloaked with the kind mantle of fiction. The process of detection is set down with the frankness of a man who took part in it. Pinkerton sends the book out as a revelation of the certain fruit of crime.
the-captain-of-the-pole-star-and-other-t:
Arthur Conan Doyle made this set of his weird tales in 1890, and it here stands in the text of the Longmans print. The set bears the name of its first tale, of a ghost ship in the polar seas. Doyle was then a young doctor, just at the start of his famed life as a writer.

Arctic ghosts walk in 'The Captain of the Pole-Star,' told as a ship's log in the ice. 'J. Habakuk Jephson's Statement' gives a ghost ship's tale, and 'The Ring of Thoth' an Egyptian one. The set holds the best of Doyle's tales of the unseen from his first years.
the-captain-of-the-polestar-and-other-ta:
The Captain of the Polestar, and Other Tales, by Sir Arthur Conan Doyle, is dedicated to Major-General A. W. Drayson, as a slight acknowledgment of his unrecognised services to science in astronomy. Doyle's preface thanks the proprietors of the Cornhill, Temple Bar, Belgravia, London Society, Cassell's, and The Boys' Own Paper for leave to reprint.

Ten tales are listed. The title story opens as the journal of John M'Alister Ray, a medical student. It is dated September 11. The place is latitude 81 degrees 40 minutes north, longitude 2 degrees east. His vessel lies-to amid the ice fields, and the diary form sets the Arctic tale in a young surgeon's own daily record from its first line.
