the-captives: The Captives, by Hugh Walpole, is dated 1920 and dedicated to Arnold Bennett with deep affection, under a long epigraph from William James. Its opening pages give the contents: Part I, The Beginning of the Journey, with the death of the Rev. Charles Cardinal, Aunt Anne, the London house, and the chapel; then Part II, The Chariot of Fire, opening on the Warlocks, expectation, and Maggie and Martin. No page of the novel is shown.
the-cat-of-bubastes:
G. A. Henty set this tale in ancient Egypt, and the heading dates it 1889. The title page calls it a tale of ancient Egypt, with five page pictures by J. R. Weguelin. Henty wrote many such history tales for boys, and his preface speaks straight to young readers as his dear lads.

In that preface he explains his method at length. Tomb walls, he notes, kept a full record of daily Egyptian life, work, sports, feasts, and home customs. He drew on Sir J. Gardner Wilkinson and other writers to make that picture lively. The scene is laid in the time of Thotmes III, named there as one of Egypt's greatest kings. The tale thus mixes story with a careful account of how people lived in that age.
the-categories:
Aristotle's short treatise on logic appears here in a translation by E. M. Edghill. It sorts the ways words name things, and the ways things themselves can be spoken of. The first part takes up names that are shared but mean different things in each case.

Three kinds of naming are set out with plain examples. Some names are shared with one shared meaning, as man and ox are both called animal. Other names are shared while the meaning shifts, as a real man and a pictured man are both called animal. A third kind borrows its name from a root word, as a grammarian takes his name from grammar. The work then moves to simple and combined forms of speech, laying ground for later study of terms and statements.
the-celibates:
Honore de Balzac grouped three tales under the title Les Celibataires in his Comedie Humaine, and this volume presents them in English as The Celibates. An introduction explains that the set is the longest single-titled group in that vast series, after Illusions perdues. Yet its parts share no single story line.

The bond between the parts is their people: bachelors and old maids stand as heroes and heroines in all three. The introduction rates at least two of the parts very high, while judging Pierrette, which opens the series, a step below its companions. Pierrette was written for the young Countess Anna de Hanska, and its manner is shaped by that aim. It also links loosely to the Arcis tales, including the Tenebreuse Affaire. Readers get Balzac's close study of single life in French towns, framed by a candid critical guide.
the-certain-hour-dizain-des-poe-tes: James Branch Cabell published this book, subtitled Dizain des Poetes, with Robert M. McBride and Company of New York in 1916. Only the front matter is present here: an epigraph on criticism, copyright lines reaching back to 1909, and a dedication poem addressed to Robert Gamble Cabell II. That poem holds that love, being God-born, abides unchanged while all other things decay.Its contents rest on the strength of the title page alone.
the-children-s-book-of-christmas-stories:
Asa Don Dickinson and Ada M. Skinner edited this gathering of Christmas stories for children. Their preface answers a need many librarians had voiced: a select set of proven tales in one volume. Each story, they note, had already won the approval of thousands of children.

The contents mix famous names with tales for different ages. Charles Dickens gives Christmas at Fezziwig's Warehouse, and Hans Christian Andersen gives The Fir-Tree. Mary E. Wilkins Freeman, Susan Coolidge, Ruth Sawyer Durand, and Olive Thorne Miller also appear. Stars in the list mark tales for younger children, and double stars mark those better suited to older ones. The editors hope the book will please parents, teachers, and librarians alike, and they claim no more for it than that it holds the true Christmas spirit.
the-children-s-hour-v-5-stories-from-sev: Eva March Tappan selected and arranged this fifth volume of The Children's Hour, a ten-volume set from Houghton Mifflin, gathering stories from seven old favorites. Only the title page and the start of the contents are present here. The first entries retell John Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress, with Christian passing the wicket gate, visiting the House of the Interpreter, and fighting Apollyon. A picture shows Ferdinand and Ariel.Readers must take the book on its title page alone.
the-children-s-six-minutes: Bruce S. Wright wrote these short talks for children, published in New York by George H. Doran Company in 1922 and dedicated to Harriet Elizabeth and Robert. Only the title page and contents are present here. The titled pieces run about two pages each and cover Happy New Year, Growth, Snow, Kindness, God's Call, a Happy Home, Easter Light, and Helping Fingers.No pages of the work itself follow the front matter.
the-chronicle-of-the-canons-regular-of-m: Thomas a Kempis wrote this chronicle of the canons regular of Mount St. Agnes, translated by J. P. Arthur and produced from the 1906 Kegan Paul, Trench, Trubner edition. Only the title page and contents are present here. The chapters tell of the first founders, of Master Gerard Groote pointing out the site, of the first house and chapel, and of the brothers' scant food and clothing. Later entries name John Kempen as first prior and the consecration of the burial ground. No chronicle text follows.
the-city-and-the-world-and-other-stories:
Francis Clement Kelley gathered these tales in a second edition from the Extension Press of Chicago in 1913. The contents list fourteen stories, among them The Flaming Cross, The Vicar-General, The Autobiography of a Dollar, and How Father Tom Connolly Began to Be a Saint. Priests, parishes, and city life supply most of his material.

The title story opens in a cloister garden. Father Denfili, old and blind, tells his beads in a corner and sighs. Father Tomasso has brought him there, and the scene sets a quiet, reflective key for the tale. Other titles promise a thousand dollar note, a Yankee tramp, an unbroken seal, and a man with a dead soul. Kelley writes as a churchman telling stories for general readers, with Catholic life in America at the center and a moral turn never far away.
the-cloister-and-the-hearth-a-tale-of-th: Charles Reade's tale of the Middle Ages appears here in a second record, taken from an International Classics volume. Only the series list is present, naming companion volumes such as Adam Bede, A Tale of Two Cities, David Copperfield, Ivanhoe, Jane Eyre, and Lorna Doone. A transcriber's note explains a markup used for a long macron over two letters.Only the frame of the book is present, not its pages.
the-club-of-queer-trades:
G. K. Chesterton opens this story set with the tremendous adventures of Major Brown. Chapter 1 begins with blocks of flats, which he compares to the giant designs of Rabelais and his illustrator Gustave Dore. Piling houses on top of each other, front doors and all, strikes him as a Gargantuan way to save space.

In the chaos of those upright streets, he argues, anything may dwell or happen. Somewhere in one such building sit the offices of the Club of Queer Trades. The odd name does not startle passers-by, since nobody in those dim hives looks beyond his own melancholy errand. A man in spectacles could answer inquiries for a strangers' assassination company, Chesterton jokes, and no inquiries would be made. That indifference lets the club reign in peace, and the tales turn on trades invented to be strange, each one a small mystery of London life.
the-collection-of-antiquities:
Honore de Balzac wrote this novel, translated here by Ellen Marriage, as part of his vast history of French manners in the nineteenth century. He dedicates it to Baron von Hammer-Purgstall, a member of the Aulic Council and author of a history of the Ottoman Empire. The dedication letter fills the opening pages with thanks.

Balzac credits the baron with warm interest in that long history and with encouragement to keep at the work. Such approval, he argues, may win the approval of others and protect this attempt. He calls the baron a leading figure of conscientious, studious Germany, famed for exhaustive research among documents. That labor produced a monumental work on the civilization of the East. Balzac says the baron's sympathy often kept up his own ardor through nights of toil on modern detail. The letter sets the novel's antiquarian theme inside a tribute to patient scholarship.
the-compleat-cook-expertly-prescribing-t:
A cookery book printed in London in 1658 by E. B. for Nath. Brook at the Angel in Cornhill forms part of the W. M. volume The Queens Closet Opened. Its title promises the readiest ways, in Italian, Spanish, or French fashion, for dressing flesh and fish, ordering sauces, and making pastry.

First comes a posset, the Earl of Arundel's way. A quart of cream with a quarter of a nutmeg goes on the fire to boil a little, while sack and ale, sweetened with sugar, warm in the chosen pot. The two are joined, stirred, and left to simmer over the fire an hour or more, the longer the better. Next comes a capon larded with lemons, trussed and boiled by itself in fair water with a little oatmeal, toward a sauce of mutton broth and white wine.
the-complete-john-silence-stories:
Algernon Blackwood's John Silence stories, headed with the year 1908, present their hero as a physician extraordinary. Blackwood dedicates the book to M. L. W., named as the original of John Silence and his companion in many adventures. The contents list six cases, from A Psychical Invasion to A Victim of Higher Space.

Case I opens in Silence's consulting room. He asks a Swedish lady, somewhat sceptically, what makes her think he could be of use in her particular case. She answers with his sympathetic heart and his knowledge of occultism, and he cuts in at the dreadful word, holding up a finger in impatience. That small clash fixes his manner: a doctor who takes strange cases seriously while disliking loose talk about them. Blackwood frames ghost work as casework, with a professional at its center.
the-conservation-of-races:
W. E. Burghardt Du Bois wrote The Conservation of Races in 1897 as Occasional Paper No. 2 of the American Negro Academy. A note at the front states the academy's aim: Black men and women with higher schooling should join forces to lift the race. They face both disunity at home and steady opposition from outside.

Du Bois begins by noting that Black Americans take a close personal interest in talk about the origins and futures of races. Such talk often hides false claims about their own powers and standing. Many, he says, have thus played down race lines and stressed one blood and human brotherhood. Yet he insists races are real, and that the meeting of two far-apart types in America poses a great question.
the-copy-cat-and-other-stories:
Mary E. Wilkins Freeman gathers twelve stories in The Copy-Cat and Other Stories, among them The Cock of the Walk, Johnny-in-the-Woods, Big Sister Solly, Noblesse, and Dear Annie. The title story opens on a secret kept by two little boys and one little girl, Lily Jennings, about Jim Simmons's cats.

Lily has no close girl friend to tempt her to talk. The only candidate is Amelia Wheeler, called The Copy-Cat by the pupils at Madame's school. Amelia is an odd child with a fixed ideal, and that ideal, unknown to anyone, is Lily herself. Her mother, a woman of strong character who does not approve of Lily, would have acted at once had she guessed.
the-corporation-of-london-its-rights-and:
William Ferneley Allen, sheriff of London and Middlesex and alderman of the ward of Cheap, defends the Corporation of London in a preface dated July 26, 1858, from Leadenhall Street. He admits he is new to civic affairs, yet says no man of spirit could sit quiet under the insulting charges aimed at the Corporation by hostile or ignorant critics.

Allen grants the civic system is not flawless, since it is of human origin. Still, he holds that the Court of Aldermen has both the power and the will to fix what is defective and to add needed reforms on its own. Outside meddling by the imperial legislature, he argues, is not required. His contents then sketch London under the Romans, the guilds, the boroughs, and the charter of William the Conqueror.
the-countess-of-saint-geran-celebrated-c:
Alexandre Dumas, pere, tells the story of the Countess de Saint-Geran in this piece from his Celebrated Crimes, in an eight-volume set dated 1910. The tale is headed 1639. About the end of that year, a troop of horsemen rides at midday into a small village at the north edge of Auvergne, coming from Paris.

Heat hangs over the party; the horses sweat and the men are caked with dust. The troop belongs to the provost of the mounted police, back from some weighty errand. Among his men rides a young man, richly dressed and plainly a prisoner of rank. Villagers crowd after the party to the wine-shop door, guessing at the great crime such a nobleman must be charged with.
the-crime-of-the-french-cafe-and-other-s:
Three complete tales of Nicholas Carter, billed as America's greatest detective, make up this volume: The Crime of the French Cafe, Nick Carter's Ghost Story, and The Mystery of St. Agnes' Hospital. The first tale opens on a well-known French restaurant in the Tenderloin district, famed for its cook and wine cellar, with small, richly fitted private dining rooms.

At half-past seven one evening, Nick Carter stands fifty yards from the restaurant's dim side door, shadowing a man over a small robbery taken on to oblige a friend. A closed carriage stops; a bare-headed waiter in a white apron hurries out, glances side to side like a man running away, and climbs in. The odd sight, Carter reflects, led him to one of the strangest criminal puzzles of his career.
the-crushed-flower-and-other-stories:
Leonid Andreyev's stories come to English readers in Herman Bernstein's translation in The Crushed Flower and Other Stories. The contents add A Story Which Will Never Be Finished, On the Day of the Crucifixion, The Serpent's Story, Love, Faith and Hope, The Ocean, and Judas Iscariot and Others.

The title story opens on Yura, six years old, for whom the world is enormous, alive, and full of mystery. He knows the daytime sky and its slow clouds well, but not the stars, since he goes to bed early. One green, bright star rises just before bedtime. It is his alone. Best of all he knows the earth of yard, street, and garden, its stones, velvet grass, hot sand, and the dust grown people never notice from their great height.
the-curious-republic-of-gondour-and-othe: Mark Twain's The Curious Republic of Gondour and Other Whimsical Sketches carries a note explaining where the pieces came from. Most came from a series he wrote for The Galaxy from May 1870 to April 1871. The rest came from The Buffalo Express. The contents list the title sketch plus pieces such as About Smells, Dan Murphy, The Tournament in A. D. 1870, Curious Relic for Sale, Our Precious Lunatic, and The Wild Man Interviewed. Only the title page, that note, and the contents are present here.
the-descent-of-man-and-other-stories:
Edith Wharton's The Descent of Man and Other Stories gathers ten tales. Among them are The Other Two, Expiation, The Lady's Maid's Bell, The Mission of Jane, The Reckoning, The Letter, and A Venetian Night's Entertainment. The title story opens on Professor Linyard coming home from a holiday in the Maine woods.

To his wife's eye he set out alone, but an unseen companion traveled with him, and his high heart came from that company. The Professor had run off with an idea. The narrator says only those who have tried it can guess the thrill. Linyard would not trade places with any hero of romance bound to a flesh-and-blood abduction, since the most charming female comes encumbered with luggage and scruples.
the-description-of-wales:
Gerald of Wales wrote The Description of Wales, shown here in the 1912 J. M. Dent edition. His first preface, addressed to Stephen Langton, Archbishop of Canterbury, recalls his earlier labors. He spent three years arranging the Topography of Ireland in three parts, and two more on the Vaticinal History of its conquest. The Itinerary of Baldwin through Cambria kept that mission from perishing in obscurity.

Now, he says, he will give some account of his native country and describe the genius of its people, so distinct from that of other nations. Some friends object, likening him to a painter of Zeuxis's skill who lavishes his colors on a cottage while the world expects a temple or palace. Others warn that gifts from above should not be wasted on remote corners like Ireland and Wales, nor spent praising ignorant princes who can neither prize nor reward fine writing.
the-development-of-the-feeling-for-natur:
Alfred Biese, director of the Gymnasium at Neuwied, wrote The Development of the Feeling for Nature in the Middle Ages and Modern Times. It is shown here in an authorized translation from the German dated 1905. A companion work on the Greeks and Romans won such a welcome, he says, that after some years he carried the subject on to modern times.

In his preface Biese grants the task's vast scope, which has daunted many a scholar since Humboldt's terse sketches. The flood of material forced him to rest on typical forerunners of each age. He keeps the thread of general growth, adding the chief phases of landscape painting and garden craft. Literature, above all poetry, he holds, is the chief source, as the most intimate medium of a nation's feelings, and he aims at readers of cultivation generally.
the-different-forms-of-flowers-on-plants: Charles Darwin dedicates The Different Forms of Flowers on Plants of the Same Species to Professor Asa Gray as a tribute of respect and affection. Its contents open with heterostyled dimorphic plants of the primula family. They compare the two flower forms of the cowslip and their fertility when united in lawful and unlawful ways. They then move to hybrid primulas, the oxlip among them, and on to flax, lungwort, and buckwheat. Only the title page, dedication, and the start of this contents are present here.
the-discovery-of-witches:
Matthew Hopkins, styling himself witch-finder, published The Discovery of Witches in 1647. It answers queries delivered to the judges of assize for the county of Norfolk, and, as the title says, is for the benefit of the kingdom. A text from Exodus stands at the head: Thou shalt not suffer a witch to live.

The work proceeds by questions raised against Hopkins and his way of finding witches, each with his answer. The first charges that he must be the witch and sorcerer himself to do what he does. He replies with the saying that if Satan's kingdom be divided against itself, how shall it stand? The second supposes he met the Devil and cheated him of his book of the witches' names in England. Hopkins answers that besting the Devil would be to his credit, and that his skill in reading faces is no more than any man's.
the-doctor-a-tale-of-the-rockies: Ralph Connor's The Doctor: A Tale of the Rockies is present here only as a title page and contents list. The chapters run from The Old Stone Mill and The Daughter of the Manse through The Young Doctor, Ben's Gang, and Love's Tangled Ways. Last heads name a fight with death. They also name a post as medical chief of the Crow's Nest mines. No story text appears in these pages.
the-door-in-the-wall-and-other-stories:
H. G. Wells gathers eight tales in The Door in the Wall and Other Stories. The contents list The Star, A Dream of Armageddon, The Cone, A Moonlight Fable, The Diamond Maker, The Lord of the Dynamos, and The Country of the Blind. In the first tale, Lionel Wallace tells a friend of a door in a white wall that haunted his life.

Wallace swears the door led to a lovely garden beyond the world's pain. His friend doubts, then believes, then doubts again. Wells uses small wonders to probe big wants: escape, power, sight, and truth.
the-easiest-way-in-housekeeping-and-cook:
Helen Campbell's The Easiest Way in Housekeeping and Cooking, first issued in 1880 and revised in this 1903 Boston printing, was made for home use and class study. Campbell says the small book stays much as first writ, though cookery books have swelled since. Its fans, she notes, are firm, above all in the South, where its need first showed.

Campbell wrote Prisoners of Poverty and Women Wage-Earners, and she brings that care for poor homes to the kitchen. Plain receipts, low costs, and clear steps rule the book. A source list ends it.
the-entailed-hat-or-patty-cannon-s-times:
George Alfred Townsend's The Entailed Hat; or, Patty Cannon's Times, a romance printed by Harper in 1884, is set for two lovers of old times: Judge George P. Fisher of Delaware and John A. J. Creswell of Maryland. Townsend, who signed as Gath, drew on the lore of the Delmarva shore. Patty Cannon led a gang that stole free Black folk and sold them south.

An entailed hat, passed down by will, knots the plot's families. Townsend mixes court tales, slave-stealing raids, and Eastern Shore speech. The book keeps a grim slice of border history alive.
the-exemplary-novels-of-cervantes:
Miguel de Cervantes Saavedra's The Exemplary Novels, in Walter K. Kelly's English rendering for Bohn's Standard Library, was printed at London in 1881. Kelly's preface defends the title: exemplary keeps the Spanish sense of giving a moral example, as with Cicero's Offices, which no one renames a treatise on duties. The word ejemplo, he notes, bore that sense since the archpriest of Hita.

Cervantes wrote these tales after Don Quixote's fame. Gypsy girls, jealous old men, and talking dogs fill them. Kelly's version carried the set to plain English homes for decades.
the-exiles:
Honoré de Balzac's The Exiles, rendered by Clara Bell and James Waring, opens in Paris in the year 1308. Few houses then stood on the island of sand the Seine had laid behind Notre-Dame, a strand prone to floods. A stern constable of the watch, Joseph Tirechair, first dared to build there, on land leased from the cathedral chapter free of feudal dues.

Seven years of fines built his house on the bank. Dante, in exile from Florence, haunts Balzac's tale of banned men and dark learning. Strange guests and banned books thicken its plot.
the-exiles-and-other-stories:
Richard Harding Davis's The Exiles and Other Stories, printed by Scribner's at New York in 1919 with an introduction by Charles Dana Gibson, gathers tales from three of Davis's books. Title notes trace the sources. The Exiles and The Boy Orator of Zepata City come from Harper's 1894 volume. The Other Woman comes from Gallagher, of 1891. On the Fever Ship and The Lion and the Unicorn come from the 1899 book of that name.

American exiles loaf in a South American port while plots brew round them. Davis, a famed war correspondent, writes with pace and polish. Gibson's drawings match the tales' dash.
the-fairy-godmothers-and-other-tales:
Mrs. Alfred Gatty, Margaret Gatty, wrote The Fairy Godmothers and Other Tales for her own children, dating her dedication at Ecclesfield Vicarage on March 27, 1851. She says the tales were written in hours of sickness but meant for healthy, glad young readers.

The title tale gives the book its name, and an Italian proverb about catching flies with honey, not vinegar, sets the tone. Gatty states plainly that the stories carry her own dearly held beliefs. Kind godmothers, small trials, and gentle lessons shape a set of tales meant to train the heart as much as to please it.
the-faith-of-the-millions-2nd-series:
George Tyrrell, a Jesuit priest, gathered past essays as The Faith of the Millions, and this second series came out in 1901 with church approval printed up front. The essays run from number thirteen to twenty-three in the set.

Juliana of Norwich opens the book, and the first essay calls her book of visions one of the great works of the middle ages. Other pieces weigh poets and mystics, the life of De Lamennais, Lippo the artist, and a book called The Making of Religion. Tyrrell asks how old faith can live in a new age of doubt and change.
the-fallen-leaves:
Wilkie Collins wrote The Fallen Leaves, and his short note to Caroline is dated from Gloucester Place, London, on July 1, 1879. He says the book's design speaks for itself and leaves it to win readers on its own merits.

A prologue comes first, then the story in three books. The hero, Amelius, appears first among socialists, then in London. A third book turns to Mrs. Farnaby's foot, a strange head for a section that hints at hidden shame. Collins builds a tale of a young idealist thrown among wealth, want, and secret pasts.
the-fireside-chats-of-franklin-delano-ro:
Franklin Delano Roosevelt gave these radio talks to the American people between 1933 and 1944, speaking straight to homes across the land. The first talk, on March 12, 1933, deals with banks and the bank holiday.

Roosevelt explains in plain words what a bank does with deposits: it lends them out in bonds, loans, and farm and trade credit, keeping only a small part in cash. He tells how fear drove crowds to pull out cash and gold faster than sound banks could pay. The talks that follow made the fireside chat a new bond between a president and the public.
the-first-and-the-last-a-drama-in-three-:
John Galsworthy wrote The First and the Last as a drama in three scenes, drawn from his Six Short Plays. Two brothers, Keith and Larry Darrant, and a woman named Wanda make up the cast.

The first scene opens at six on a November night in Keith's study, a dark room lit by one lamp and a log fire. Keith, a famed lawyer, sleeps in his chair. Larry slips in, thin, worn, and sighing, with a dreadful secret to lay on his brother. Thirty hours pass before the next scene in Wanda's room, and two months before the last. Guilt and rank pull the brothers apart.
the-flower-of-the-chapdelaines:
George W. Cable wrote The Flower of the Chapdelaines as a tale of old New Orleans, printed at New York in 1918 with a front picture by F. C. Yohn. A young lawyer stands at the start.

The hero has just opened a law office off Bienville Street when he meets a fair stranger at a Royal Street corner. A small Black boy in a broad white collar walks at her side like a guard. Cable, famed for tales of Creole life, sets love and mystery among the old French streets, where fine manners hide old wounds and lost kin wait to be found.
the-forged-coupon-and-other-stories:
Leo Tolstoy wrote The Forged Coupon and the tales gathered with it, short works of his late years. An introduction praises Tolstoy's rare force of soul in an age of greed and goods.

With the title tale stand After the Dance, Alyosha the Pot, My Dream, There Are No Guilty People, and The Young Tsar. The introduction calls Tolstoy both a great realist and a mystic who fought his own flesh all his life. In these tales one small sin, a forged note of money, spreads harm from hand to hand, while plain folk and kings alike face the claims of conscience.
the-former-philippines-thru-foreign-eyes:
Austin Craig edited The Former Philippines Thru Foreign Eyes, a set of old travelers' tales of the islands. Five main pieces make up the book, with two short ones at the end.

Jagor's travels fill the first and longest part, in an English version checked against the German. Then come an account of the islands in 1810 by Tomas de Comyn, Commodore Wilkes on Manila and Sulu in 1842, and Lieutenant John White on Manila in 1819. Rudolf Virchow writes on how the islands were peopled. Foreign eyes, friendly and harsh alike, show the land before American rule.
the-garden-party-and-other-stories: Katherine Mansfield's 1922 collection, the high point of her art: "The Garden Party," "The Daughters of the Late Colonel," and other perfect stories of New Zealand and London life. Delicate, ironic, and quietly devastating, they made her one of the great modern short-story writers.
the-gerrard-street-mystery-and-other-wei:
John Charles Dent wrote The Gerrard Street Mystery and the weird tales gathered with it, and a sketch of his life opens the book. Dent was born in Kendal, England, in 1841 and came to Canada as a child.

The sketch tells how Dent read law, found it dull, and left for London, where high-class magazines took his work. Back in America he wrote for Boston papers, then joined the Toronto Telegram and the Weekly Globe, where his lives of eminent Canadians made his name. The tales here turn to mystery and the strange, the field where his deft, quick pen found its strangest effects.
the-girl-s-cabinet-of-instructive-and-mo:
The Girl's Cabinet of Instructive and Moral Stories is by Uncle Philip. Philip J. Cozans printed it in New York in 1856. It holds short moral tales for girls, each with a picture. The first tale is A Doll's Party. It shows good girls who have done their lessons. Santa Claus left each of them a doll at Christmas.

The tales praise duty before pleasure. They praise prayer at bedtime and good conduct at school and at home. The next tale is The Vain Girl. It starts long ago in one of the New England states. Each short piece gives a clear model of how a girl should act. It holds up one fault or one good trait at a time. Young readers can copy the good and shun the bad.
the-girl-with-the-golden-eyes:
Honore de Balzac wrote The Girl with the Golden Eyes. Ellen Marriage translated it. A note says the tale is the third part of a trilogy. The other parts are Ferragus and The Duchesse de Langeais. The three are often joined as The Thirteen. The book is dedicated to the painter Eugene Delacroix.

The tale opens with a grim view of the Paris crowd. Balzac calls the people of Paris gaunt and worn. Their faces are masks of want, joy, weakness, and greed. He asks what they seek: gold or pleasure. He sets out to explain the soul of the city. That harsh first look at Paris frames the story. It is a story of desire and wealth, as the title promises.
the-girl-with-the-green-eyes: Clyde Fitch wrote The Girl with the Green Eyes. It is a play in four acts. The Macmillan Company printed it in New York in 1905. Fitch dedicated it to Clara Bloodgood. He called her his good friend and the ideal interpreter of Jinny. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page, the copyright page, and the dedication. It also gives the heading of Act I. Act I is set at the Tillmans' house in New York. It opens with a wedding. No dialogue is present.
the-glory-of-the-trenches:
Coningsby Dawson wrote The Glory of the Trenches. It is subtitled An Interpretation. The book is dated 1917. It has an introduction by his father, W. J. Dawson. A line from Dawson's Carry On stands at the front. The glory, it says, is all in the souls of the men. A frontispiece shows Lieutenant Coningsby Dawson.

A poem, To You at Home, opens the book. It tells how men in the trenches waited each night for runners. The runners bore letters through battle smoke, gas, and wire. Some nights no letters came. The men then knew the runners had fallen. The poem frames the book's theme. It is the bond between soldiers at the front and the folk at home. The folk at home wrote to keep despair away.
the-golden-fleece-and-the-heroes-who-liv: Padraic Colum wrote The Golden Fleece and the Heroes Who Lived Before Achilles. The book is dated 1921. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page and a full contents list in three parts. Part I is The Voyage to Colchis. It tells of the youth Jason, King Pelias, and the building of the Argo. Part II is The Return to Greece. It names King Aeetes, Medea the sorceress, and the winning of the fleece. Part III gives lives of heroes: Atalanta, Peleus, Theseus, Heracles, and Orpheus.
the-golden-mean-or-ratio-1-sqrt-5-2-to-2:
The Golden Mean gives the golden ratio to 20,000 places. The ratio is written as (1 plus the square root of 5) over 2. It starts 1.6180339887498948482045868343656381177203091798057. It runs on in long blocks of digits. No story or essay is present. The numbers are the work.

The file also lists other math constants by name. It names Catalan's constant and 170,000 digits of Euler's constant. It names Artin's constant and the Backhouse constant. It names Zeta(3), or Apery's constant, and the Feigenbaum numbers. It names the Gauss-Kusmin-Wirsing constant and Khinchin's constant. It names the twin primes constant, and more. The set is a reference table. It serves readers who work with these constants and need them in one place.
the-golden-sayings-of-epictetus-with-the: Hastings Crossley translated and arranged The Golden Sayings of Epictetus. The Hymn of Cleanthes goes with it. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page and a contents list. The list runs to forty-four numbered parts in Roman numerals. It gives no heads and no text of the sayings. Nothing of Epictetus's teaching can be summed up from what is here. Only this can be said: the book joins his sayings with the Hymn of Cleanthes. Crossley made the translation and the arrangement.
the-goodness-of-st-rocque-and-other-stor:
Alice Dunbar wrote The Goodness of St. Rocque and Other Stories. A contents list names fourteen tales. They name Tony's Wife and The Fisherman of Pass Christian. They name M'sieu Fortier's Violin and By the Bayou St. John. They name A Carnival Jangle, Little Miss Sophie, and The Praline Woman. They name Titee.

The title tale opens with Manuela. She is tall, slender, and graceful. She sweeps down Marais Street with quick glances from under a heavy veil. She acts as if she feared she was followed. Her dark eyes are swollen from a sleepless, tearful night. The day before, a merry crowd of Creole girls and boys went by train to a picnic. The picnic was at Milneburg-on-the-Lake. There was dancing in a weather-beaten pavilion by the bayous. The tales are set in Creole New Orleans.
the-grandissimes: George W. Cable wrote The Grandissimes. Pictures are by Albert Herter. The book is dated 1899. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page and a contents list. The heads open with Masked Batteries and The Fate of the Immigrant. They name Family Trees and Honore Grandissime again and again. They name a philosophe, a rent-spectre, and Aurora as historian. They name a ride and a rescue. A long central tale, The Story of Bras-Coupe, is told in two parts. No chapter text is present.
the-great-shadow-and-other-napoleonic-ta: A. Conan Doyle wrote The Great Shadow and Other Napoleonic Tales. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page and a contents list. The title tale has fifteen chapters. They open with The Night of the Beacons and Cousin Edie of Eyemouth. They name The Man from the Sea and The Gathering of the Nations. They end with The Tally of Death and The End of It. Two further tales are named. No tale text is present.
the-great-speeches-and-orations-of-danie:
Edwin P. Whipple wrote the essay on Daniel Webster in The Great Speeches and Orations of Daniel Webster. The essay treats Webster as a master of English style. This edition is dated 1923. Its preface states the book's aim. It is not to supersede the standard edition of Webster's Works in six volumes. That edition was edited by Edward Everett and issued in 1851. This book calls attention anew to Webster's genius. It presents him as lawyer, statesman, diplomatist, patriot, and citizen.

The preface owns the limits of a selection. Among the speeches left out are passages of the highest eloquence. They hold maxims of political and moral wisdom fit for mottoes. In a hundred and twenty years, the preface says, only two men who shaped legislatures stand in the first class of English and American letters. They are Edmund Burke and Daniel Webster.
the-greatest-thing-in-the-world-and-othe:
Henry Drummond wrote The Greatest Thing in the World and Other Addresses. Fleming H. Revell Company published the book. Its copyrights are dated 1891 and 1898. The contents name six addresses. They open with Love, The Greatest Thing in the World. They name Lessons from the Angelus and Pax Vobiscum. They name First!, an address to boys. They name The Changed Life and Dealing with Doubt.

An introduction by another hand tells how the first address began. In 1884 the writer stayed with friends in England. On a Sunday evening the party asked him to expound some Scripture. Tired, he passed the task to Henry Drummond, one of the party. Drummond drew a small Testament from his hip pocket. He opened it at the thirteenth chapter of First Corinthians. He began to speak on the subject of Love. The hearer brought Drummond to Northfield to deliver it.
the-grey-wig-stories-and-novelettes: I. Zangwill wrote The Grey Wig: Stories and Novelettes. This edition is dated 1923. The book is dedicated to the author's mother and sisters, as mainly a study of woman. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page, the note, and a contents list. The pieces named run from The Grey Wig and The Woman Beater to The Big Bow Mystery and Merely Mary Ann.
the-guests-of-hercules: C. N. and A. M. Williamson wrote The Guests of Hercules. Doubleday, Page and Company published it at Garden City, New York, in 1912, with pictures by Bracker and Buckland. It is dedicated to the Lord of the Garden. Only front matter is present here. It gives a list of the Williamsons' other books and the title page. The list names The Golden Silence, The Motor Maid, and The Lightning Conductor. A frontispiece caption calls Mary a goddess on a golden pinnacle. No chapter text is present.
the-happiest-time-of-their-lives:
Alice Duer Miller wrote The Happiest Time of Their Lives, published in 1918. She is named on the title page as the author of Come Out of the Kitchen, Ladies Must Live, and Wings in the Night. Chapter one introduces Little Miss Severance, who sits with cold hands in her mother's drawing-room in a New York brownstone in the upper Sixties, waiting for a visitor due about five.

Miller fills the room with care. Old crystal, ivory, carved wood, and roses give the space its charm, though Miss Severance prefers her own plain third-floor room with chintz and maple pieces from her mother's family, the Lanleys. Her wait, begun early on purpose, turns a social call into a small study of hope and nerves.
the-happy-prince-and-other-tales: Oscar Wilde wrote The Happy Prince and Other Tales, with pictures by Walter Crane and Jacomb Hood. The title page shows a seventh impression, printed in London by David Nutt in 1910, after a first edition in May 1888. The contents list The Happy Prince, The Nightingale and the Rose, The Selfish Giant, and The Devoted Friend. The record present here holds front matter only.
the-haunted-mind-from-twice-told-tales:
Nathaniel Hawthorne wrote The Haunted Mind, a sketch from Twice Told Tales. The piece begins at the first moment of waking after midnight sleep. The dreamer seems to catch the figures of a dream still gathered around the bed, then hears a distant church clock and a nearer one strike in the sleeping town.

Hawthorne lingers on that in-between hour. Rest has lifted the weight of the day, morning still feels far off, and the mind can drift with one hour for thought and more for dreams. Yesterday has faded and tomorrow has not yet come. The sketch turns a brief waking spell into a quiet study of time, rest, and the border between sleep and thought.
the-heritage-of-dedlow-marsh-and-other-t:
Bret Harte wrote The Heritage of Dedlow Marsh and Other Tales. The contents list the title tale plus A Knight-Errant of the Foot-Hills, A Secret of Telegraph Hill, and Captain Jim's Friend. The title tale opens at sunset on the Dedlow Marshes, where the tide runs out fast and pools left behind catch the last light like dying embers.

Sand-pipers rise in a white cloud, geese point toward the upland, and the dark marsh is cut by hidden creeks. Two human figures come ashore from an unseen boat and pick a slow, winding path inland. Harte builds the scene from light, birds, and water before the men can be clearly seen.
the-hermit-and-the-wild-woman-and-other-:
Edith Wharton wrote The Hermit and the Wild Woman and Other Stories, published in New York in 1908, shown in Roman numerals as MCMVIII. The table of contents lists seven stories: the title piece, The Last Asset, In Trust, The Pretext, The Verdict, The Pot-Boiler, and The Best Man.

The title story opens with a hermit living in a cave in the hollow of a hill, above a glen with a stream and oak woods. Across the valley stands a walled town under a Guelf lord. Wharton recalls the day armed men crossed the valley, battered the gates, and filled the streets with fighting, while a boy fled from the town that would shape the hermit's life.
the-hidden-places:
Bertrand W. Sinclair wrote The Hidden Places, copyright 1922 by Little, Brown, and Company. He is named as the author of Big Timber and Poor Man's Rock. A frontispiece caption shows fingers probing damage done by an exploding shell. Chapter one opens with Hollister standing in the middle of his room, staring at the door without truly seeing it.

A feeling close to terror has settled on Hollister like a fog. Sinclair stresses that the dread did not take him by surprise. It had been gathering over him for weeks, and his sharp awareness of thought makes the room itself fade from his sight.
the-high-school-failures: Francis P. OBrien wrote The High School Failures, a study of the school records of pupils failing in academic or commercial high school subjects. The title page notes that the work was submitted for the degree of Doctor of Philosophy at Columbia University and published by Teachers College, Columbia University, in New York City in 1919. The contents outline chapters on the meaning of failure, the field covered, and the sources of the data. Front matter is all that is present here.
the-historic-thames:
Hilaire Belloc wrote The Historic Thames, issued in The Wayfarer's Library by Dent & Sons of London. Belloc opens with a broad claim: England was built up on the framework of her rivers, and the chief line in that pattern is the line of the Thames. He gives reasons in turn, from highway use to tides.

The Thames served as the main highway of southern England, faced east toward the Continent, and no other channel had so helpful a tide. Belloc contrasts Britain's many close-packed navigable rivers with the far-apart great rivers of the Continent. Short portages link one basin to the next, and island tides carry wealth deep inland.
the-historical-nights-entertainment-firs:
Rafael Sabatini wrote The Historical Nights' Entertainment, First Series. A preface explains the task Sabatini set himself. He would rebuild famous events in full detail. He would use all the color the records hold. He chose events that were strange in themselves. Human passions at play drove most of them.

Each tale must follow the recorded facts with care. It must owe nothing to fiction. Imagination may serve only as color. The color fills the grey outlines history leaves. Speech should rest on real words kept by chroniclers. Sabatini admits one case where he broke the rule on purpose.
the-historical-nights-entertainment-seco:
Rafael Sabatini wrote The Historical Nights' Entertainment, Second Series. A letter dated at London in June 1919 dedicates the volume. The dedication goes to David Whitelaw, editor of The Premier Magazine. Sabatini says the tales owe their being to Whitelaw's suggestion. The narratives first ran in that magazine.

The contents name eleven tales with their subjects. The Absolution treats Affonso Henriques, first king of Portugal. The False Demetrius and The Hermosa Fembra follow. Later tales treat the killing of Henry IV. Sir Judas treats the betrayal of Sir Walter Ralegh. The last tale treats Charlotte Corday and Jean Paul Marat.
the-history-of-tom-thumb-and-other-stori:
The History of Tom Thumb and Other Stories was printed in Chicago by M. A. Donohue & Co. and marked profusely illustrated. No editor is named in the pages present. The title story opens in the days of King Arthur, when Merlin, the famous enchanter, stops at the cottage of an honest ploughman to ask for refreshment.

The ploughman's wife serves milk in a wooden bowl and brown bread on a wooden platter. Merlin sees that the neat cottage holds sorrow: the pair have no children, and the wife would be the happiest creature alive with a son no bigger than his father's thumb. Merlin carries the wish to the Queen of the Fairies, and a thumb-sized son is granted.
the-hound-of-the-baskervilles:
A. Conan Doyle wrote The Hound of the Baskervilles, subtitled another adventure of Sherlock Holmes. A letter at the front thanks Robinson: the tale owes its start to his account of a West Country legend, and to his help in the details. The contents list fifteen chapters, from Mr. Sherlock Holmes and The Curse of the Baskervilles to Death on the Moor and A Retrospection.

Chapter one opens at breakfast. Holmes sits at the table while Watson stands on the hearth-rug, holding the stick a visitor left behind the night before. The stick is a fine, thick, bulbous-headed piece of wood of the sort known as a Penang lawyer. A sibling record in the library opens with the same breakfast scene and the same stick.
the-house-of-a-thousand-candles: Meredith Nicholson wrote this novel. His earlier books include The Main Chance and Zelda Dameron. It appeared in 1905 with pictures by Howard Chandler Christy. Nicholson dedicated it to his sister Margaret. Only the front matter and contents are present here. The narrative itself does not appear. The chapter titles hint at an inheritance story. The first chapter concerns the will of John Marshall Glenarm. Later headings mention a face at a restaurant. Others name a voice from the lake, a hidden passage, and eavesdroppers. A girl in gray also appears.
the-house-of-cobwebs-and-other-stories: George Gissing wrote the short fiction in this volume. It appeared in 1906. Thomas Seccombe supplied an introductory survey of Gissing's work. A chronological record of his career follows it. Only the title pages and contents are present here. The stories themselves do not appear. Fifteen pieces are listed in all. They include the title story and A Capitalist. Others are Christopherson, Humplebee, and The Scrupulous Father. A Poor Gentleman and A Lodger in Maze Pond also appear. The titles point to lodgings, money worries, and modest London lives.
the-house-of-the-whispering-pines: Anna Katharine Green wrote this mystery, published in 1910. A quotation from Milton opens it, about intricate mazes. Her earlier successes include The Leavenworth Case and That Affair Next Door. Only the contents pages are present here. The narrative itself does not appear. The headings divide the story into books. The first, called Smoke, moves through a hesitating step and an odd candlestick. A scrap of paper follows, and a lawyer takes the narrator's case. The second book brings the detective Sweetwater to the front.
the-huge-hunter-or-the-steam-man-of-the-: Edward S. Ellis wrote this frontier adventure. A mechanical marvel drives it. A steam-powered man walks the western prairies. Only the title and chapter list are present here. The story itself does not appear. The headings still trace the machine's career. A genius and an artisan build it. It travels on the Yellowstone. It joins miners and a buffalo hunt. A grizzly bear and a ravine attack follow. The final chapter promises the concluding catastrophe. Twenty chapters carry it homeward in all.
the-hungry-stones-and-other-stories:
Rabindranath Tagore's short stories fill this volume. The title tale leads the contents. The Victory and The Home-coming follow. The Kingdom of Cards and The Cabuliwallah appear. The preface explains the translation work. Tagore himself Englished The Victory. C. F. Andrews translated the seven stories after it. The author helped him with them. Other hands assisted as well. They include E. J. Thompson and Sister Nivedita.

The title story opens on a train. The narrator and his kinsman return to Calcutta. A fellow passenger discourses on every subject. His confidence seems total. He quotes science, the Vedas, and Persian poets. He hints that secret forces move the world. Russian advances and English policies fill his talk. Two travelers who never left home sit dumb with wonder. Tagore lets the man's magnetism grow on them. A tale then comes from a voice they cannot judge.
the-ice-maiden-and-other-tales: Hans Christian Andersen's tales appear here in Fanny Fuller's translation. F. Leypoldt published the volume in Philadelphia in 1863. Copyright was entered that year in Pennsylvania. Only the title page, copyright page, and contents heading are present here. The tales themselves do not appear. The title promises the Ice-Maiden as the lead piece. Other tales were to join it. No story titles or page numbers survive in what is shown. The record holds the wrapper of an early American Andersen edition.
the-indian-lily-and-other-stories:
Hermann Sudermann's stories appear here in English. Ludwig Lewisohn translated them in 1911. Six pieces stand beside the title story. They include The Purpose and The Song of Death. The Victim, Autumn, and Merry Folk follow. Thea closes the list. The Indian Lily opens at seven on a May morning. Herr von Niebeldingk opens his iron gate. He steps into a front garden. Blossoming bushes wall it from the street.

Sunlight tints the greyish walls gold. Open window-panes flash with flame. A carpet-beater sounds dully from the second story. The master glances up at it. He thrusts his key rapidly into the lock. A desire stirs in him. He wants to slip past the porter's lodge unseen. Sudermann builds the opening on that small evasion. A respectable house hides a man sneaking out.
the-iroquois-book-of-rites:
Horatio Hale edited this Iroquois record. It is number two in Brinton's Library of Aboriginal American Literature. His preface argues strong claims for it. Accept the custodians' chronology, he says, and a fact follows. Authentic history here reaches fifty years before Columbus. Iroquois tradition links them to still earlier peoples. The Alligewi, or Moundbuilders, stand behind them. Conquerors and conquered meet in that link.

The annals of this continent need not start with colonists, Hale says. The book's chief value is ethnological, though. It shows Iroquois political and social life from inside. Love of peace and human brotherhood appear. Strong domestic affections and respect for law stand out. Hale gathered his material over many visits. Iroquois reservations in Canada and New York supplied it. The volume prints the rites with notes and an appendix.
the-island-pharisees:
John Galsworthy's preface builds a parable of the high road. Every man is born like Shelton in this book, he writes. A road his fathers made waits for him. As a toddler he is charmed by the broad white way. He splashes through puddles without care. He sleeps under roofs raised by those before him. One day he notices a path in the hedge. After that he stops at every opening. One day, heart beating, he tries one.

Nine of ten who try it come back, Galsworthy says. They pity the silly tenth who fares on alone. They miss the irony under their feet. The broad road was once a trackless heath itself. The preface announces the novel's subject precisely. Comfortable England's pharisaism is the target. The rare man who leaves its road is the hero.
the-itinerary-of-archbishop-baldwin-thro:
Giraldus Cambrensis wrote this itinerary of Archbishop Baldwin's Welsh tour. Gerald the Welshman is his other name. The text here comes from the 1912 J. M. Dent edition. The introduction begins with Gerald himself. He was born probably in 1147 at Manorbier Castle in Pembroke. His father was the Norman noble William de Barri. His mother Angharad descended from the famous Princess Nesta. Nesta was called the Helen of Wales.

The editor revels in that ancestry. Rhys ap Tewdwr died against the Normans past fourscore. Gwenllian fell in a skirmish at Kidwelly. Nesta's sons undertook the conquest of Ireland. Gerald called himself a Welshman despite mixed blood. The introduction catalogs his character warmly. Vanity and credulity stand beside shrewd common sense. Wit and eloquence complete the portrait. He counts as a lovable South Walian type.
the-jimmyjohn-boss-and-other-stories:
Owen Wister opens this story collection with a teasing verse. What grows too much the fashion grows vulgar, it says. Excess and cheap copies follow fame. The stranger who writes books should stop, it advises. Leave the masses and join the select few by reading him. The title story begins at Nampa, Idaho. A ruddy, massive, jovial old man stands by the Silver City stage. He pats his beard. He pats the shoulder of a boy beside him.

The old man is a careful German. He is a great cattle man in Oregon and California. He has ridden the branch train from Boise. For nineteen miles he repeated his business orders. He likes to say everything twice when business matters. Vogel and Lex, the ranch partners, are still spoken of. The boy is being sent south on a new mission. Wister builds his western tale from a stagecoach farewell.
the-junior-classics-volume-1-fairy-and-w:
William Patten selected this ten-volume library for boys and girls. He was managing editor of the Harvard Classics. Charles W. Eliot wrote the introduction. William Allan Neilson supplied a reading guide. Volume one is Fairy and Wonder Tales. The introduction explains the purpose. About five thousand pages of tales and poems fill the set. They serve readers from six to sixteen years old.

Eliot argues that taste in reading forms early. The first ten or twelve years decide it. A child's mind prefers good writing if access is easy. Children should choose for themselves from the set. Their enjoyment is the object in view. The set stocked homes with proved material. Anxiety about random reading ran high then. This first volume starts with fairy tales. Children's literature itself starts there too.
the-junior-classics-volume-6-old-fashion: Volume six of The Junior Classics gathers Old-Fashioned Tales. William Patten selected the set for boys and girls. Charles W. Eliot wrote its introduction, and William Allan Neilson supplied a reading guide. Only the title pages and opening contents are present here. The stories themselves do not appear. The contents begin with Mary Mapes Dodge's Race for the Silver Skates. Louisa M. Alcott's Nelly's Hospital follows. Rebecca H. Davis's A Fox and a Raven comes next. Tales by Whitney, Cooke, and Lucretia P. Hale fill the list shown.
the-junior-classics-volume-8-animal-and-: Volume eight of The Junior Classics covers Animal and Nature Stories. William Patten selected the set for boys and girls. Charles W. Eliot wrote its introduction, and William Allan Neilson supplied a reading guide. Only the title pages and contents are present here. The stories themselves do not appear. The contents promise W. T. Hornaday's Little Cyclone, a grizzly cub's story. W. H. G. Kingston treats tigers, wolves, foxes, and bears. Anna Sewell's What Ginger Told Black Beauty appears. Dogs, cats, and a faithful little lizard close the list shown.
the-kreutzer-sonata-and-other-stories: Leo Tolstoy's Kreutzer Sonata appears here in Benjamin R. Tucker's translation, joined by other stories. Only the cover and contents are present here. The tales themselves do not appear. The contents show the title novella in twenty-eight chapters. A piece called Lesson of The Kreutzer Sonata follows. Ivan the Fool comes next, with chapters of its own. The bare listing shows the design. Tolstoy's fierce story of marriage and murder comes first. His own commentary follows. The folk tale of the fool closes it.
the-ladies-vase-or-polite-manual-for-you:
An American lady compiled this polite manual for young ladies. It is original and selected work. This copy is the eighth edition, from Hartford in 1849. H. S. Parsons and Company issued it. Her preface is dated April 16, 1847. She apologizes for adding another volume to a crowded shelf. Similar works were rich in merit, she admits. Their size and expense put them beyond many readers. Those readers were the class the books meant to improve.

She calls female character and manners a matter of great weight. The age is swayed by moral rather than physical force, she says. Her selections gather the best advice on female education. Judicious writers supplied it. The cheaper form puts it within all girls' reach. Only the preface and contents heading are present in full here. The design is plain anyway. A gift-book of conduct was made cheap enough for its readers.
the-laird-s-luck-and-other-fireside-tale:
A. T. Quiller-Couch published these fireside tales in 1901. He signed himself Q. Charles Scribner's Sons of New York issued them. The title tale arrives wrapped in a frame. He prints the frame as an editor's note. A general order of New Year's Day 1836 set it going. Accounts of every regiment's services were to be published. The records of a distinguished regiment fell to Major Reginald Sparkes. The regiment is disguised here as the Moray Highlanders.

Among them Sparkes found manuscript pages sealed and docketed. They concerned Ensign D. M. J. Mackenzie. Their date was January 3, 1816. Sir James Ross, the Waterloo commander, had written them. Private was marked twice underlined. None of the four eyewitnesses survived. The regiment preserved not a rumor. Sparkes left the matter out of his report. Quiller-Couch now prints it in Ross's very words.
the-land-war-in-ireland-a-history-for-th:
James Godkin, former Irish correspondent of The Times, published his history of the Irish land question in London in 1870. His preface says no subject drew more debate over the prior half century. Commissions and committees had filled libraries with reports, yet the cause of Irish distress stayed disputed.

Godkin rejects claims that Ireland was simply perverse or incurable. He argues that boons and experiments failed because they missed the root trouble in landholding. Readers get a reform minded history written for a moment when Parliament faced pressure to act at last. He writes as a witness with a remedy in mind.
the-last-galley-impressions-and-tales:
Arthur Conan Doyle gathers historical tales and modern stories in two parts. Part one holds nine pieces set in the ancient world, from the title tale to the coming of the Huns and the last of the legions. Part two shifts to pieces such as the silver mirror and the terror of Blue John Gap.

The title tale opens in spring, one hundred forty-six years before Christ, off the North African coast. A lone red galley sails toward Carthage through a calm sea. Doyle uses small scenes to test courage, faith, and pride across long spans of history.
the-last-spike-and-other-railroad-storie: Cy Warman published his railroad story collection with Scribner in New York in 1906. Only the title page and contents are present here. Nine pieces are listed, opening with the title story. The list also names the Belle of Athabasca, pathfinding in the Northwest, a mysterious signal, and chasing the white mail. The stories themselves, set on western and Canadian lines, do not appear in this record beyond those titles.
the-laughing-prince-jugoslav-folk-and-fa: Parker Fillmore retold Jugoslav fairy tales and folk tales in a volume illustrated by Jay Van Everen. Only the publisher front pages are present here, praising bright imagery, rolling humor, and tales shaped where Slav, Turk, Greek, and Roman peoples met. The note calls Jugoslavia a highway and battlefield between East and West. The tales themselves, and Fillmore earlier Czechoslovak stories listed beside them, do not appear in this record beyond that praise.
the-law-breakers-and-other-stories:
Robert Grant opens his story collection with George Colfax in an outraged mood. Colfax counts as a passive reformer who reads the Nation, opposes the spoils system, and gives one dollar a year to civil service reform. He votes for the best men after cutting candidate names from a league list.

Grant notes that Colfax still does little beyond talk and complaint about national and city politics. Other stories in the contents include a romance of a soul, an exchange of courtesies, and a surrender. Grant satirizes respectable citizens whose good views rarely turn into action.
the-lazy-tour-of-two-idle-apprentices:
Charles Dickens tells of two idle apprentices who ran from their employer in September 1857. Their mistress is a meritorious lady named Literature, respected everywhere except, perhaps, in the City of London. The pair want a perfectly idle trip with no fixed direction.

They plan to see nothing in particular and to do nothing on purpose. The 1905 Chapman and Hall edition names Dickens alone on its title page and adds illustrations by Harry Furniss and A. J. Goodman. Comic travel writing grows from idleness itself, as the apprentices drift through northern towns and inns.
the-light-princess-and-other-fairy-stori:
George MacDonald gathers three fairy tales in this volume, and the contents name the title tale plus The Giant Heart and The Golden Key. Its opening pages match the single tale record held here, starting with a childless king and queen. The king sulks, counts other queens children, and calls himself ill used.

His patient queen at last bears a lovely daughter, as the opening here shows. Readers should note both records share the same first chapter wording. The princess curse of lightness, the giant child eater, and a golden key quest fill the three tales.
the-light-that-lures:
Percy J. Brebner published his novel in 1911, noting that the English edition bore the title A Gentleman of Virginia. A prologue opens across the waters of Chesapeake Bay. A strong, well knit boy sits on a green hummock with his head in his hands, lost in dreams of real deeds.

Other boys play at battles, sieges, and assaults drawn from the strenuous talk around them. This boy, their master at running, swimming, wrestling, and riding, wants a true future instead of mimicry. Brebner sets a Virginia coming of age story under the shadow of coming war.
the-lily-s-quest-from-twice-told-tales:
Nathaniel Hawthorne tells of two lovers who plan a summer house shaped like an antique temple. Adam Forrester and Lilias Fay mean to consecrate it to refined and innocent enjoyments. Music, fruit, poetry, fiction, and daydreams would fill its pillar shade.

One breezy afternoon they walk her father estate to choose a site, hand in hand down an elm avenue. A dismal figure in a black velvet cloak follows them on the same path. Hawthorne lets Death trail young hope through a bright landscape, turning a building plot search into an allegory of how sorrow attends every human plan.
the-line-of-love-dizain-des-mariages:
James Branch Cabell published his book of marriage tales in 1921, dedicated to Robert Gamble Cabell the First under a Chaucer portrait of a perfect gentle knight. An introduction, by a writer not named on these pages, calls the Cabell case a comedy in the grand manner. Fine, original work sat unnoticed for fifteen years, the introducer says.

Suppression of Cabell novel Jurgen by a purity society then made him famous overnight. Bookshops hunted out his romances at once. The tales here, a dizain on marriages, weigh love, honor, and freedom inside polished, ironic medieval settings.
the-little-dream-an-allegory-in-six-scen: John Galsworthy's The Little Dream, an allegory in six scenes, is dated 1919 in its heading. Only the series lists and title page are present here, so the play itself does not appear. The title page places the play in Galsworthy's second series of plays, numbering it No. 2, alongside The Eldest Son and Justice. A companion record for the same play numbers it No. 1 of that series instead, so the two records disagree on its series number.
the-little-man-a-farcical-morality-in-th:
John Galsworthy's The Little Man, subtitled A Farcical Morality in Three Scenes, appears among his Six Short Plays. Its cast is built from types rather than named people. They include the Little Man, an American, an Englishman and his wife, a German, and a Dutch boy. A mother with her baby and several railway staff complete the list. Scene one is set on the departure platform of an Austrian railway station, at little tables outside the buffet.

The opening dialogue is light and sharp. An English traveller pays for two coffees and settles the sugar with his wife. An American with field-glasses and a pocket camera complains that his eggs have not come. Galsworthy sets national habits side by side in a crowded station, letting small talk and impatience carry the comedy.
the-lonesome-trail-and-other-stories:
B. M. Bower, also writing as B. M. Sinclair, published The Lonesome Trail and Other Stories with Grosset and Dunlap in 1904. The contents list seven western stories, including First Aid to Cupid, When the Cook Fell Ill, The Lamb, The Spirit of the Range, and The Unheavenly Twins. The title story opens by comparing a man to a horse that shies again at the spot where it was once frightened.

The man in question is Will Davidson of the Flying U, known to the Happy Family as Weary. Bower explains that a high-keyed man with pride will deny he was ever afraid, quite sincerely, once the danger proves imaginary. Her cowboy fiction mixes range settings with close attention to pride, fear, and reputation among the crew.
the-lost-hunter-a-tale-of-early-times:
The Lost Hunter, a tale of early times, was published in New York by Derby and Jackson in 1856 and entered for copyright in 1855. No author's name is printed in what is present. An epigraph from Halleck praises a rough land of rock and tree where thoughts, tongues, and hands are bold and free. The book then opens with a playful section called Apology.

The anonymous writer compares bursting before the public without an introduction to barging unannounced into a company of strangers. Such a clown, he says, would deserve an unceremonious invitation to leave at once. Writing from his obscure retreat in the quiet village of Addlebrains, he follows the fashion of introductions before the tale begins. The humor promises a frontier story told with a wink.
the-magic-egg-and-other-stories:
Frank R. Stockton's The Magic Egg and Other Stories gathers a dozen tales. Among them are "His Wife's Deceased Sister," The Widow's Cruise, Captain Eli's Best Ear, A Piece of Red Calico, The Christmas Wreck, and Our Archery Club. The title story opens in the pretty little theatre of the Unicorn Club, hired for a January afternoon by Mr. Herbert Loring. Loring, a handsome man of about thirty, has lately made a long stay in the far East. He means to show invited friends some wonderful things he brought from that country of wonders.

He was very particular with his invitations, saying he could not talk to a crowd. The exclusiveness stirred gossip among the uninvited, yet nearly everyone asked came. Stockton sets up a private exhibition whose mystery depends as much on the audience as on the marvels.
the-magician-s-show-box-and-other-storie:
Lydia Maria Child's The Magician's Show Box and Other Stories collects seven tales, including The Violet Flame, Floribel, The Lady Intelletta, Venus's Dove, and Earning One's Own Living. The title story opens with Gaspar, a boy whose uncle voyages to China and brings home chessmen, queer toys, porcelain vases, and embroidered skullcaps. The uncle's grand descriptions of foreign countries leave Gaspar dissatisfied with his small village and its commonplace dress.

At school Gaspar covers his slate with Turks in turbans as large as small mosques and Chinese with queues several yards long. One day he can bear it no longer. Taking an oaken dagger he carved himself, he sets off on a conquering expedition, stoning a bullfrog on the way. Child writes a child's hunger for adventure with humor and sympathy.
the-magnificent-lovers-les-amants-magnif:
Molière's The Magnificent Lovers, translated into English prose by Charles Heron Wall with short introductions and explanatory notes, began as a royal command. An introductory note says Louis XIV gave the subject; the play was acted before him at Saint-Germain-en-Laye on February 4, 1670, yet never represented in Paris and only printed after Molière's death. The note calls it one of Molière's weakest plays, with his attack on astrology its most interesting part. Molière's own preface explains the design.

The king wanted an entertainment joining everything the stage can furnish. So two rival princes, in the vale of Tempe during the Pythian Games, compete in fêting a young princess and her mother. The cast names Iphicrates and Timocles as the rival lovers, a general, Sostratus, also in love, an astrologer, and Clitidas, a court jester played by Molière himself.
the-majesty-of-calmness-individual-probl:
William George Jordan, author of The Kingship of Self-Control, wrote The Majesty of Calmness, a set of essays on individual problems and possibilities. The contents list Hurry, the Scourge of America, The Power of Personal Influence, and The Dignity of Self-Reliance. Failure as a Success, Doing Our Best at All Times, and The Royal Road to Happiness follow. The title essay opens by calling calmness the rarest quality in human life: the balanced poise of a great nature, at one with itself and its ideals. Jordan is careful about what calmness is not.

The Sphinx is no true type of it, since petrifaction is death, not calm. The fatalist is not calm either, only a coward slave of his environment, drifting like a rudderless ship. The calm man, by contrast, has his course clearly marked on his chart and his hand ever on the helm.
the-man-eaters-of-tsavo-and-other-east-a:
Lieut.-Col. J. H. Patterson wrote The Man-Eaters of Tsavo and Other East African Adventures, with a foreword by Frederick Courteney Selous. In his preface Patterson confesses great diffidence: friends who heard of his unique experiences in the wilds urged him to write, and only after much hesitation did he agree. Readers far from civilization may think some incidents exaggerated, he warns, but he has toned the facts down rather than otherwise.

He stresses the setting's rawness. When these events occurred, British East Africa's railway was still being built through country in a primitive state, and away from the line it remained so. His account covers two years of work and play in the wilds. Patterson hopes it may draw attention to a beautiful and valuable country on the Equator, and thanks the photographers whose pictures appear.
the-man-that-corrupted-hadleyburg-and-ot:
Mark Twain's The Man That Corrupted Hadleyburg and Other Stories and Sketches gathers the title tale with eighteen other pieces. A note points out that the title story may also be found as its own e-text file, and a companion record here carries that story alone. The contents range widely: My First Lie and How I Got Out of It, The Esquimaux Maiden's Romance, Christian Science and the Book of Mrs. Eddy, Concerning the Jews, Travelling with a Reformer, Luck, and In Memoriam.

The title story begins the same way as in the companion record. Hadleyburg, honest for three generations, taught honesty from the cradle and shielded its young from temptation until honesty became bone. Its pride, Twain shows, was also vanity, and vanity is exactly the weakness a revengeful stranger needs when he decides to corrupt the whole town at once.
the-man-upstairs-and-other-stories: P. G. Wodehouse's The Man Upstairs and Other Stories appears here with only its title page and contents, so the stories do not appear. The contents list nineteen tales. First come the title story, Something to Worry About, Deep Waters, When Doctors Disagree, and By Advice of Counsel. The Man Who Disliked Cats, Ruth in Exile, Archibald's Benefit, Pots o' Money, and Out of School follow. Three from Dunsterville, The Tuppenny Millionaire, Sir Agravaine, and The Goal-Keeper and the Plutocrat are among them. Nothing beyond the list is present.
the-man-with-two-left-feet-and-other-sto: P. G. Wodehouse's The Man with Two Left Feet and Other Stories is dated 1917. Only the title page, contents, and the opening lines of the story are present here, so the stories themselves do not appear beyond that start. The contents list Bill the Bloodhound, Extricating Young Gussie, Wilton's Holiday, The Mixer in two parts, and Crowned Heads. At Geisenheimer's, The Making of Mac's, The Romance of an Ugly Policeman, and the title story follow. The opening lines introduce Henry Pifield Rice, who is really only a sort of detective.
the-man-without-a-country-and-other-tale: Edward E. Hale's The Man Without a Country and Other Tales was published in Boston by Roberts Brothers in 1891. Only the title page and contents are present, so the tales do not appear. After the title story come The Last of the Florida, A Piece of Possible History, and The South American Editor. The Old and the New, Face to Face, The Last Voyage of the Resolute, and My Double, and How He Undid Me follow. Named are In His Name and Ten Times One is Ten among Hale's books.
the-man-wolf-and-other-tales: Émile Erckmann and Alexandre Chatrian wrote The Man-Wolf and Other Tales, dated 1876. The record holds only a title page and part of the contents, leaving the tales themselves unread. The contents give The Man-Wolf thirteen numbered chapters with no titles shown, then begin a second tale, Myrtle, with its own first and second chapters before the list breaks off. Nothing further about either story's setting or characters is printed in what is present.
the-mariner-of-st-malo-a-chronicle-of-th:
Stephen Leacock wrote The Mariner of St Malo, a chronicle of the voyages of Jacques Cartier, as volume two of the Chronicles of Canada, published at Toronto in 1915. Chapter one begins with a portrait. In the town hall of St Malo hangs a picture of Cartier, the great sea-captain of that port, whose name is joined for all time with the title Discoverer of Canada. He stands on a ship's deck, chin on hand, eyes gazing over the western ocean as if seeking to penetrate its mysteries. Leacock reads the face closely: firm and strong, tight-set jaw, prominent brow, the full inquiring eye of a man used to thinking and acting.

The contents trace three voyages: Newfoundland, Labrador, and the Gulf of St Lawrence; the river, Stadacona, and a winter there; and Hochelaga. The close of Cartier's career follows, with an itinerary and bibliographic note.
the-marriages:
Henry James wrote the novella The Marriages, printed here from the 1922 Macmillan edition of his collection Daisy Miller, Pandora, The Patagonia and Other Tales. The opening scene follows a large dinner at the London home of Mrs. Churchley, a wealthy and imposing hostess. Young Adela Chart lingers with her father, Colonel Chart, and studies the grand rooms around her.

Adela wonders whether Mrs. Churchley's fortune matches her huge sofas, jewels, and tall horses. Her father addresses their hostess with a familiarity that suggests more than a dinner invitation. James lets small signals carry the tension, from a flourished fan to a resentful tone of voice. Readers get a sharp study of manners, money, and a daughter watching her father's interest in a widow take shape.
the-mason-bees:
J. Henri Fabre's essays on mason-bees appear here in English in a translation by Alexander Teixeira de Mattos. The translator's note explains that the volume gathers every essay on the Chalicodomae, the mason-bees proper, from Fabre's Souvenirs entomologiques. Two extra studies join them: an essay on Fabre's cats and his single study of red ants. Both bear on the sense of direction that the bees display.

De Mattos notes that essays on the Osmiae, also mason-bees, wait in a companion volume called Bramble-bees and Others. Some chapters had already appeared in English and American magazines, while others reach English readers for the first time here. Two chapters on experiments and exchanged nests come in a fresh translation made for the uniform edition of Fabre's works. Readers get close observation of how these bees build, orient themselves, and find home.
the-matador-of-the-five-towns-and-other-: Arnold Bennett published The Matador of the Five Towns and Other Stories in 1912. Only the title page and a list of Bennett's other books are present here, so the stories themselves do not appear. The list shows his range by that year: novels such as The Old Wives' Tale and Clayhanger, fantasias such as The Grand Babylon Hotel, and earlier Five Towns story collections. His nonfiction includes How to Live on Twenty-Four Hours a Day.
the-memoirs-of-sherlock-holmes:
Arthur Conan Doyle's The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes gathers twelve cases narrated by Dr. Watson. The contents run from Silver Blaze and The Yellow Face to The Greek Interpreter and The Naval Treaty. The collection closes with The Final Problem, the story that sends Holmes against his great enemy. Silver Blaze opens at breakfast in Baker Street, where Holmes announces that he must go to Dartmoor, to King's Pyland.

Watson is unsurprised, since the case has filled every newspaper in England. A favorite racehorse for the Wessex Cup has vanished, and its trainer has been murdered. Holmes has paced the room for a day, chin on chest, recharging his pipe with strong black tobacco and ignoring questions. Fresh editions of the papers arrive only to be tossed into a corner. Readers join a detective whose silence means the problem has already engaged his full powers of analysis.
the-memorable-thoughts-of-socrates:
Xenophon's Memorabilia of Socrates appears here as The Memorable Thoughts of Socrates, in Edward Bysshe's translation, printed by Cassell in 1888. The introduction explains that Bysshe first published his version in 1712 and revised it in 1722. It kept a good reputation, with another edition in 1758. The editor notes he has changed Bysshe's 'Things' into 'Thoughts,' since a wise man's sayings and doings both express his thought.

The introduction then sketches Xenophon's own life as Socrates' pupil. At Delium in 424 B.C., Socrates reportedly carried the fallen Xenophon from the field on his back. Xenophon later marched with Cyrus the Younger into Persia and helped lead the Greek retreat told in his Anabasis. He fought beside Sparta, settled at Scillus for some twenty years, and wrote there. Readers approach Socrates through the soldier-student who preserved his conversations, in an English version already old when Cassell reprinted it.
the-mercenaries:
H. Beam Piper's story The Mercenaries was produced from Astounding Science Fiction of March 1950, illustrated by Brush. Its opening line of commentary observes that wars were once won by maneuvering hired fighting men, while modern wars need different hired experts. The human problems, the editor promises, remain. Duncan MacLeod, the hero, begins by hanging up his suit and sealing his laundry at a research establishment's gate.

Naked except for a plastic identity disk, MacLeod submits to a search by attendants with searchlights, magnetic detectors, and patient hands. Soldiers passing through receive the same treatment. MacLeod counts himself a connoisseur of security after fifteen years of research and development work for a dozen nations.
