Even so, the Tonto Basin Research Establishment of the Philadelphia Project exceeds anything he has seen. Readers enter a Cold War laboratory where expertise itself is the mercenary trade.
the-moon-endureth-tales-and-fancies:
John Buchan's The Moon Endureth: Tales and Fancies, dated 1912, is present here only through a contents list that stops at the seventh section, so none of the tales appear. A sibling record of the same collection carries a longer contents and the opening poem; this one ends earlier, at The Riding of Ninemileburn and its accompanying verses, Plain Folk.

Earlier headings pair stories with songs. The Company of the Marjolaine comes with Avignon 1759, A Lucid Interval with a revised Shorter Catechism, and The Lemnian with Atta's Song. Space, Streams of Water in the South, and The Grove of Ashtaroth complete the visible list, each trailed by a short poem title.
the-mysterious-affair-at-styles:
Agatha Christie's The Mysterious Affair at Styles lays out thirteen chapters in its contents, from I Go to Styles through Poirot Investigates and The Inquest to Poirot Explains. Chapter I opens with the narrator explaining why he writes. Public interest in the Styles Case has cooled, yet worldwide notoriety and persistent rumours persuade him, at Poirot's request and the family's, to set down the whole story.

Invalided home from the Front, the narrator spent months in a depressing convalescent home before receiving a month's sick leave. With no near relations or friends, he ran into John Cavendish, a man fifteen years his senior whom he had known since boyhood visits to Styles, the Cavendish place in Essex. Their talk of old times ended with an invitation to spend the leave there.
the-mysterious-stranger-and-other-storie:
Mark Twain's collection The Mysterious Stranger and Other Stories carries an honest warning at its head. The title story was written in 1898 and never finished. Editors of Twain's Collected Works completed it before publication, and the printed copy does not make clear where Twain stopped and the editors began. Three shorter pieces follow it in the contents: A Fable, Hunting the Deceitful Turkey, and The McWilliamses and the Burglar Alarm.

Chapter 1 of the title story opens in Austria in the winter of 1590. The boy narrator remembers a country far from the world and asleep, still in the Middle Ages by its mental and spiritual clock. His village drowsed by a tranquil river beneath a vine-covered castle, in a prince's hereditary lands, content and almost untouched by news.
the-naturalist-on-the-thames:
C. J. Cornish's The Naturalist on the Thames is present here only in title page and contents, so the river essays do not appear. A frontispiece shows a fox flushing pheasants, from a drawing by Lancelot Speed. Cornish's fellowship of the Zoological Society is printed after his name.

Seventeen pieces are listed. The Thames at Sinodun Hill, The Filling of the Thames, and The Shells of the Thames begin the book, followed by river plants and insects. The Chavender or Chub, The World's First Butterflies, and Butterfly Sleep mix natural history with sport. Crayfish and trout, bird migration down the Thames, Wittenham Wood, a February fox hunt, and eel-traps close the visible list.
the-nest-in-the-honeysuckles-and-other-s:
The Nest in the Honeysuckles, and Other Stories was written for the American Sunday-School Union and published at Philadelphia, with offices in New York, Boston, Cincinnati, and Louisville. Only a frontispiece caption, title page, and the start of a contents list are present here, so the stories themselves do not appear. No author is named on the pages shown. Copyright was entered in 1855 by the Union.

A printed notice explains the Union's committee of publication: fourteen members drawn from seven denominations, no more than three from any one, and no book issued over any member's objection. The frontispiece shows Mrs. Dudley standing by her little boy at a window. Contents begin with the title story at page 7.
the-new-boy-at-hilltop-and-other-stories:
Ralph Henry Barbour's The New Boy at Hilltop and Other Stories, dedicated To Belinda, collects twelve school and college tales listed in its contents. The Proving of Jerry, McTurkle the Band, Patsy's story, Pemberton's Fluke, The Seventh Tutor, and A Race with the Waters are among them, alongside The Triple Play and The Dub.

The title story opens with a small arithmetical mystery. Hilltop School ended its fall term counting just ninety-five students. When it reopened on the third of January, two weeks later, it had ninety-six, and thereby hangs the tale, Barbour writes. The explanation begins with Kenneth Garwood, whose entry at Hilltop had been arranged back in the autumn.
the-ninth-vibration-and-other-stories:
L. Adams Beck's The Ninth Vibration and Other Stories collects eight tales named in its contents. The Interpreter, a romance of the East, and The Incomparable Lady, a story of China with a moral, follow the title story. The Hatred of the Queen, a story of Burma, Fire of Beauty, The Building of the Taj Mahal, and two tales with quoted titles complete the list.

The title story opens on an ancient track running from India into Tibet, nine thousand feet up in the purest air. It leaves Simla by a stately road, then narrows beside steep drops called khuds, where baggage goes by coolie and travellers ride or are pushed in a small carriage. Deodar trees darken the way toward a rambling bungalow known as the House in the Woods.
the-nomad-of-the-nine-lives:
A cat tells the story of his own life in a book by A. Frances Friebe, with pictures by Clara R. Atwood. The book is dedicated to the Rev. Francis H. Howley, president of the S.P.C.A. In the preface the cat explains that his nephew Tom urged him to write, after hearing many tales told beside the fire.

The cat argues that cats earn their place in a home. They give company to lonely people, kill rats and mice, and guard corn in barns. He also quotes a Boston newspaper report that thousands of abandoned cats and dogs are killed each year after owners move away and leave them behind.
the-odds-and-other-stories:
Ethel M. Dell published The Odds and Other Stories in 1922. Dell had already written The Bars of Iron, The Keeper of the Door, and The Way of an Eagle. The contents list seven tales: The Odds, Without Prejudice, Her Own Free Will, The Consolation Prize, Her Freedom, Death's Property, and The Sacrifice.

The title story opens with Dot Burton, a tanned, boyish young woman who vows to shoot a man named Buckskin Bill if he crosses her path. Her brother Jack warns her not to shoot a policeman by mistake. The banter sets up a western-flavored tale of threats, pride, and romance.
the-old-nurse-s-story-and-other-tales:
Elizabeth Gaskell wrote The Old Nurse's Story, the lead tale in a group of her stories dated 1852. An old nurse tells the children of her former charge how she came into the family. She was a village schoolgirl in Westmoreland when the young clergyman's wife chose her as nurse-maid for the coming baby, Miss Rosamond.

Both parents died within a fortnight when Rosamond was four or five, and the child was sent to Furnivall Manor House in Northumberland. There an old Miss Furnivall lived alone with a few servants in a grand, empty house. The nurse, not yet eighteen, found herself and her pet left among strangers, far from home.
the-only-true-mother-goose-melodies:
An exact reproduction of the original edition of Mother Goose's Melodies comes with an introduction by the Rev. Edward Everett Hale. Hale leaves the history of Madam Vergoose and her son-in-law Mr. Fleet to the editor's preface. He points readers to William Whitmore's paper, printed in Albany in 1889, which reproduced Isaiah Thomas's 1785 edition in facsimile.

Hale instead recalls the Mother Goose of his own Boston childhood, the small quarto on which a whole line of Bostonians was raised. He remembers an old nurse who said "weal" and "winegar" like a London Cockney, and children playing English games. His piece ties the rhymes to a vanishing old Boston.
the-opera-a-sketch-of-the-development-of: R. A. Streatfeild wrote The Opera, a sketch of the development of opera with full descriptions of all works in the modern repertory. J. A. Fuller-Maitland wrote the introduction, and this third edition, revised and enlarged, came from Routledge in London. Front matter and a contents list are present, with no chapter text after them. The list begins with the beginnings of opera, naming Peri, Monteverdi, Lully, Purcell, and Handel, and reaches Rossini, Donizetti, and Bellini.
the-pacha-of-many-tales:
Captain Marryat wrote The Pacha of Many Tales. A prefatory note explains that the book imitates the Arabian Nights. A pacha, charmed by Scheherazade's stories, wants a stock of tales of his own and, helped by a wily barber-vizier, gathers tellers to entertain him. An English sailor dragged before him is told he must tell lies and will have gold.

The list of tales names the Story of the Camel-Driver, the Story of the Greek Slave, the voyages of Huckaback, The Scarred Lover, and The Wondrous Tale of Han. The note praises the tales as stories of intrigue and adventure told with a straight face.
the-path-of-duty-and-other-stories: H. S. Caswell wrote The Path of Duty, and Other Stories, published by John Lovell at Montreal in 1874. Only the title page and the start of the contents are present here, so the stories themselves do not appear. The contents are given to the first tale, Clara Roscom; or, The Path of Duty, in numbered chapters. They run from A Sudden Bereavement and Success at School through Clara as governess in Mr. Leighton's family, to A New England Home and New Occupations.
the-philistines: Arlo Bates wrote The Philistines. A dedication thanks three friends who acted as amanuenses, his secretaries, so the book could be finished. Only that front matter and the contents are present here, so the novel itself does not appear. The chapter titles are lines from Shakespeare. They overlap heavily with the titles in Bates's The Pagans, a sister record in the library. In Place and In Account Nothing stands near the head of both lists. Some Speech of Marriage and In Way of Taste appear in both as well.
the-piazza-tales:
Herman Melville's The Piazza Tales came out in New York from Dix and Edwards in 1856, with a London issue by Sampson Low, Son and Co. Six pieces make up the volume: The Piazza, Bartleby, Benito Cereno, The Lightning-Rod Man, The Encantadas, and The Bell-Tower. Melville is named on the title page as the author of Typee and Omoo.

The opening piece begins with a narrator who has moved into an old farmhouse in the country. The house lacks a piazza, a fault he regrets, because the country round about is so fine a picture. Painters plant their easels in every nook there during berry season. His house is old, and the frame tale sets a quiet, watchful tone for the stranger stories after it.
the-poems-of-goethe-translated-in-the-or: The Poems of Goethe, translated in the original metres by Edgar Alfred Bowring, reaches this record through an old Project Gutenberg header. The header is numbered Etext 1287 and dated April 1998. Only that header is present here, so the poems themselves do not appear. It gives the title and names Bowring as translator before the usual Gutenberg notices. Nothing of Goethe's verse can be seen in what is present. No contents list or title page from a printed edition appears either.
the-poetical-works-of-beattie-blair-and-: The Poetical Works of Beattie, Blair, and Falconer was issued with lives and critical dissertations by the Reverend George Gilfillan. Here only the title page and contents appear, so the poems themselves are absent. Beattie's section opens with an account of his life and poetry, then The Minstrel, or the Progress of Genius. Miscellaneous poems follow: odes to hope and peace, The Judgment of Paris, The Triumph of Melancholy, and The Hermit. Epitaphs and fables appear too. Blair's section is headed by his life and The Grave; Falconer's works follow.
the-poetical-works-of-oliver-wendell-hol:
Verses from the Oldest Portfolio close The Poetical Works of Oliver Wendell Holmes. A bracketed note calls the file Volume 3 of the 1893 three-volume set. The pieces come from The Collegian of 1830, illustrated annuals, and similar early outlets. Titles include The Mysterious Visitor, The Toadstool, and The Spectre Pig. To a Caged Lion, The Star and the Water-Lily, A Roman Aqueduct, Our Yankee Girls, and The Ballad of the Oysterman appear too.

Holmes frames the section with a candid note. These verses, he says, have always been printed in his collected poems. Most, he admits, will bear only one reading, so he allows them to appear again. They stand in a less conspicuous position than his other productions. The apology, offered with Latin mottoes from Horace and Quintilian, presents the juvenilia as a chick not yet fledged beside the mature work.
the-poetry-of-wales:
The Poetry of Wales, edited by John Jenkins and published by Houlston and Sons at London in 1873, offers Welsh poetry in English translation. Jenkins's preface explains the want the volume supplies. English friends eminent in literature had told him they had heard of the value of Welsh writing. They asked why no one translated it, when versions existed for almost every other nation. Jenkins says he took no payment for the work. He wants only to extend the treasures of his native country's literature.

His introduction argues that a people's literature reflects its character and history. The age of Homer was heroic, and Virgil's Rome gallant. Chaucer, Spenser, and Sidney moved through feudal halls and enchanted vistas. Shakespeare, he writes, portrayed the British mind in both its grave and comic moods. Milton mirrors a sober, spiritual age.
the-politeness-of-princes-and-other-scho:
P. G. Wodehouse's The Politeness of Princes and Other School Stories collects early tales written between 1905 and 1910, in a selection assembled for Project Gutenberg. The contents date each story. The title piece, Shields' and the Cricket Cup, and An International Affair all come from 1905. The Guardian comes from 1908, and Pillingshot, Detective from 1910. All are set in the world of the English public school.

The title story opens by asking readers to examine the painful case of G. Montgomery Chapple, a bachelor of Seymour's house at Wrykyn. Chapple's speciality, the narrator says, was being late for breakfast as a daily habit. Sometimes he scrambled in while coffee was still going round, fastening his waistcoat as he came. More often he waited for Mr. Seymour to leave. Then he made his private bargain with Herbert, the house factotum, whose standing with the cook could win him something hot.
the-portent-and-other-stories:
George MacDonald's The Portent, leading story in The Portent and Other Stories, is subtitled a story of the inner vision of the Highlanders, commonly called the second sight. MacDonald inscribes the volume, in a letter dated Kensington, May 1864, to a friend of his father's.

The letter defends the tale as a romance. MacDonald grants that the word romance condemns a story with many readers. Yet he argues for a place for any tale founded in the marvellous that stays true to human nature and to itself. Even The Rime of the Ancient Mariner meets that test. Shakespeare allows any amount of the marvellous on the same condition. He also apologises that a story built on his ancestors' belief in second sight must differ in tone from his other work. He asks for a shadowy nook where a reader may dream.
the-pot-of-gold-and-other-stories: Mary E. Wilkins's The Pot of Gold and Other Stories was published by D. Lothrop Company at Boston in 1893, under an 1892 copyright. Here only the title page, contents, and illustration list appear, so the stories themselves are absent. Sixteen stories are listed, opening with the title piece and The Cow with Golden Horns. The Christmas Monks, The Pumpkin Giant, The Silver Hen, and Toby follow. Later entries include The Patchwork School, The Bound Girl, and Deacon Thomas Wales's Will.
the-prehistoric-world-or-vanished-races: E. A. Allen's The Prehistoric World, or Vanished Races, was published at Nashville by the Central Publishing House in 1885. Allen is named as author of The Golden Gems of Life. The page shown is the title page, and it carries an unusual feature: a list of scholars who reviewed chapters and made suggestions. They include C. C. Abbott, F. W. Putnam of Harvard's Peabody Museum, and A. F. Bandelier. Charles Rau of the Smithsonian, Alexander Winchell, and Cyrus Thomas are also named. No chapter text is shown here.
the-pretentious-young-ladies:
Molière's comedy The Pretentious Young Ladies, a one-act prose play from 1659, opens with an introductory notice on what the piece changed. With it, the notice says, Molière began to portray men and women exactly as they are. Living characters and existing manners became the groundwork of his plays. From that time he gave up imitating Italian and Spanish intrigue plots.

The notice traces the fashion the play mocks. Parisian ladies had once worked to refine coarse language, and the Hôtel de Rambouillet did that work well. By 1658 a new clique cared only for phrases out of the common way. Their style was pretentious and affected, spoiling the national idiom instead of improving it. Every lady in Paris and the provinces kept a drawing-room where borrowed, exaggerated talk ruled. The novels of Mademoiselle de Scudéry served as the textbook of these would-be wits.
the-princess-elopes:
Harold MacGrath's The Princess Elopes was issued at New York by Grosset and Dunlap under a 1905 copyright. MacGrath is named as author of The Puppet Crown, The Grey Cloak, and The Man on the Box. Harrison Fisher drew the illustration, showing Princess Hildegarde at the piano. The book is dedicated to the author's wife.

Chapter I opens with a former diplomat as narrator, confessing he cannot recall where the Grand Duchy of Barscheit or the principality of Doppelkinn exactly lie. Berlin and Vienna were easily reached, he says, and three hours brought one under the Carpathians. Her sister states knew Barscheit as a meddler and troublemaker, ruled by a duke nicknamed Old Grumpy. In the narrator's Yankee phrase, she had a finger in every pie and a ladle in every political broth.
the-princess-passes: The Princess Passes, a romance of a motor-car by C. N. and A. M. Williamson, authors of The Lightning Conductor, was published by Henry Holt in 1905. The opening pages hold the title page and a dedication to a princess who makes the Riviera sunnier. The first contents entries are Woman Disposes, Mercédès to the Rescue, and In Search of a Mule. The motoring story itself is not reached in the pages provided, which stop at the chapter list.
the-principal-navigations-voyages-traffi: Richard Hakluyt's Principal Navigations, Voyages, Traffiques and Discoveries of the English Nation appears here in Edmund Goldsmid's edition. Transcriber's notes explain that Hakluyt's sixteenth-century spelling is kept, with manuscript abbreviations silently expanded. This record is Volume II, Northeastern Europe and Adjacent Countries, Part I: Tartary. The pages at hand hold the notes and the volume's title pages only; none of the voyage narratives themselves are shown.
the-prophetic-pictures-from-twice-told-t:
Nathaniel Hawthorne's Prophetic Pictures, from Twice Told Tales, begins with Walter Ludlow praising a painter in Boston. The man talks Hebrew with Dr. Mather and lectures on anatomy to Dr. Boylston, meeting every instructed man on his own ground. He adapts himself to every character, so all find a mirror in him. Walter lowers his voice for the greatest wonder: the painter renders not features but mind and heart, catching secret sentiments like sunshine, or infernal fire in dark souls.

Elinor asks whether Walter describes a painter or a wizard, and whether Boston is safe for him. Walter begs her not to let the man paint the frightened, sad look she wears at that moment. A headnote says the story grew from an anecdote of the painter Stuart in Dunlap's History of the Arts of Design.
the-real-thing-and-other-tales: Henry James gathers short tales in an edition issued at London by Macmillan in 1893 for circulation in India and the British colonies. A short note explains that the second tale first appeared in The Cosmopolitan under a different title. Here only the title pages and that note are present, so the tales themselves do not appear.
the-red-book-of-heroes: Mrs. Lang wrote and Andrew Lang edited a companion to the fairy books, issued by Longmans at London in 1909 with plates and illustrations by A. Wallis Mills. Contents open with a lady-in-chief and prisoners and captives, then give lives of Hannibal, a missionary to lepers, a constant prince, Montrose, Gordon, and others, closing with the crime of Theodosius. Here only the title pages and contents list are present, so the hero lives themselves do not appear.
the-red-redmaynes: Eden Phillpotts published his mystery at New York in 1922. Macmillan issued it. Contents open with a rumour and a problem stated. A mystery and a clue follow. Robert Redmayne is seen, and then he is heard. A compact and a death in a cave come next. A piece of wedding cake closes the opening list. Only the title pages are present here. A list of the author's books and the chapter list appear with them. The investigation itself does not appear.
the-redheaded-outfield-and-other-basebal:
Zane Grey turns from westerns to baseball in these stories. Delaney's outfield trio all wear red hair on the field. Red Gilbat plays left, and Reddy Clammer plays right. Reddie Ray covers center between them for the club. Their manager counts them a pride and a trouble together.

Gilbat hits for a very high average in the opener. Yet he vanishes like a will-o'-the-wisp before games begin. Scouts have found him peeping through knotholes with small boys. Clammer plays to the grandstand with circus catches instead. Easy plays look hard when Clammer handles them daily. A rube's rise, pennant, honeymoon, and Waterloo fill companion tales. Grey's affection for the game shows in every detail.
the-return-of-sherlock-holmes:
Arthur Conan Doyle lists thirteen adventures, from an empty house and a Norwood builder through dancing men, a solitary cyclist, Black Peter, Charles Augustus Milverton, and six Napoleons to a second stain. Watson opens the first case in spring 1894 with London fascinated by the murder of Ronald Adair.

Watson explains that police facts were partly suppressed because the prosecution case was already overwhelming, and that only after nearly ten years can he supply the missing links. The sequel, he promises, outshocked the crime itself. A companion record in the set carries the same opening with magazine details, and readers should expect the same stories in both.
the-romance-of-the-milky-way-and-other-s:
Lafcadio Hearn published his Japanese studies and stories with Houghton Mifflin at Boston and New York in October 1905. Contents list the title romance, goblin poetry, ultimate questions, a mirror maiden, a story of Ito Norisuke, a piece stranger than fiction, and a letter from Japan.

The title piece opens with an ancient scholar calling the Milky Way, the River of Heaven, a ghost of waters that shifts its bed through the year like an earthly river. Hearn then turns to the many charming festivals of old Japan. Folklore, astronomy, and quiet wonder meet in his characteristic blend of study and story.
the-rudder-grangers-abroad-and-other-sto:
Frank R. Stockton's The Rudder Grangers Abroad and Other Stories is dated 1891 and 1894. It gathers six pieces. They include Euphemia Among the Pelicans and The Rudder Grangers in England. Pomona's Daughter, Derelict, and The Baker of Barnbury follow. The Water-Devil closes the contents.

The first story opens on a little yacht. Winter sunshine warms the semi-tropics. Seven pelicans labor slowly through the air. Mullet spring from the river ahead of a shark. The narrator lies on the cabin roof. Euphemia stands below, her elbows on its edge. A paying teller writes at a hanging shelf. A little lady keeps a note-book nearby. At the tiller stands their boatman. His sombre eye stays fixed south-by-east.
the-safety-curtain-and-other-stories: Ethel M. Dell's The Safety Curtain and Other Stories was issued by Grosset and Dunlap under arrangement with G. P. Putnam's Sons. The title page lists many earlier Dell novels, including The Way of an Eagle and The Knave of Diamonds. The portion shown here gives the title matter and contents alone, with no story text following. The contents names three pieces: The Safety Curtain, The Experiment, and Those Who Wait. Readers can see the collection's shape, but none of its narratives are shown.
the-satyricon-volume-06-editor-s-notes:
Volume six of W. C. Firebaugh's unexpurgated Satyricon translation gathers the editor's notes. The Petronius text itself gives way to commentary here. The first note is headed Prostitution. It opens with a claim about two basic instincts. They are the will to live and the will to propagate the species.

From their interplay, the note argues, prostitution took origin. It calls the profession the oldest in human experience. Roman evidence is then marshalled at length. Livy is cited, along with the Bacchanalian cult and the comedies of Plautus and Terence. A passage from Cicero's Pro Coelio is quoted in support. The Floralia festival, introduced about 238 B.C., is said to have sped the spread of the practice.
the-satyricon-volume-07-marchena-notes:
Volume seven of W. C. Firebaugh's unexpurgated Satyricon translation prints six notes by Marchena. The first is addressed to the Army of the Rhine. Marchena credits French conquests with a boon to knowledge and letters. Convent libraries were ransacked, he says. Precious manuscripts came to light.

His note claims a fragment of Petronius was found at St. Gall. Soldiers sent the manuscript for examination. The text of St. Gennadius on the duties of priests covered it. Beneath that writing lay an earlier, almost effaced text. Marchena says the deciphered morsel fills a gap in the Quartilla episode. He insists its Latin style makes forgery impossible to believe. Readers should note that the wider set openly labels Marchena's contributions as forgeries.
the-science-of-fingerprints-classificati:
The Federal Bureau of Investigation made The Science of Fingerprints for police use. Its subtitle is Classification and Uses. The title page names the Department of Justice. John Edgar Hoover is listed as the Bureau's chief. An introduction tells who the book is for. It serves offices that may start print files of their own.

The book rests on the Bureau's long work with prints, the introduction says. That work built the largest set of filed prints in the world. The Bureau's own systems are set forth in full. How to read print patterns gets close treatment. Prints help catch men and women on the run, the text argues. Past arrests can be proved with them. Courts can then set fairer terms, and parole boards gain firm facts.
the-sea-fairies:
L. Frank Baum wrote The Sea Fairies for readers who had followed Dorothy's adventures in Oz. John R. Neill illustrated the book. Baum dedicated it to Judith of Randolph, Massachusetts. His preface is dated Hollywood, 1911. Two-thirds of the earth's surface is covered with water, he begins. What people inhabit that water has always roused curiosity on land.

The story is fanciful, Baum admits. Its sea people talk and act much as land people do. The mermaids are not unlike familiar fairies, he says. Yet they are real sea people in his telling, except Zog the Magician. Learned people deny mermaids exist, he notes. Proving that would require living under water, as Trot and Cap'n Bill did. Young correspondents had implored him to write about mermaids, he adds.
the-second-class-passenger-fifteen-stori:
Perceval Gibbon's The Second Class Passenger gathers fifteen stories. Methuen first published it in 1913. Chapman and Dodd issued it in the Abbey Library in 1922. Titles include The Sense of Climax, The Murderer, and The Victim. The Poor in Heart, The Strange Patient, and The Widower also appear.

The title story opens in Mozambique. A party from a big German mail-boat has nearly finished inspecting the town. They walked the main street, admired the palms, and lunched at Lazarus's costly table. They bought curios as mementoes, including Indian silks and Birmingham metal-work. Miss Paterson invested in a heavy bronze image. She cherished the delusion that it was an object of local worship. Dawson, her favored courtier, carried it for her. Having lunched, he was fated to leave it behind at the hotel.
the-seven-vagabonds-from-twice-told-tale:
Nathaniel Hawthorne's The Seven Vagabonds, drawn from Twice-Told Tales, casts its narrator as a rambling pedestrian. In the spring of his life he reached a crossroads one afternoon. The main road ran straight to Boston. A left branch went toward the sea, and a right-hand path led over hills to Canada.

At the guidepost stood a huge covered wagon, like a small house on wheels. Music proceeded from its interior, and a shower was climbing the western sky. The narrator hailed the doorkeeper and stepped up a short ladder. A respectable old personage appeared, mild as an aged schoolmaster. He was bound for the camp-meeting at Stamford, he said. He merely tarried to refresh his cattle on this dull day for business.
the-silent-places:
Stewart Edward White published The Silent Places with McClure, Phillips and Company in 1904. Philip R. Goodwin illustrated it, and White dedicated it to his mother. A list of illustrations precedes the text. Its captions show woodsmen raising their rifles and a hound sniffing deep in feather snow.

Chapter one opens at about eight o'clock on an early summer evening. A group of men sits on a grass-plot overlooking a broad river. The sun is just setting through the forest fringe behind them. Some men recline in the short grass, White writes. Others lean against the carriages of two highly ornamented field-guns. The guns' embossed muzzles gape silently at an eastern shore. That shore lies nearly two miles distant, across the river.
the-sister-years-from-twice-told-tales:
Nathaniel Hawthorne's The Sister Years, drawn from Twice-Told Tales, opens on the last night of the year. Between eleven and twelve o'clock, the Old Year sat down on the steps of the new City Hall. She looked weary of body and sad of heart, Hawthorne writes. Her garments were ruined by foul weather and rough usage. Her shoes were scarcely worth mending.

She set down a capacious bandbox beside her. Under her arm she carried a folio book like a newspaper's annual volume. She rested her elbows on it and sighed over her past existence. Then a young maiden came lightsomely from the railroad depot. Her face smiled with cheerfulness and confidence in a kind reception. Her dress was too airy for the season, Hawthorne notes. Still, hardly anybody could meet the New Year without hope, he says.
the-smiling-hill-top-and-other-californi: Julia M. Sloane wrote The Smiling Hill-Top and Other California Sketches. Charles Scribner's Sons published it in New York, with a 1919 copyright. Carleton M. Winslow illustrated the book. Sloane dedicated it to her three companions of the road, one large and two small. The pages shown give the title matter and contents only. An introduction comes first, then the title sketch at page five. A California poppy, gardeners, and thorns follow. The gypsy trail, an adventure in solitude, and a Sabine farm appear later.
the-spell-of-the-yukon-and-other-verses:
Robert W. Service, the British-born Canadian poet, gathers his northern ballads in a volume also published in Britain as Songs of a Sourdough, matching American editions of 1907 and 1916. The poems are present here, opening with The Land God Forgot. That poem is a grim salute to a land of lonely sunsets and lordly mountains. A lone wolf howls under a gibbous moon.

That opening poem calls the Yukon an outcast land whose hate and abysmal loneliness the wolf-cry expresses. A contents list pairing titles with first lines follows. It promises the rhyming tales of gold-rush camps, trails, and hard winters. Those tales made Service the best-known verse chronicler of the Canadian north.
the-spirit-of-st-francis-de-sales: Jean Pierre Camus, bishop of Belley and friend of the saint, wrote this portrait of Francis de Sales, translated here by J. S. in a new and enlarged edition carrying a 1910 Westminster imprimatur and a preface by the Archbishop of Westminster. Only the title pages and contents are present here. The contents name chapters on perfect virtue and the lesser virtues. They also cover temptations against faith, confidence in God, and waiting upon God. Camus's recollections themselves do not appear.
the-spread-eagle-and-other-stories: Gouverneur Morris published this story collection in 1910. The pages present here hold the title page and his playful dedication verses. The verses address Elsie, Patsie, and Kate. Morris pretends that three pretty girls now rule him from the chair he thought was his. He does what he is told. He must even produce stories and get them sold. The tales themselves do not appear.
the-story-of-the-guides: Colonel G. J. Younghusband of the Queen's Own Corps of Guides wrote this regimental history, published by Macmillan in London in 1908 and dedicated, by special permission, to King Edward VII as the corps' colonel-in-chief. Only opening pages and a contents heading appear here. Younghusband gives thanks there. He thanks past and present officers of the Guides. He thanks two authors too. They are Lumsden of the Guides and the memoirs of General Sir Henry Dermot Daly. The history itself does not appear.
the-story-of-the-hymns-and-tunes: Theron Brown and Hezekiah Butterworth compiled this history of hymns and tunes, published in New York in 1906 with Thomas Ken's portrait as frontispiece. Only title page and contents appear here. The contents show sections. Hymns of great witnesses come first. Hymns of devotion and experience follow. Missionary hymns and hymns of suffering and trust come next. Christian ballads and old revival hymns appear too. Sunday school hymns and patriotic hymns follow. Sailors' hymns and hymns of Wales close the list. The hymn stories themselves do not appear.
the-story-of-the-innumerable-company-and: David Starr Jordan, president of Leland Stanford Junior University, published this volume of sketches in San Francisco in 1896, dedicating it to his wife, Jessie Knight Jordan. Only the title pages, a short prefatory note, and the contents appear here. Jordan explains the bond of the sketches. They are historical or allegorical. All share the idea of the higher sacrifice. The list names The California of the Padre among them. The Last of the Puritans appears too. The sketches themselves do not appear.
the-story-of-versailles: Francis Loring Payne wrote this history of Versailles. Moffat, Yard and Company of New York published it in 1919. A frontispiece statue shows Louis XIV, Versailles' builder. Only the title pages and contents appear in this record. The contents list nine chapters. They cover the beginning and making of Versailles. Its luxury, gardens, and fountains follow. The Grand Trianon and a day with the Sun King come next. The women of Versailles appear too. The twilight of the Bourbon kings closes the list. Payne's history itself does not appear.
the-strength-of-gideon-and-other-stories: Paul Laurence Dunbar published this story collection in 1900, dedicating it to his good friend and teacher Captain Charles B. Stivers. Only the title page and contents are present in this record, naming the title story and companions such as Mammy Peggy's Pride, Viney's Free Papers, The Fruitful Sleeping of the Rev. Elisha Edwards, The Ingrate, The Finish of Patsy Barnes, and An Old-Time Christmas, so Dunbar's tales themselves do not appear.
the-swindler-and-other-stories: Ethel M. Dell's stories, first published in the Red Magazine, were gathered by Grosset and Dunlap by arrangement with G. P. Putnam's Sons. Only title pages, a contents list, and the opening words appear here. The list names The Swindler's Handicap and The Nonentity. Her Hero, The Example, and The Right Man follow. The Knight-Errant and A Question of Trust close the list. The first story opens with a reflection. Only a few planks separate a ship's company from the sea. The tales themselves do not appear.
the-tale-of-ginger-and-pickles:
Beatrix Potter published Ginger and Pickles with Frederick Warne in 1909, dedicating it to old Mr. John Taylor. The story opens in a tiny village shop whose counter stands at just the right height for rabbits. Ginger the yellow tom-cat and Pickles the terrier keep the shop together. Their regular customers include the dolls Lucinda and Jane Doll-cook, who buy all their groceries there.

The shop sells red spotty handkerchiefs, sugar, snuff, and galoshes, and nearly everything else except things wanted in a hurry. Potter notes dryly that rabbits always feared Pickles a little. Young readers get a gentle, funny picture of village trade run by two very different animal shopkeepers.
the-tale-of-the-flopsy-bunnies:
Frederick Warne issued Beatrix Potter's Flopsy Bunnies in 1909, dedicated to the little friends of Mr. McGregor, Peter, and Benjamin. Potter begins by doubting that lettuce makes anyone sleepy, since she is not a rabbit. The Flopsy Bunnies certainly grow drowsy on it. Benjamin Bunny has married his cousin Flopsy, and their large family is improvident and cheerful.

Food often runs short, so Benjamin borrows cabbages from Flopsy's brother Peter Rabbit, who keeps a nursery garden. That borrowing leads the young bunnies toward Mr. McGregor's rubbish heap and real danger. Potter turns a sleepy meal into a rescue story, with Benjamin and Peter facing their old enemy again.
the-tale-of-timmy-tiptoes:
Frederick Warne published Beatrix Potter's Timmy Tiptoes in New York in 1911, dedicating it to many unknown little friends, including Monica. Timmy is a fat, comfortable grey squirrel with a leaf-thatched nest high in a tall tree. His wife Goody pushes moss under the thatch while Timmy enjoys the breeze. Timmy announces that the nuts are ripe and they must store food for winter and spring.

Goody answers that the nest is so snug they will sleep soundly all winter, then wake thinner with nothing to eat. Potter grounds the tale in a real squirrel habit, gathering and hiding nuts. The opening promises trouble over buried stores, stolen caches, and a hero wrongly blamed.
the-ten-pleasures-of-marriage-and-the-se:
The Ten Pleasures of Marriage, attributed to Aphra Behn, was printed at London in 1682, and the Navarre Society reissued it in 1922 with an introduction by John Harvey. Its publisher's preface tells the book's own story first. The original was a small thick volume, and only one perfect copy was known. That copy lay unappreciated in an antiquarian bookseller's shop in the heart of London until a colleague spotted it.

The preface argues the little book matters to students of the manners of ordinary people of its period. The volume also includes the second part, The Confession of the New Married Couple, and twenty re-engraved plates. Readers get a Restoration marriage satire rescued from near-loss, framed by a bibliophile's tale of its survival.
the-testimony-of-the-bible-concerning-th: S. E. Wishard's Testimony of the Bible Concerning the Assumptions of Destructive Criticism was published in Los Angeles by Johnson and Haney, Bible Institute Press, in 1909. This record shows the title page and a brief foreword rather than the argument itself. The foreword sends the booklet out to Sabbath-school teachers, to young people of the Christian churches, and to all believers in the living Word. A line from Philippians about defence of the truth stands as its motto. Wishard's case against the critics begins beyond these pages.
the-three-brides:
Charlotte M. Yonge's Three Brides, dated 1876, opens in a family council about an influx of daughters-in-law. Three sons have married at once, and their mother jokes with the two boys still at home about the pity of her case. Each bridegroom swears his bride resembles the mother, giving her three mirrors, and each claims he married for her benefit. She turns briskly to practical plans for bringing the brides home.

Raymond and Cecil need the carriage in full state at Holford's Gate, Julius and Rosamond come by train to Willansborough, and poor Miles's wife arrives alone from a strange country at Backsworth. One reluctant son agrees to fetch 'Miles's little African.' Yonge mixes family teasing with a household bracing for three new brides at once, her domestic world drawn in quick, affectionate dialogue.
the-three-brides-love-in-a-cottage-and-o:
Francis A. Durivage collected The Three Brides, Love in a Cottage, and Other Tales at Boston in 1853, inscribing the volume to his mother, the first to encourage his efforts. His preface explains that the stories are selections from his contributions to the American press. Most were written in intervals of relaxation from serious labor and daily business. They would have vanished into the forgetfulness awaiting old magazines and newspapers, he says, had their wide circulation not argued for saving them.

Durivage offers the book as rescued periodical fiction, tales that readers already enjoyed in print once. A namesake collision is worth noting: Charlotte Yonge's novel elsewhere in the library is also called The Three Brides, but Durivage's is an American story collection, wholly separate. His preface gives the volume its honest, modest frame.
the-three-comrades:
Kristina Roy of Stara Tura, Slovakia, wrote The Three Comrades, translated by Charles Lukesh in a first edition of November 1941. Chapter one declares that no comrades in the wide world loved each other better than Petrik, Ondrejko, and Fido. All three are orphans who have had a hard time. Petrik's parents died of a malignant fever, and the passed-along child found a poor hut with old Bacha Filina, the shepherd overseer, that felt like paradise.

Ondrejko, a lord's son in name, was sent to the mountains to grow strong on whey and black bread, like a candle ready to go out. His mother, a famous singer, left him with strangers and vanished. Roy, a beloved Slovak Christian writer, builds her children's story from lonely boys gathered into one mountain household, with faith and friendship as the cure.
the-three-eyes: Maurice Leblanc's Three Eyes, translated by Alexander Teixeira de Mattos and copyrighted in 1921 by the Macaulay Company, is shown here in title pages and the head of a contents list only. A frontispiece caption gives one tantalizing line: 'Bérangère stopped....' The title page notes Leblanc as author of The Secret of Sarek and credits G. W. Gage with the frontispiece. No chapter of this scientific mystery follows in the pages present. Readers can identify the book and its makers, while the three eyes themselves keep their secret.
the-three-hostages:
John Buchan's Three Hostages, fourth of the Richard Hannay novels, was first published in 1924 and dedicated to a young gentleman of Eton College. Buchan's letter explains that the boy complained a godfather's gift of dry historical research had let him down, and demanded more Hannay. Buchan met Sir Richard, now a country neighbour, noticed his mauled left hand, and got the tale from him. The affair, he promises, was a pure contest of wits.

Chapter one finds Hannay blissfully retired at Fosse Manor in the Cotswolds, walking the Mill Meadow on a mid-March day of blackthorn and primroses. His son Peter John is teething, the estate is nearly repaired, and Mary whispers that such peace is too good to last. Buchan lets the idyll glow just before three kidnappings drag Hannay back to work.
the-threefold-destiny-from-twice-told-ta:
Nathaniel Hawthorne's Threefold Destiny, from Twice-Told Tales, is labelled a fairy legend, and Hawthorne prefaces it with his method. He imagines incidents that wed fairy legend's spirit to familiar, everyday characters. A muted wildness lies over New England persons and scenery. Rather than a story of real events, he calls it an allegory given more lifelike warmth than an Eastern tale.

In summer twilight a tall, dark traveller enters his native village unrecognized, leaning on a staff grown in the jungles of Hindostan. His cheek bears Arabian desert wind and Arctic frost, and an ataghan hides beneath his vest. A young woman half-utters his name: Ralph Cranfield, marked from youth for a high destiny. Hawthorne's tale tests prophecy, love, and ambition in one wandering life.
the-tidal-wave-and-other-stories: Ethel M. Ethel M. Dell's Tidal Wave and Other Stories is dated 1919. This record gives its title pages, a list of her many novels, and a contents list. The first story reaches only its chapter heading, Still Waters. Six stories are promised: The Tidal Wave, The Magic Circle, The Looker-On, The Second Fiddle, The Woman of His Dream, and The Return Game. Dell was a bestselling writer of intense romantic fiction, and the volume's shape is plain. Its love stories themselves, however, do not begin within the pages shown.
the-time-of-roses: Mrs. L. T. Meade's Time of Roses, issued in Chicago by M. A. Donohue, takes its title from a quoted couplet about plucking roses in passing. This record gives the title page and first contents entries only. Those entries promise Home at Last, a character called the Little Mummy and her arrangements, a startling meeting, an evil genius, Maurice Trevor, and Mrs. Aylmer's strategy. Meade wrote popular girls' fiction, but her chapters do not appear here, so Bertha's quandary waits outside.
the-toll-gatherer-s-day-from-twice-told-:
Nathaniel Hawthorne's Toll-Gatherer's Day, a sketch of transitory life from Twice-Told Tales, envies the man who watches life rather than plunging into it. For a nature too indolent or sensitive for dust, sunshine, and turmoil, no retreat could be better than a toll-house beside a thronged thoroughfare. There the great globe performs its revolutions before his eyes while he sits still. Hawthorne imagines himself on the bench of a toll-house set mid-bridge between shores.

His friend's day begins in dim, gray, dewy morning as ponderous wheels mingle with slumber and hay wagons creak across groaning timbers. Then the never-tiring mail dashes over at a headlong rate. Hawthorne turns one workman's routine into a meditation on observation itself, the whole travelling world paying toll to a man who goes nowhere.
the-torch-and-other-tales:
Eden Phillpotts collects fifteen tales in The Torch and Other Tales, published by Macmillan in New York, opening with 'Santa Claus.' No one in Little Silver knew Teddy Pegram's origins, or why he settled there. He lodged with Mrs. Ford, the policeman's wife, then took a tumble-down cottage and made it to his liking with his own hands. A handy, kind man, he did odd jobs for neighbours and could cook and sew like the clever ones.

Pegram's learning let him talk business with the shopkeeper and patent medicines with the chemist, yet his past stayed his own. The contents promise Dartmoor-flavoured pieces: a returned native, John and Jane, an old soldier, the hound's pool, and the wise woman of Walna. Phillpotts writes village mystery with affection, letting an unknown stranger's usefulness deepen the question of who he is.
the-trampling-of-the-lilies: Rafael Sabatini's Trampling of the Lilies is his French Revolution novel, dated 1906. It is laid out here as a contents list in three parts. They are named The Old Rule, The New Rule, and The Everlasting Rule. Chapters open with Monsieur the Secretary and the lords of life and death. They pass to the disciples of Rousseau. Then come sheep turned wolves, a citizen commissioner, and La Boulaye discharging a debt. Part three begins with Cecile Deshaix. The drama is charted in these headings; the narrative itself stays outside.
the-treasure-of-heaven-a-romance-of-rich: Marie Corelli's Treasure of Heaven, a romance of riches, was published by Dodd, Mead in 1906. This record shows its title page. It also shows a dedication to Bertha: 'A faithful friend is better than gold.' A contents list starts, but reaches only chapter one. Corelli, author of The Sorrows of Satan and Thelma, was among the bestselling novelists of her age. Her story of wealth and its spiritual price does not begin within these pages. A companion record adds her author's note on the frontispiece portrait.
the-trojan-women-of-euripides:
Gilbert Murray's translation of Euripides' Trojan Women, Englished in rhyming verse with notes and published in 1915, is introduced here by an essay quoting Murray's own preface. Murray calls the play imperfect, a great wrong of the world cried aloud and turned into music. Yet in one situation, with little movement and few figures, it flashes out the infinite pathos of a successful wrong. Through pity and terror, it hints that beyond defeat may come a glory greater than the victors'.

First performed in 415 B.C., the play's pathos is called as modern as it was to the Athenians, since war's terrors have not changed in three thousand years. Poseidon's lament over Troy is quoted for the cities of today. Murray's version let English readers meet Greek tragedy as a living argument against war.
the-troll-garden-and-selected-stories:
Willa Cather's Troll Garden and Selected Stories joins her 1905 collection to four earlier tales, and opens with On the Divide. Near Rattlesnake Creek stands Canute's shanty, with the level Nebraska plain of rust-red grass stretching north, east, and south. A strip of timber winds along the turbid little stream to the west. If not for the few stunted cottonwoods and elms along its banks, the narrator says, Canute would have shot himself years ago, for Norwegians are a timber-loving people.

Canute built the shanty alone when no human being lived within twenty miles. The volume then gathers the Troll Garden stories: The Sculptor's Funeral, A Wagner Matinee, Paul's Case, and others about artists and the provinces that made and starved them. Cather's prairie realism and her art-haunted exiles meet in one book.
the-twelve-tables:
P. R. Coleman-Norton of Princeton's classics department presents The Twelve Tables, Rome's earliest law code, prefaced, arranged, translated, and annotated by himself. Table One governs proceedings preliminary to trial. If a plaintiff summons a defendant to court, he shall go; if he will not, the plaintiff calls a witness and takes him by force. If the defendant flees, the plaintiff may lay hand on him. If disease or age impedes him, the summoner shall grant a conveyance, though he need not spread a cushioned carriage.

Freeholders must have freeholders as sureties, while any willing person may stand for a proletary. Parties plead in the comitium or forum before noon, and sunset ends the proceedings. Coleman-Norton's plain translation, with bracketed supplements, lets students read the foundation text of Roman law clause by clause.
the-twilight-of-the-gods-and-other-tales: Richard Garnett's Twilight of the Gods and Other Tales, dated 1903 in Roman numerals, is dedicated to Horace Howard Furness and Georg Brandes. This record gives title page, dedication, and a contents list of ten tales. They include the title story, The Potion of Lao-Tsze, and Abdallah the Adite. Ananda the Miracle Worker, The Demon Pope, and The Dumb Oracle are also named. The Cupbearer and Duke Virgil close the list. Garnett's mythological fables are named here, not told. A companion record prints a fuller contents.
the-twins-of-table-mountain-and-other-st:
Bret Harte's Twins of Table Mountain opens on a vast stony plateau, lifted so high that its outlines seem a cloud-streak on the lesser hills. The turbulent river's roar is lost at that height, and winds spend their fury below the summit. An eternal calm invests the serene altitude, where rain and snow fall straight down over granite boulders. Even Alpine flowers seldom thrill their petals to a passing breeze on Table Mountain.

Such a place, Harte says, should speak in a whisper, and ordinary voices on the night of 15 May 1868 sound grotesquely incongruous in the darkness. The volume adds four stories, including An Heiress of Red Dog and The Great Deadwood Mystery. Harte's California local colour here turns hushed and strange, altitude itself becoming a character.
the-two-destinies:
Wilkie Collins opens The Two Destinies with a prelude in which the guest tells the story of a dinner party. Years have passed since the narrator and his wife left the United States for their first visit to England, carrying the usual letters of introduction. One, from his wife's brother, presented them to George Germaine, an old and valued friend just married. The brother knew nothing of the lady or the meeting, but promised a hearty welcome for his sake.

The Germaines returned their call the same day and invited them to the first dinner given after the wedding tour, with only a few old friends expected. Collins also digresses on the English custom of arriving half an hour late to dinner. Behind the polite frame waits his tale of two children betrothed by a dying grandmother's vision, separated, and drawn together by destiny.
the-valet-s-tragedy-and-other-studies:
Andrew Lang gathers studies in secret history in The Valet's Tragedy and Other Studies. The contents list twelve pieces on enduring mysteries. Subjects include the valet's master, Sir Edmund Berry Godfrey's death, a false Jeanne d'Arc, the voices of the true Maid, Amy Robsart, Fisher's ghost, and the Shakespeare-Bacon dispute.

Lang's preface warns readers not to expect neat solutions. Public pleasure favours certainty, he says, but science and conscience forbid it, since nobody truly knows who killed Godfrey or how Robsart died. The essays can only restate each case and clear away errors and confusion. Restoration intrigues around James de la Cloche and a valet condemned to lifelong captivity anchor the title studies.
the-village-uncle-from-twice-told-tales:
Nathaniel Hawthorne frames The Village Uncle, from Twice Told Tales, as an imaginary retrospect spoken by an old man on Thanksgiving night. He calls for another log, wanting the blaze to dance high and light the cottage windows reddest in the village. Susan and the children draw chairs around his armchair by the fire.

The figures quiver indistinctly in the flame, looking like visions that will vanish when the fire sinks. Surf sounds faintly from a mile inland, and the old man's ears, eyes, and perhaps mind are failing. The past peeps over the present's shoulders: fifty years shrink to moments, and he thanks Heaven he is old, done with the hermit vanities of his scribbling youth.
the-vision-of-the-fountain-from-twice-to:
Nathaniel Hawthorne recalls reaching, at fifteen, a village over a hundred miles from home. Next morning, a September day bright as July, he rambles into oak woods along cattle-paths. A track leads him to a crystal spring ringed with fresh grass and shaded by a great oak, where one sunbeam plays like a goldfish in the water.

Hawthorne has loved gazing into springs since childhood, and he imagines the Naiad who might rise from this one in a gown of water-moss. Leaning over the grassy border, he meets his own reflected eyes first. Then a second face appears deeper in the fountain, a fair young girl with pale gold locks and a mirthful, dimpling expression.
the-vultures:
Henry Seton Merriman opens The Vultures aboard an Atlantic steamer, in a chapter called All at Sea. Joseph P. Mangles lounges in a deck-chair with an excellent cigar, a tall, thin man of fifty years' dyspepsia and patient disgust with the world. Moderating weather annoys him, since fine weather will bring women on deck.

His sister remarks that Joseph growls over meals like a dog. The only other non-business man aboard, Reginald Cartoner, leans silently at the rail nearby, a big, quiet Englishman whose soft voice makes people ask him to repeat himself. Four days out from New York, the two have drifted together like ships on a sea of commercial interests.
the-wanderer-or-female-difficulties: Frances Burney published The Wanderer, or Female Difficulties, in 1814. The material present here is a title heading and a partial contents list, so the novel itself does not appear. Contents promise a preface, then volume one divided into at least seventeen chapters. No chapter titles are printed, only roman numerals, and the list breaks off within the first volume. Readers can confirm the book's identity, its subtitle about female difficulties, and its multi-volume scale from this record alone.
the-war-and-the-churches: Joseph McCabe wrote The War and the Churches for the Rationalist Press Association, issued by Watts and Company in London in 1915. The pages present here give the title page and a long list of McCabe's earlier works, so his wartime argument does not appear. That list includes Modern Rationalism, lives of Peter Abelard, Saint Augustine, Talleyrand, and Goethe, plus Twelve Years in a Monastery. A candid history of the Jesuits also appears. Readers can place the pamphlet within a rationalist catalogue from this record.
the-war-of-the-wenuses:
C. L. Graves and E. V. Lucas published The War of the Wenuses in 1898 with J. W. Arrowsmith of Bristol, as a parody of H. G. Wells. A mock title page claims translation from the Artesian of H. G. Pozzuoli, author of The Treadmill and The Isthmus of Dr. Day. The dedication is blunt: to H. G. Wells, this outrage on a fascinating and convincing romance.

The pages present here stop within the contents, so the parody's chapters do not appear. Book one, The Coming of the Wenuses, lists chapters called Just Before the Battle, Mother, The Falling Star, The Crinoline Expands, and How I Reached Home. Feminised Martians and music-hall titles signal the joke's direction from the headings alone.
the-water-babies:
Charles Kingsley's Water Babies, a fairy tale for a land-baby, appears here in an 1889 Macmillan edition from London and New York. Linley Sambourne supplied one hundred illustrations for this new edition. Kingsley dedicates the book to his youngest son, Grenville Arthur, and to all other good little boys, under a riddle verse daring grown-ups to read what children can.

The pages present here stop at the front matter and a picture of water babies playing leap-frog with frogs, so Tom's chimney-sweep story itself does not appear. Publication history on the title pages shows the tale's long life in print. Readers learn the edition's illustrator, dedication, and intended child audience from this record alone.
the-water-goats-and-other-troubles:
Ellis Parker Butler, author of Pigs Is Pigs, gathers three comic pieces in The Water Goats and Other Troubles. The title story opens with a landscape gardener advising Mayor Dugan and the city council on a new public park. In the lake, the gardener insists, the committee should place two gondolas, amply sufficient for its size, since children and adults both like riding in them.

Mayor Dugan agrees warmly but cannot get his tongue around the word gondolas, and clerk Toole vows to hold them fast in mind. Butler builds the joke from small-town officialdom meeting artistic certainty. Contents add two more troubles: Mr. Billings's pockets and the committee's first burglar.
the-water-of-the-wondrous-isles: William Morris published The Water of the Wondrous Isles with Longmans, Green in 1897. The pages present here give a long contents list for the romance's first two parts, so Morris's prose itself does not appear. Part one, Of the House of Captivity, follows Birdalone, a stolen child who waxes into maidenhood under a witch-wife. Chapters cover skin-changing, her raiment, swimming, fishing, and a serpent-ring. Part two reaches the wondrous isles, a witch's prison in a wailing tower, and the isle of the queens.
the-westcotes:
Arthur Thomas Quiller-Couch dedicates The Westcotes to Henry James in a letter dated October 25, 1901. He borrows a joke: a spinster excused a borrowed man's hat in her hall because the house wanted a something. Inscribing James's name, Quiller-Couch says, risks showing readers exactly what his little story wants, meaning James's penetrating subtleties of insight on behalf of its heroine Dorothea.

The dedication letter is the only material present in this record, so the story itself does not appear. Quiller-Couch goes on to praise James's sustained pride in good workmanship as a common example to every practitioner of their art. He calls James a master whose genius in operation remains a mystery to him, admired with almost personal loyalty.
the-white-bees: Henry van Dyke published The White Bees and Other Poems with Charles Scribner's Sons in New York in 1909. The pages present here give the title page and contents, so the poems themselves do not appear. The collection's first pages hold lyrics, then sonnets, odes, and readings in natural history. Sonnets named include The House of Life, The Cherry-Blooms of Yeddo, and Mother Earth. Odes follow to light, to music, and to the poet Robert Burns. Readings treat salmon rivers, golden-rod, and the midsummer daisy.
the-white-old-maid-from-twice-told-tales:
Nathaniel Hawthorne opens The White Old Maid, from Twice Told Tales, in a moonlit chamber richly furnished in antique fashion. Light through one lattice falls on a bed between heavy silken curtains, illuminating a young man's face. He lies too quietly, too pale, with the sheet wound like a shroud: a corpse in its burial clothes.

A girl steals to the bedside and presses her living lips to the dead man's cold ones, with a gleam of triumph in her eye. Then a second girl, soft and fragile, glides in ghost-like. The proud first visitor cries that the dead is hers, since the other had him living. Edith, named at last, sinks beside the corpse with her hair mingling in his dark locks, bewildered by her first draught of sorrow.
the-white-people-and-other-weird-stories:
Arthur Machen's White People and Other Weird Stories is a modern Penguin Classics gathering, and the pages present here are its front matter: a contents list and editor S. T. Joshi's biographical sketch, so the tales themselves do not appear. Contents name The Inmost Light, the novels of the black seal and the white powder, The Red Hand, the title story, The Bowmen, The Great Return, and The Terror. Machen is a different author entirely from Frances Hodgson Burnett, whose unrelated White People also appears in this library.

Joshi's sketch follows Machen from his 1863 birth at Caerleon, Monmouthshire, through Hereford Cathedral School and a move to London in 1881. Journalism, tutoring, and a publisher's clerkship supported night writing until an inheritance freed him. The Great God Pan succeeded in 1894 despite scandal, and American fame in the nineteen-twenties arrived alongside deepening poverty at home.
the-white-wolf-and-other-fireside-tales: Arthur Quiller-Couch, writing as Q, published The White Wolf and Other Fireside Tales with Methuen in 1902. The pages present here give the title pages and a contents list, so the tales themselves do not appear. Fourteen stories are named. The White Wolf, the Murder at the Towers, and My Grandfather, Hendry Watty open the collection. Hugh Miller's Story and Captain Dick and Captain Jacka follow, then the dispossession of the Meynack estate and the tale of Maurice the milk boy. Seven Sisters closes the list.
the-wiradyuri-and-other-languages-of-new:
R. H. Mathews wrote a study of the Wiradyuri and other languages of New South Wales. A synopsis lists sections on orthography and on three languages. Those languages are Wiradyuri, Burreba-burreba, and Ngunawal. Word lists for Wiradyuri and Ngunawal follow the grammar sections. Mathews notes his ties to anthropological societies in Washington.

Wiradyuri speakers occupied a huge region in central and southern New South Wales. Mathews says their language covered more ground than any other tongue in the colony. Earlier maps from his 1898 papers mark its boundaries. Readers get a short outline of how the language is built. The vocabularies let readers compare words across neighboring peoples.
the-wonder-book-of-bible-stories:
Logan Marshall edited and arranged The Wonder Book of Bible Stories for the John C. Winston Company. The contents run from Adam and Eve through the Old Testament. Noah, Hagar, Abraham, and Jacob follow in order. An illustration shows Pharaoh's daughter finding the baby Moses. His own mother, by chance, is called to nurse him.

The edition carries copyrights from 1904 and 1925. Stories are shortened and arranged for young readers. Familiar episodes come in simple sequence. Pictures reinforce the best-known scenes. Families and Sunday schools used such books to introduce children to scripture. The volume treats the Bible as a storehouse of wonder tales.
the-world-english-bible-web-1-chronicles:
First Chronicles stands as book thirteen in the World English Bible, a modern English translation of scripture. Verse numbers mark every line in a chapter-and-verse layout. The book opens with a long genealogy. Adam, Seth, and Enosh begin the line. Noah and his sons follow, then the nations descended from Japheth, Ham, and Cush.

Name after name links Israel's story to the first humans. Nimrod appears as an early mighty figure. The Philistines' origins get a brief note. Readers who want Israel's roots traced carefully will value these lists. The genealogy sets up the histories of David and the kingdom that follow.
the-world-english-bible-web-2-chronicles:
Second Chronicles, book fourteen of the World English Bible, opens with Solomon secure on his throne. God, the text says, magnified him greatly. Solomon addresses captains, judges, and princes across Israel. The whole assembly travels to the high place at Gibeon. Moses' tent of meeting stands there. A bronze altar made by Bezalel waits before it.

Solomon offers a thousand burnt offerings on that altar. That night God appears and invites his request. The scene sets up Solomon's famous choice of wisdom. Temple building and Judah's kings follow in the book. Readers trace a kingdom's rise and slow decline through its rulers' faithfulness.
the-world-english-bible-web-ecclesiastes:
Ecclesiastes, book twenty-one of the World English Bible, opens with the Preacher's bleak verdict. Vanity of vanities, he says; all is vanity. The speaker is a son of David, king in Jerusalem. He asks what profit human labor brings under the sun. Generations pass while the earth remains. The sun rises, sets, and hurries back again.

Wind circles south and north without rest. Rivers fill the sea, yet the sea never fills. Nothing under the sun is truly new, the Preacher argues. The eye never sees enough, nor the ear hears enough. Readers get scripture's most candid meditation on weariness, pleasure, and meaning.
the-world-english-bible-web-judges:
Judges, book seven in the World English Bible, opens after Joshua's death. Israel asks God who should fight the Canaanites first. Judah receives the assignment. Judah invites Simeon to join the campaign. Together they strike down ten thousand men at Bezek. Their king, Adoni-Bezek, flees but is captured. His thumbs and big toes are cut off.

The captured king recalls doing the same to seventy kings. Cycles of victory, compromise, and decline structure the book. Charismatic deliverers rise when Israel cries out. Order remains fragile between their victories. Readers see tribal Israel before monarchy. Violence and heroism sit side by side in these rough stories.
the-young-step-mother-or-a-chronicle-of-:
Charlotte M. Yonge opens The Young Step-Mother under the beeches at Fairmead vicarage. Mr. Ferrars talks with his slender wife about her sister Albinia. They have discussed Albinia's future with her already. The vicar doubts the conversation promised much success. Giving Albinia up will hurt them both, they admit. He jokes that his wife married him partly for his sister.

Albinia's suitor Kendal may not match the vicar's imagined hero. Yet the imaginary man, he concedes, might please her less. Yonge builds domestic drama from affectionate family negotiation. A young stepmother's arrival will test this household's kindness. Mistakes, as the subtitle promises, will teach through consequences.
their-crimes:
Their Crimes, translated from the French in 1917, catalogues German conduct in occupied France and Belgium. Its contents list robbery, incendiarism, and murder as chapters. Killing the wounded and martyrdom of civilian prisoners follow. Profits were pledged to the League of Remembrance and relief work in Lorraine. The preface states the book's purpose bluntly. English-speaking readers must remember the destruction of 1914.

Time, the preface warns, has dimmed those horrors in many minds. War weariness might sap resolution toward a patched-up peace. The authors demand true perception of reparation and punishment due. German excuses get a chapter of rebuttal. Belgian workmen add their own appeal. The book stands as wartime atrocity literature aimed at Allied resolve.
theobald-the-iron-hearted-or-love-to-ene: Theobald, the Iron-Hearted; or, Love to Enemies came from the French of the Rev. Cesar Malan, dated 1808. Chapter headings sketch a rescue story. Gottfried and Erard pursue a horseman and save a wounded chevalier. Later headings bring Theobald face to face with Arnold the Lion, his enemy, and show kindness returned in unexpected ways. Family worship and Hildegarde also appear. Just the contents pages are given in this record, so Malan's narrative itself stays unseen.
there-are-crimes-and-crimes:
August Strindberg wrote There Are Crimes and Crimes at fifty, in 1899, the same year as three major historical dramas. Edwin Bjorkman translated the comedy from Swedish and supplied an introduction. Bjorkman places it just after Strindberg's confessional works Inferno and Legends.

He calls the play a first step beyond a mental crisis spent in Paris chasing gold-making and mystical heaven. Strindberg himself later summed up this period as light after darkness. Readers get a drama about Maurice's fall from success, framed by champagne, faith, and recovered certainty. Bjorkman's German title for it, Rausch, means intoxication.
things-mother-used-to-make-a-collection-:
Lydia Maria Gurney collected old-time recipes, some nearly one hundred years old and never printed before, in a New York book of 1914. Her foreword says good food depends on the cook's judgment as much as on materials. The recipes are written plainly for inexperienced housekeepers.

The breads section opens with bannocks made from sour milk, sugar, egg, flour, and Indian meal, dropped into boiling fat. Boston brown bread follows. Readers get simple, inexpensive period cooking, plus household hints, meant to be followed closely by beginners. Maple syrup is the serving she suggests for the warm bannocks.
thirteen-stories:
R. B. Cunninghame Graham published Thirteen Stories with William Heinemann in London in 1900. He dedicated the sketches to George Morton Mansel, recalling long rides together over the Pampa. Several pieces had already appeared in the Saturday Review, the Westminster Gazette, and Justice.

His preface mourns the lost art of slow literary approaches, comparing old prefaces to old warfare's manoeuvres. Modern writers, he says, rush at readers like torpedo boats. Readers get a storyteller who defends grace and ceremony while promising tales shaped by travel in South America and beyond. He calls such slow approaches a grace that modern books have lost.
thoughts-on-the-present-discontents-and-:
Edmund Burke's Thoughts on the Present Discontents appears in an 1886 Cassell edition together with several speeches. Cassell's introduction begins a life of Burke, born at Dublin on January 1, 1730. His attorney father had fifteen children, and delicate Edmund was taught at home and at Ballitore school.

The contents add speeches on the Middlesex election, juries in libel cases, shorter parliaments, and reform of Commons representation. The introduction recalls his 1756 Vindication of Natural Society and essay on the sublime and beautiful. Readers get political writing framed by a compact Victorian biography. The introduction follows him from school to Trinity College and London.
three-comedies:
Björnstjerne Björnson, poet, dramatist, novelist, and politician, receives a long introduction in Three Comedies. He was born in December 1832 at Kvikne in northern Norway, where his father was pastor. The remote Österdal district had been pastorless after a predecessor fled its wild folk.

At six Björnson moved to Naes at the mouth of the Romsdal, among Norway's fairest scenery. School at Molde and Christiania led to university in 1852 and early dramatic criticism. Readers get a biography stressing lonely independence, beauty, and a young author who withdrew his first accepted play after learning its defects.
three-elephant-power-and-other-stories:
Andrew Barton 'Banjo' Paterson, Australian poet and reporter, shares Three Elephant Power and Other Stories with a closing piece by Knott Gold. A 1917 edition notes the stories first appeared in Australian journals. Contents promise tales about an oracle, a cast-iron canvasser, a merino sheep, and a bullock.

The title story opens with Alfred the chauffeur tapping a speed indicator and doubting its honesty. He asks whether the narrator heard about Henery, who drove for old John Bull, and Henery's elephant. Readers get bush and town humour told through drivers, dogs, gardeners, and racing men.
three-ghost-stories:
Charles Dickens gathered three ghost stories from his Christmas Stories in an 1894 Chapman and Hall edition. The Haunted House comes first, followed by The Trial for Murder and The Signal-Man. Dickens stresses that he first saw the haunted house in plain daylight, with sun on it and no thunder.

He had arrived from a nearby railway station for his health, following a friend's suggestion. Northern lights, broken sleep, and an ordinary autumn morning frame the discovery. Readers get Christmas supernatural tales that ground their hauntings in railways, rented houses, and everyday travel rather than Gothic castles.
three-john-silence-stories:
Algernon Blackwood's three John Silence stories open with a contents list naming A Psychical Invasion, Ancient Sorceries, and The Nemesis of Fire. Blackwood dedicated the book to M. L. W., called the original of John Silence and his companion in many adventures. Case one begins with a Swedish lady consulting the doctor.

She praises his sympathetic heart and psychic knowledge, while Silence winces at the word occultism. Her real case concerns a lost sense of humour, which no ordinary medicine can restore. Readers get supernatural tales investigated like medical cases by a calm, clairvoyant physician.
three-more-john-silence-stories:
Algernon Blackwood's three more John Silence stories list Secret Worship, The Camp of the Dog, and A Victim of Higher Space. He again dedicated the book to M. L. W., the original of John Silence. The first case follows Harris, a silk merchant travelling home through south Germany.

Harris impulsively revisits his old school after thirty years, while Silence happens to be tramping the same mountains. The school belonged to a strict Protestant community whose mental discipline shaped Harris deeply. Readers get a supernatural investigation where two men converge on one inn from opposite directions.
time-and-life-mr-darwin-s-origin-of-spec:
Thomas H. Huxley wrote on Darwin's Origin of Species under the heading Time and Life, beginning with the earth's thin accessible film of strata. Beds of former sea and lake mud lie deeper and older in sequence. Geologists group them as palaeozoic, mesozoic, and cainozoic formations.

Huxley poses a choice: either natural forces always worked near their present intensity, requiring prodigious time, or primeval forces were far stronger and time was short. Early geologists chose the second, reading deep time like children reading Rome. Readers get a clear Victorian argument for vast geological ages beneath Darwin's theory.
time-s-laughingstocks-and-other-verses: Thomas Hardy collected Time's Laughingstocks and Other Verses, first published in 1909 and reprinted in a 1928 Macmillan pocket edition. His short preface thanks periodical editors for permission to reclaim poems. Hardy warns that poems written far apart in time and in unlike moods may not sit well together. Edition history fills the opening pages, from second edition in 1915 through several pocket reprints. The preface breaks off before Hardy's poems begin. What is present here is the edition history and preface opening, so Hardy's verses themselves do not appear.
time-s-portraiture-from-the-doliver-roma:
Nathaniel Hawthorne's Time's Portraiture appeared as a carrier's address to patrons of the Salem Gazette for January 1, 1838, inside The Doliver Romance and Other Pieces. Newspaper carriers, Hawthorne jokes, are Time's errand boys, seized each New Year by a fit of rhyme.

This carrier has been forgotten by the Muse and must offer plain prose instead of verses. He proposes describing Father Time's person and habits, known from long service as an errand boy. Readers get a humorous New Year piece where a boy apologises for missing poetry while asking patrons for their customary bounty.
tiverton-tales:
Alice Brown published her story collection in 1899, with twelve tales including Dooryards, A March Wind, The Mortuary Chest, and The Experience of Hannah Prime. The first tale praises Tiverton's breezy upland roads and damp, sweet valleys. A summer visitor, Brown says, need not travel far.

Family living spills into dooryards, the outer courts of domestic life where children riot and work finds its channel. Monday washing, churning timed to the cow Sweet-Breath, and butter that sometimes refuses to come fill the opening. Readers get New England village stories grounded in household routine and local character.
tom-dot-and-talking-mouse-and-other-bedt: J. G. and C. Kernahan wrote Tom, Dot and Talking Mouse and other bedtime stories, published at New York by Platt and Munk, copyrighted in 1916. Four stories are listed in the contents. Their titles are The Miller's Mouse, The Old Rocking Horse, The Message of the Lily, and Water-Lily's Mission. Illustrations promise little girls with flowers, Tom dreaming, and a mouse at its mouse-hole. The title pages and contents are what is held in this record, so the Kernahans' bedtime stories themselves do not appear.
tom-slade-boy-scout-of-the-moving-pictur: Percy K. Fitzhugh adapted Tom Slade, Boy Scout of the Moving Pictures from the photo play The Adventures of a Boy Scout. Contents list twenty chapters, from sticks and stones through jail, Camp Solitaire, burglars, and Tom turning detective. A frontispiece caption quotes Tom swiping quarantine signs off doors. Chapter one begins by placing its action in Barrel Alley, with Tom Slade, as usual, responsible, then breaks off. The contents and that opening line are what is given in this record, so Fitzhugh's story itself does not appear beyond them.
