tom-swift-and-his-big-tunnel-or-the-hidd: The Hidden City of the Andes waits at the end of the Tom Swift big tunnel story by Victor Appleton, presented through twenty-five chapter headings. An appeal for aid, a face at the window, a bomb, and Professor Bumper lead Tom off to Peru. Chapter one starts with Tom in his laboratory puzzling over an invention, then breaks off mid-sentence. The contents and that opening fragment are what is given in this record, so Appleton's Andes adventure itself does not appear beyond them.
tomaso-s-fortune-and-other-stories:
Henry Seton Merriman opens his story collection with a contents list of nineteen tales, ending with The Prodigal's Return. Titles include Sister, A Small World, The Tale of a Scorpion, The Mule, In Love and War, Stranded, and For Juanita's Sake. The first story, Sister, begins with a narrator hiding names.

He hopes the woman called Sister never sees the piece, fearing she would count it a breach of professional etiquette. They met once, when their names stood together on a return of deaths now filed at the War Office. Readers get restrained military and colonial stories framed by secrecy and duty.
tractus-de-hermaphrodites-or-a-treatise-:
An anonymous treatise on hermaphrodites was printed at London for E. Curll in Fleet Street in 1718. Its contents promise descriptions of several sorts of hermaphrodites and how law regards them in matrimony. Intrigues, outward distinguishing marks, causes, unnatural births, and monsters follow.

The preface refuses apology for the subject and attacks a libeller who condemned such books while practising worse iniquity daily. The design, it insists, is innocent entertainment for curious persons, and publication will not add one hermaphrodite to the world. Readers get an early sexological tract defending curiosity against scandal, in period language and categories.
traffics-and-discoveries:
Rudyard Kipling's collection mixes stories and poems in its contents, from The Captive and The Bonds of Discipline to A Sahibs' War, Steam Tactics, Wireless, Mrs. Bathurst, and They. Poems such as Poseidon's Law and The Wet Litany stand between the stories in italics. The Captive opens the book.

Its verse begins not with a poem but a prose-framed captive answering his name at muster without complaint. Anklets are welded on the chain-gang, yet he greets the armourers like brothers and moves statelily in chains. Readers get Kipling's imperial stories and verse about discipline, captivity, machinery, and soldiers' lawful occasions.
travels-with-a-donkey-in-the-cevennes: Stevenson's beloved travel memoir of a twelve-day hike through the Cévennes mountains of France with a stubborn donkey named Modestine. Full of comic battles with his four-legged companion, lonely nights under the stars, and reflections on solitude, it is one of the great walking books. The trail he followed is still hiked today and bears his name.
trent-s-trust-and-other-stories: Bret Harte's Trent's Trust and other stories: California tales of honor and adventure. Varied and vivid in his best manner. The master of the Western story in fine form. Harte's miners are rough diamonds every one.
twice-told-tales: Nathaniel Hawthorne's Twice-Told Tales (1837) gathers his early New England stories together. Guilt and ghosts haunt these pages persistently. The Tower library holds the full complete text. It made his literary reputation slowly but surely. Puritan past shadows present lives darkly. The tales blend moral lessons with mystery. Readers discovered a true master here.
two-penniless-princesses: Two poor princesses, brave and kind, fill Yonge’s gentle history. It was made for girls who love the days of old. Sweet and good from the first page to the last. Sweet and good from first to last.
two-years-in-the-french-west-indies: Lafcadio Hearn, the writer who later became famous for his books on Japan, spent two years in Martinique in the 1880s. These sketches capture Creole markets, voodoo-tinged folklore, tropical storms, and the slow rhythms of island life. Hearn writes with a poet's ear for color and sound, preserving a Caribbean world on the edge of change.
un-doc-draft-united-nations-declaration-:
The Draft United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples was adopted by a UN rights panel on 26 August 1994. Indigenous peoples had suffered seizure of lands and loss of rights for centuries. The draft came out of years of work with their own delegates at the table. It later fed the final text of 2007.

The draft calls indigenous peoples equal in dignity to all others. It grants them self-rule over their political path and growth. No one may drive them off their lands without free, informed consent and fair payment. Forced blending into other cultures is barred. Their tongues, faiths, schools, and sacred places win clear protection. So do their lands, waters, and the wealth beneath them.
un-doc-international-review-of-criminal-:
The Coercive Powers of Prosecuting Authorities belongs to the United Nations manual on computer crime, printed in the International Review of Criminal Policy, Nos. 43 and 44. Proof in these cases sits inside machines. Old search law was built for desks and filing rooms. The passage tests how far that law can stretch.

Three powers get the focus. Search and seizure strain when facts have no fixed home or sit on networks abroad. Duties to help raise hard cases: a witness can be made to print a file out, but a suspect keeps the right to stay silent. Wire taps and quiet watching of systems cut deep into free life. Britain's 1984 police act is cited as one fix, letting officers demand computer facts in readable form.

The Extent of Crime and Losses forms part of the United Nations manual on computer crime, printed in the International Review of Criminal Policy, Nos. 43 and 44. Counting this crime turns out to be half the fight. Most of it never reaches the police. One expert called it the biggest cover-up since Watergate.

A 1992 world meeting put the reported share at near five per cent. A 1987 American survey found 72 of 300 firms and offices had been hit in one year. Losses were guessed at 145 million to 730 million dollars. A 1991 poll of computer sites found most had seen a breach. Speed and dense storage hide the acts, staff lack training, and firms fear the shame of telling.
un-un-res-draft-united-nations-declarati:
Rights for the world's first peoples were drafted in this text, a 1994 draft of the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples. Indigenous leaders and state delegates argued over its wording for more than a decade. The final declaration was not adopted until 2007.

The draft affirms rights to land, language, culture, and self-rule for native peoples. It rejects forced removal and demands a say in projects on ancestral lands. Comparing this draft with the final 2007 text shows which claims survived the long fight and which were trimmed away.
uncle-josh-s-punkin-centre-stories: Cal Stewart's vaudeville tales of Uncle Josh Weathersby, the drawling New England farmer whose "punkin centre" stories delighted millions on phonograph records. Folksy, funny, and full of rural wisdom, they capture small-town America at the turn of the century. A charming relic of the days when the phonograph was the family entertainment.
under-the-andes: An early adventure novel by Rex Stout, later famous for the Nero Wolfe detective stories. Set amid the peaks and ruins of the Andes, it sends its heroes into a lost world of Incan legend, hidden treasure, and strange underground realms. Written in 1914, it shows Stout before the mysteries, working in the popular lost-civilization vein of H. Rider Haggard.
under-western-eyes:
Joseph Conrad wrote Under Western Eyes, a novel of Russian revolutionaries seen through English eyes. Its narrator, an elderly teacher of languages, opens by denying that he owns the gifts to invent such a tale. Words, he says, are the great foes of reality, and years of teaching have smothered whatever imagination he once had. What he offers instead rests on a document, which his knowledge of Russian lets him present.

The document tells of a student who called himself, in the Russian way, Cyril son of Isidor, or Razumov. A line from Miss Haldin stands at the head of the book, about taking liberty from any hand as a hungry man snatches bread. Conrad builds a story of betrayal, guilt, and exile in Geneva around Razumov's secret. Readers get a tense study of a man trapped between the police and the revolutionaries he betrayed.
understanding-the-scriptures:
Francis J. McConnell, a bishop of the Methodist Episcopal Church, delivered the talks printed as Understanding the Scriptures as the Mendenhall Lectures, third series, at DePauw University. His first chapter starts from a puzzle. Many people claim the Bible is plain English that anyone can read with a dictionary, yet ordinary readers soon run into trouble with it.

McConnell lists the sources of that trouble plainly. The Bible reports events unlike anything in daily life, and some seem to go against the way nature works. Its points of view feel foreign, some passages seem to clash with others, and its teaching on losing life to save it defies common sense. His lectures take up how such a book can still hold its grip on the world's life, and how readers should approach it.
une-vie-a-piece-of-string-and-other-stor: Guy de Maupassant's Une Vie stands at the head of this first volume of his stories in English, rendered by Albert M. C. McMaster, A. E. Henderson, Mme Quesada, and others. The pages here give the title page and contents only, so the stories themselves do not appear. Contents list an introduction by Pol Neveux, then Une Vie in fourteen chapters that follow Jeanne from her home by the sea through marriage, Corsica, loss, and old age. Two shorter pieces, A Vagabond and The Fishing Hole, follow the novel.
urbain-grandier-celebrated-crimes:
Alexandre Dumas, the elder, told the story of Urbain Grandier in his Celebrated Crimes, and this telling comes from the eight-volume set of 1910. Grandier was a priest of Loudun whose fall in 1634 became one of France's most famous cases. Chapter one opens on Sunday, November 26, 1631, when the little town buzzed with talk in the narrow streets near the church of Saint Pierre.

The cause of the stir was a man coming back to town, a figure much argued over of late. Friends and foes alike awaited him, and doorsteps turned into small debating clubs as people took sides with sharp local feeling. Dumas sets the scene years before the end, letting readers watch a town divide over one man. His method mixes court record and drama, so the case reads like a novel built on real events.
urban-sketches:
Bret Harte's Urban Sketches gathers thirteen short pieces about city and town life. The contents name a venerable impostor, a boy's dog, and sidewalkings. Other pieces recall neighborhoods he has moved from, and the surprise adventures of Master Charles Summerton. The first sketch opens at the narrator's own table. A venerable head keeps rising into view across from him. A very small hand reaches with it, in vain, for the inkstand.

The joke lands slowly: the solemn elder is a small child. His arrival in the family came with odd circumstances, which the narrator plans to explain. Harte writes these pieces as light essays with a storyteller's timing. He finds comedy in daily scenes. Readers who know his mining tales will find the same sharp eye turned on parlors, streets, and steamers. The sketches stay short, warm, and quick.
v-v-s-eyes: Henry Sydnor Harrison, author of Queed, wrote V.V.'s Eyes, issued with pictures in 1913 and dedicated to a reader named Norvell. The pages given here hold the title page and a contents list whose long chapter headings tell the story in outline, so the novel itself is not shown. Headings name Dr. V. Vivian, Miss Carlisle Heth, a beach trip in October, an upset boat, and a pursuer called Hugo Canning whose chase stops at a summer house. Two houses with a great gulf between them open the tale.
vaninka-celebrated-crimes:
Alexandre Dumas, the elder, told the tale of Vaninka in his Celebrated Crimes, and this copy comes from the eight-volume set of 1910. The story opens in St. Petersburg near the end of the reign of Emperor Paul I, in the first year of the nineteenth century. One afternoon a crowd gathers before the house of General Count Tchermayloff, once a military governor in the government of Pultava.

The draw is a public punishment. In the courtyard, men prepare the knout, a heavy whip, for the general's serf, who works as his barber. Such scenes were common then, Dumas notes, yet they still pulled in every passerby. At half past four a young aide-de-camp, about twenty-five and covered with medals, steps out before the crowd. The tale turns on that officer, the general's household, and a crime the punishment hints at.
varied-types: G. K. Chesterton gathered the literary essays of Varied Types at New York with Dodd, Mead and Company in 1905. A note says the papers first ran, with changes, in The Daily News and The Speaker. Pages present here hold that note, the contents, and the first line of the opening essay, so the essays themselves are not shown. Contents promise pieces on Charlotte Bronte, William Morris, Byron, Pope, Rostand, Charles II, Stevenson, Carlyle, Tolstoy, Savonarola, Scott, Bret Harte, Alfred the Great, Ruskin, Tennyson, and Elizabeth Barrett Browning.
verses: Susan Coolidge published her poems under the plain title Verses. Pages present here hold a long dedication poem and the start of the contents, so the body of the book is not shown. The dedication honors two friends, named only by initials. Their youth grew under peaceful suns, and they held wealth, ease, and love as a trust. Coolidge says they shared their light with darker days. She compares them to the saint whose loaves turned to roses.
victorian-short-stories-of-troubled-marr:
Victorian Short Stories of Troubled Marriages gathers five tales. The Bronckhorst Divorce-Case, by Rudyard Kipling, leads the set. Irremediable, by Ella D'Arcy, and A Poor Stick, by Arthur Morrison, follow. Arthur Conan Doyle adds The Adventure of the Abbey Grange, and George Gissing adds The Prize Lodger. Kipling's story is marked as first printed in the Civil and Military Gazette in September 1884.

Kipling introduces Bronckhorst as a grey, middle-aged army man. He is not nice in any way, and he has no respect for the soft lies that make life bearable. His wife is fifteen years his junior, large, pale, and quiet, with heavy eyelids over weak eyes. His coarse manner toward her sets the marriage's tone at once. The set as a whole tests marriage at its breaking points: divorce, dull hatred, poverty, and crime.
victorian-short-stories-stories-of-succe:
Stories of Successful Marriages pairs five tales. Elizabeth Gaskell leads with The Manchester Marriage. Thomas Hardy adds A Mere Interlude, and George Moore adds A Faithful Heart. Walter Besant and Henry James complete the set. Gaskell's story is marked as a Christmas piece from Household Words in 1858.

She brings Mr. and Mrs. Openshaw from Manchester to London. He is to run a new warehouse there for his firm. Openshaw rather enjoys the change. He burns with a curiosity about London he has never fed. Yet he also holds a shrewd contempt for its people, whom he pictures as fine, lazy, and fashion-mad. He hides his pleasure even from himself. Set against the troubled-marriage volume, these tales test how wedlock works when it works, through money, habit, and affection.
villa-rubein-and-other-stories: John Galsworthy published Villa Rubein and Other Stories in 1900, as the file header notes. Pages present here hold that header and a partial contents list only, so the stories themselves are not shown. The list gives Villa Rubein in eighteen numbered sections and stops there, without naming the other stories of the title. A companion record of the same book gives the full contents and the start of a preface. Readers learn from these pages only the frame of Galsworthy's early story volume and its lead tale's length.
violets-and-other-tales:
Alice Ruth Moore published Violets and Other Tales in 1895, under copyright of the Monthly Review, and called it in her introduction a maiden effort. She owns that the world teems with good books, books with motives, morals, and lessons, and that one more seems almost too great a presumption. Room for amateurs is scant, she says, and even the worthiest writers are poorly repaid.

Her little book, she insists, wants only to amuse. Some sketches and verses had run in newspapers and magazines; others see print for the first time here. If the collection whiles away an hour or two, or lifts the load of care from some mind for a brief space, its purpose is served and she is satisfied. The contents mix tales and poems: Violets, Three Thoughts, The Woman, Ten Minutes' Musing, and A Plaint among them.
visionaries: James Huneker wrote the tales in Visionaries. Charles Scribner's Sons issued the book at New York, with copyright in 1905 and a title page dated 1916. He dedicated it to Remy de Gourmont of Paris. Pages present here hold the title page and contents only, so the tales themselves are not shown. Contents list eight pieces. They name A Master of Cobwebs, The Eighth Deadly Sin, and The Purse of Aholibah. Rebels of the Moon, The Spiral Road, A Mock Sun, Antichrist, and The Eternal Duel follow.
voyager-s-tales:
Voyager's Tales draws its sea stories from the collections of Richard Hakluyt. An introduction first tells Hakluyt's own life. For all the Dutch look of his name, he came of good British stock, from Wales or its borders. An ancestor, Hugo Hakelute, sat in Parliament for Leominster in the early fourteen hundreds. Richard was born about five years before Queen Elizabeth took the throne.

A schoolboy visit to a cousin in the Middle Temple first fired him for study of the wider world. At Christ Church, Oxford, he spent all his spare time gathering accounts of voyages. He took his degrees in 1574 and 1577, and lectured in public on geography with new maps and globes. In 1582 he issued Divers Voyages, on the discovery of America. The tales that follow rest on that life's work of saving sailors' records from loss.
war-of-the-classes:
Jack London gathered his socialist essays in War of the Classes. Macmillan copyrighted the book in 1905, and this copy was transcribed from the edition of 1912. The contents name The Class Struggle, The Tramp, and The Scab. The Question of the Maximum and How I Became a Socialist follow. His preface recalls his youth, when his neighbors took him for a weird creature because he was a socialist.

For standing in his native town for city ownership of public services, London says, he was branded a red-shirt, a dynamiter, and an anarchist. Decent fellows who liked him drew the line at his walking out with their sisters. Times changed: he later heard a Republican mayor of that town proclaim city ownership a fixed fact. The essays argue the class war from the road, the picket line, and his own conversion.
war-time-silhouettes:
Stephen Hudson's War-Time Silhouettes gathers seven tales. Among them stand Mr. Reiss's Final Grievance, Business Is Business, and a piece called Bobby. A War Victim and one titled with the old Latin tag about dying for one's country complete the set. The first story opens on a gloomy December afternoon. Mr. Adolf Reiss, a merchant past seventy, sits alone and gazes into the fire with jaundiced eyes. He turns over his grievance against life.

His room matches the man: rich furniture placed without taste, and no air of home. Pictures cover the walls, some at the forced sales of bankrupt friends. Making and musing on money left Reiss no time for comfort. For art as a saleable thing he holds respect, since well-bought pictures can rise in value once their makers are dead. Hudson sketches a speculator whom war and age corner at last.
webster-s-unabridged-dictionary-1st-100-:
Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary of 1913 opens here at page one, with the letter A. The first entry traces the letter's long descent. The capital and small forms of western Europe come from the Latin A, borrowed from the Greek Alpha. That came from the first letter of the Phoenician alphabet, the Hebrew Aleph, itself of Egyptian origin. The Aleph, the entry explains, was a consonant with a guttural breath, which Greek ears took as their vowel.

The entry moves from history to sound and use. In English the letter serves several vowel sounds. The long a of fate is a fairly modern sound. It took the place of an older one, near the a of far, by the early sixteen hundreds. These first hundred pages run from A through the early letters. Origins, senses, and quoted uses stand under each word.
webster-s-unabridged-dictionary-2nd-100-:
The second hundred pages of Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary of 1913 open at page one hundred, in the thick of the A's. The first word is Attractivity, the quality or degree of attractive power. Entries on this page run through a Latin family: Attractor, and Attrahent, an old word for a thing that draws, as a magnet does. In medicine, the word names a blistering stuff laid on the skin, to excite action in the part below.

Attrap, from the French, means to entrap or ensnare. In an older sense it means to deck a horse with trappings, as a line of Holland quoted here shows. Attribute gets a long entry, with senses from grammar to theology. A line from Archbishop Tillotson treats what men may attribute to God. A companion record holds the dictionary's first hundred pages, from the letter A itself.
wee-ones-bible-stories:
Wee Ones' Bible Stories, dated 1903, retells short sketches of the Bible for little folks, with pictures made for them. No author's name stands on the pages here. The story shown is Feeding the Multitudes. Jesus had chosen twelve of those who flocked to him as disciples, called apostles. He sent them out to preach, to cast out evil spirits, and to heal disease.

When the twelve return and tell what they have done, they cross the Sea of Galilee with Jesus to a quiet place. The people walk around the lake to join them. Jesus, sorry for the crowds, teaches and heals them again. At evening the disciples urge him to send the people away to buy food. He bids them give the crowd to eat, though all they hold is five loaves and two fishes. The telling keeps the gospel plain for small readers.
welsh-fairy-tales:
William Elliot Griffis published Welsh Fairy Tales in 1921. Griffis opens with a letter to his grandfather, Captain John Griffis, a Welsh sea captain who came to America in 1783. The letter praises Welsh gifts to freedom and to the world of story.

The contents promise tales of a huge beast called Afang, two cat witches, and a boy named Trouble. One tale asks how the Welsh land first got its people, and one tells of a golden harp. Readers meet Welsh folk tales retold in clear English. The book ties family pride to an old store of myth and magic.
welsh-fairy-tales-and-other-stories: Only the opening pages are present here for a set of Welsh tales gathered by P. H. Emerson. His note says he took the tales down in Anglesey during the winter of 1891 and 1892, close to how they were told. The contents list stories of fairies, a blacksmith from Craig-y-Don, old Gwilym, and the famed dog Gelert. One French tale is the lone piece not heard in Wales. The tales themselves do not appear in these pages.
wessex-poems-and-other-verses:
Thomas Hardy wrote the poems gathered in Wessex Poems and Other Verses. The 1919 Macmillan book joins that set with Poems of the Past and the Present. Hardy notes in his preface that most of the verse had not been printed before. Some pieces were old, and a few had first been turned into prose.

Hardy also defends his use of old district words where plain English had no match. The poems draw on the rural world he called Wessex. Readers find an older poet looking back at love, loss, and country life. The mix of new print and old drafts gives the book its range.
wessex-tales:
Thomas Hardy set the short tales in Wessex Tales in his home region of rural England. The set holds six stories, among them The Three Strangers, The Withered Arm, and Fellow-Townsmen. His preface talks about hangmen, smuggling, and old local tales told near county towns.

Hardy tells how one tale grew from a real woman and a strange daytime dream. He also recalls goods hidden in caves and pits under planted trees. The stories turn village gossip and old customs into fiction with a dark edge. Readers get both the tales and Hardy's own notes on where they came from.
weymouth-new-testament-in-modern-speech-:
James is book 59 in R. F. Weymouth's modern speech New Testament, third edition, 1913. The writer calls himself a servant of God and of Christ. He writes to the twelve tribes scattered across the world. His first charge is bold: count trials as pure joy.

Trials test faith, and tested faith builds the strength to endure. Those who lack wisdom should ask God, who gives freely and does not scold. Doubt, though, makes a man like a wave tossed by wind. Rich men will fade like flowers in hot sun. Weymouth keeps the counsel brisk and clear. Readers get hard, practical faith in short, sharp verses.
what-men-live-by-and-other-tales:
Leo Tolstoy wrote the tales in What Men Live By and Other Tales. Verses from the first letter of John head the book, all on love of one's brother. The title tale starts with Simon, a poor shoemaker with no house or land of his own. He and his wife share one torn sheepskin coat.

Simon has saved a small note and is owed a few roubles by village customers. One morning he sets out to buy skins for a new coat at last. Work pays little while bread costs much in his world. Tolstoy builds a tale of kindness and faith from this plain errand. Simple lives carry deep lessons here.
what-to-see-in-england-a-guide-to-places: The pages present here give the title page, picture lists, and a long station index for Gordon Home's guide, but the guide text itself does not start. Home published What to See in England in 1908. His book points travelers to spots of past fame, natural beauty, or links to books. The station list names London stops from Broad Street to Waterloo. York Minster and Bootham Bar head the named pictures. Readers learn how the trip was planned, not what Home said of each place.
when-a-man-marries:
Mary Roberts Rinehart wrote When a Man Marries, a comic novel told by a young woman hostess. A nursery rhyme heads the book, warning that marriage starts a man's troubles. Chapter titles promise an omelet, a roof garden, a clash, and a kiss. The narrator opens by saying that when a dreadful thing happened one night, every guest turned on her.

She insists she meant well and suffered ten times more than the rest. She had planned the dinner and begged friends to give up other plans for it. The party landed in the papers, and all the town laughed. Dallas Brown, coal shovel in hand, gets the first sharp words. Rinehart sets a farce of pride, mix-ups, and young love.
when-god-laughs-and-other-stories:
Jack London gathered twelve tales in When God Laughs and Other Stories, issued in a 1911 Mills and Boon edition. The title tale opens on a stormy night in a California bungalow. A man named Carquinez sits by the fire with a glass of local wine. Rain and a south-east gale roar at the windows.

Carquinez praises the wine as fit for saints in gray robes. The narrator notes that wine loosens the artist's thought, which runs dull when he is sober. Other tales in the set include The Apostate, A Piece of Steak, and The Chinago. London mixes high talk, labor, and the sea in this set. Wine and storm set the title tale's rich mood.
when-the-sleeper-wakes:
Herbert George Wells wrote When the Sleeper Wakes, a novel that opens on the Cornish coast. A young artist named Isbister walks from Boscastle toward the caves at Pentargen. Partway down the cliff path he finds a man sitting in deep distress. The stranger's eyes are red, his face wet with tears, and his hands hang limp.

The man confesses that he has not slept at all for six nights. Drugs are of little use, and he fears strong doses. Isbister, awkward but kind, keeps him talking. Wells builds a tale of a sleeper who wakes in a changed future London. Sleepless dread at the start gives way to wonder and revolt.
where-the-trail-divides: Only the title page and contents are present here for Will Lillibridge's Where the Trail Divides, printed in 1907, so the novel itself does not appear. Lillibridge also wrote Ben Blair. The contents begin with Presentiment and Fulfilment, then a Discovery. Later chapters name the red man and the white, a glimpse of the unknown, and the curse of the conquered. A tree of knowledge gives two chapter titles. The list ends with The Reckoning and Sacrifice. The Kinneys drew a colored frontispiece for the book.
whistler-stories:
Don C. Seitz collected and arranged Whistler Stories, printed by Harper and Brothers in 1913. Seitz also wrote a book of writings by and about the artist James McNeill Whistler. The tales begin in the studios of Chelsea, said to be full of Whistler lore. One tale concerns a model owed fifteen shillings for sittings.

The model knew nothing of Whistler's fame and cared little for his art. She told another artist of a little Frenchman who jumped about his studio and griped about all things. Seitz dedicates the book to Sheridan Ford, named as a finder of the art of folly. Short, sharp tales show Whistler's wit, pride, and temper.
white-lies:
Charles Reade opens White Lies in late eighteenth-century Brittany. The Baron de Beaurepaire lives in his family chateau, held by his line for ages. One young son of the house once rode with the Duke of Normandy to England and won land there. More than twenty lords of the name have held the Breton house since.

The present baron, Henri de Beaurepaire, has health, rank, wealth, and a loving wife and two daughters. Two months a year he visits Paris and the court, where all know his face. Content is his chief treasure, and he shuns ambition. Reade sets this calm house at the edge of the French upheaval to come.
wide-courses: Only the title page, contents, and picture list are present here for James Brendan Connolly's Wide Courses, printed in 1912, so his sea tales do not appear. Connolly also wrote Out of Gloucester and The Seiners. The contents name eight tales, opening with The Wrecker. A tale of a seized ship, the Aurora Borealis, follows. Other titles name a light-ship, Captain Blaise, and a pump-man styled as Don Quixote. A picture caption quotes a diver whose boy wished to go down in his place.
wieger-histoire-croyances:
Léon Wieger, a Jesuit sinologist in China, wrote his great survey in French in 1922. His History of Religious Beliefs and Philosophical Opinions covers all China. Confucian thought, Taoism, Buddhism, and the hundred schools fill its span.

Wieger spent his life among Chinese texts and Chinese teachers alike. He traces each school's birth, growth, and clash with its rivals. Dates, names, and key texts anchor his vast, ordered narrative. French readers treated the work as their standard guide for years. Few single books map two thousand years of Chinese thought so fully in French. Wieger's charts and lists help readers hold the vast span together.
wieger-textes-philosophiques:
Wieger's Textes philosophiques, in French from 1906, gathers the sources themselves. Chinese thinkers speak here in the Jesuit scholar's lucid French versions. Confucius, Laozi, and Zhuangzi lead a cast of lesser masters.

Short texts let readers test the claims of Wieger's great history. The wells from which that history drew stand open in this book. Moral maxims sit beside wild tales of sages who scorn all rule. Wieger picks and renders with a teacher's care for the new reader. The volume remains a fine first path into Chinese thought in French dress. Its short pieces suit readers new to the sages and schools.
wild-apples:
Henry David Thoreau wrote Wild Apples, an essay in nine short parts. The parts trace the apple tree's history, the crab, how wild fruit grows, and its flavor and beauty. Thoreau begins by linking the apple's story closely to man's own. The apple family, he notes, appeared on earth just before man did.

Ancient lake dwellers in Switzerland, he says, ate crab apples long before Rome was founded. A whole black, shriveled crab apple was found in their stores. Tacitus tells of old Germans who fed on wild apples. Thoreau calls the apple tree a sign of peace, like the olive. His essay mixes lore, botany, and praise of wild taste.
willard-glimpses:
Frances Willard published Glimpses of Fifty Years in 1889, her autobiography and the story of a movement. Willard led the Woman's Christian Temperance Union, the largest women's group in America. Her pen name for the cause was 'Home Protection.'

She tells of her Illinois girlhood, teaching, and grief at her brother's death, which turned her to reform. Under her lead the temperance fight joined suffrage, labor, and prison reform. Her famous tale of learning to ride a bicycle at fifty-three symbolizes her push for women's freedom. The book blends memoir, speeches, and the record of a vast campaign.
winnemucca-life-among-piutes:
Sarah Winnemucca Hopkins published Life Among the Piutes in 1883, the first autobiography by a Native American woman. Winnemucca, a Paiute interpreter and teacher, wrote in English for white readers whose help she sought. The book is both a life story and an indictment.

She tells of her grandfather Truckee's friendship with whites, her schooling in California, and her work as an interpreter. Then she charges reservation agents with theft, hunger, and broken promises to her people. Her account of the Bannock War pleads the Paiute case. Few nineteenth-century books speak so directly from inside a Native nation.
winning-his-spurs-a-tale-of-the-crusades:
G. A. Henty wrote Winning His Spurs, a tale of the Crusades, in an edition dated 1895. The contents list twenty-six chapters, from outlaws in England to King Richard's return. Chapter one opens on a bright August morning. A lad of about fifteen sits on a low wall and watches armed men ride up to Evesham Castle.

The boy's curling hair and open face draw the eye, Henty says. Ahead lie a rescue, the lists, pirates, and the Holy Land. Saracen hands, a hermit's tale, and a siege fill the later list. A twin record in the set holds only a shorter contents list. Henty sends a young squire east to win his spurs under Richard.
winter-evening-tales:
Amelia E. Barr wrote the tales in Winter Evening Tales, printed by the Christian Herald in New York in 1896. A publisher's preface praises the set in warm terms. Barr, it says, spreads a feast for leisure hours. Her fancy carries readers along like a magic current, and few writers of the day match her glow.

The tales touch many sides of human nature, the preface notes. Some sparkle with mirth, while others show the sadder side of life. Broad sympathy runs through all of them, by this account. Her people feel like flesh and blood, not puppets, the preface insists. Barr writes heart to heart in these romances of home and faith.
with-the-allies:
Richard Harding Davis sailed to the war in With the Allies, his report of the Great War's first months. Chapter one opens aboard the Lusitania on August 4. The ship slips from New York with lights doused and ports sealed. For three days those aboard know nothing of events in Europe. Sailors then paint out the Cunard colors and cover the funnels in mouse gray.

Breakfast brings the ship's paper with news caught from the air: England and Germany have declared war. The contents promise Brussels under the Germans, the burning of Louvain, and Paris in war time. Rheims under shellfire and the waste of war follow. Davis writes as an eyewitness with a flair for scene.
with-the-boer-forces: Only detailed contents summaries are present here for Howard C. Hillegas's With the Boer Forces, so his reporting itself does not appear. Hillegas wrote as a correspondent of the New York World. Methuen printed the book in London in 1900, with twenty-three pictures and a plan. The summaries open with the way to the Boer country, through Delagoa Bay and Lorenzo Marques. A second chapter moves from farm to battlefield by way of lion hunts. Commandant-General Louis Botha fronts the pictures.
within-the-enemy-s-lines: Oliver Optic wrote this Civil War story for his Blue and the Gray series. Pages present here hold series lists and title pages dated Boston, 1890, but no story chapters. The front pages name companion volumes Taken by the Enemy and On the Blockade. They also list many other Optic series for boys, from Army and Navy to Boat Club stories. The tale itself does not begin in these pages.
wolfert-s-roost-and-miscellanies: Washington Irving gathered these chronicles, sketches, and legends in one volume. Pages present here show only a contents list, and the tales themselves do not appear. The list opens with a chronicle of Wolfert's Roost and a Sleepy Hollow piece. It also names recollections of the Alhambra, Spanish romance, and legends tied to Communipaw and the Bermudas. History, travel memory, and tall tales sit side by side in the plan of the volume.
women-of-the-romance-countries:
John R. Effinger, of the University of Michigan, wrote this survey of women in Italy, Spain, and kindred lands. It was copyrighted in 1907 and 1908 for a series on women in all ages and countries. Part one treats Italian women. Chapter one opens in the age of Countess Matilda of Tuscany, around the First Crusade.

Effinger warns that the age was not simply pious. Europe was still emerging from the gloom after Rome's fall, he writes. Superstition filled the air, and liberty was not yet a popular watchword. Portraits of strong women carry the history forward from there.
worldwide-effects-of-nuclear-war-some-pe:
The U. S. Arms Control and Disarmament Agency issued this 1975 study of nuclear war's worldwide effects. Its foreword says most research covered only the country hit directly. Long-term global harm got far less study. Sound arms control policy needs wider public knowledge, the agency argues. A National Academy of Sciences study from 1974 anchors the findings.

Sections explain blast basics, local fallout, and worldwide fallout in plain terms. Later parts treat high-altitude dust and harm to the ozone layer. Short notes define yield, weapon design, and half-life. Readers get a calm, factual warning about effects far past any target zone.
yankee-gypsies:
John Greenleaf Whittier wrote this prose sketch about wandering Yankee pedlars and tinkers. He opens by confessing a sharp sensitivity to weather. Winter cold, summer storms, and equinox gales all earn his praise. Each has some grandeur to redeem it. A dull autumn day of thaw and rain gets no mercy. Whittier calls it spiritless, soaked, and melancholy beyond comfort.

That bravura weather passage sets the essay's voice. Humour and fine description carry a slight subject. The gypsies of the title are New England wanderers, not Romani travellers. Readers get a magazine sketch built on mood, memory, and sharp local observation.
yorkshire-coast-and-moorland-scenes: Gordon Home painted and described these Yorkshire coast and moorland scenes. The second edition appeared in April 1907, three years after the first. Pages present here hold a contents list and a list of illustrations, but no chapter text. Chapters run from Pickering to Whitby, along the Esk valley, and down the coast to Scarborough. Named plates show Barnby Moor and Goathland Moor. The descriptive writing itself does not appear in these pages.
young-canada-s-nursery-rhymes:
No compiler is named in the pages present here for this gathering of nursery rhymes. It opens with an alphabet rhyme about an apple pie. Each letter acts on the pie, from bit to stole, until all wish for a piece in hand. Old favourites follow at once. A crooked man walks a crooked mile with a crooked cat. Curly Locks is promised strawberries, sugar, and cream.

Short rhymes about Tom Tucker's dog and hard school sums round out the pages shown. The tone stays playful and brief throughout. Young Canadian children were the clear audience. Readers get a compact treasury of verses many families already knew by heart.
young-lives: Richard Le Gallienne published this novel in 1899, dedicated to Alfred Lee in memory of Angel. Pages present here hold the title page, a verse motto about friendship's flame, and a chapter list. No chapter text appears. Chapter titles follow Henry and Esther's love, a Mike Laflin, and chapters called Damon and Pythias. Later titles promise Dot's decision and Mike and his million pounds. The story itself does not begin in these pages.
youth-challenges:
Clarence Budington Kelland wrote this novel about a family firm ruled by custom. Chapter one opens as Bonbright Foote VI welcomes his son into partnership. The father's smile is formal and practised, built over generations of correct manners. He unlocks an office kept shut for twelve years. That room belongs to the heir apparent alone. It stays open until the son takes command in turn.

Young Foote knows the ritual well from family lore. His grandfather's death had emptied the room before his father filled it. Tradition here works like a crown passing down. Readers get a business dynasty tale about duty, pride, and a son proving useful.
zola-four-short-stories:
Four short tales by Zola gather in this 1906 volume of his briefer fiction. Zola is best known for huge novels and a twenty-volume family saga. Here his range shows in a far smaller frame, tale by tale.

Love, war, country life, and Paris streets pass in a few vivid pages each. Compression suits him: scenes strike fast and leave a lasting mark. New readers often fear the scale of the Rougon-Macquart set. For them, these stories offer the easiest door into his world. They prove that the master of the vast canvas could also cut a gem in miniature, with the same clear eye.
zweig-jeremiah-a-drama-in-nine-scenes:
The prophet Jeremiah warns Jerusalem not to resist Babylon and gets condemned as a traitor for preaching peace. Stefan Zweig's Jeremiah, a drama in nine scenes from 1917, appears here in English. Written while the First World War raged, the play turns scripture into protest against the madness of nations.

Jeremiah's warnings fail, the city falls, and yet the prophet's vision of a renewed people survives the ruins. Zweig poured his own horror at the war into the ancient story. Nine powerful scenes move from court intrigue to exile's road. The drama stands as his most passionate public statement of the war years. It also launched his European fame as a writer of conscience.
